And Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed group that … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
If there’s one issue that seems to activate all kinds of voters in 2026, it’s data centers. The rapid buildout of these massive server storage facilities — and the infrastructure construction and expenses that come with them — has sparked local opposition in communities across the country and become a major issue in many congressional and gubernatorial campaigns.

At the same time, tech money has been pouring into many of these races. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, has already spent $45 million in a year. And Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed group that says it supports AI safeguards, says it’s raised $80 million. Both have funded Democratic and Republican-aligned groups. Other super PACs see an opportunity to push for stricter AI policies, like the recently created Tomorrow Together, which launched $4 million in ads for battleground House races, with messages about data center development and AI safety.

All sorts of candidates appear to be distancing themselves from data centers and taking steps to assuage voters’ concerns about unconstrained buildouts in their backyards. How far they’re willing to go — including by backing an outright moratorium on development — varies. While many Democratic candidates seem likelier to back a pause, that’s not always the case. And though some Republicans have leaned on party messaging about putting development in local control, rather than supporting a ban, others say a pause is exactly what the moment calls for.

Texas gubernatorial and Senate races

Deep red Texas has the second-highest number of planned data center projects in the country after Virginia, and across multiple races, data centers have emerged as a key wedge issue. Democratic and Republican candidates are all trying to look tough on data centers but emphasize different messages in their plans. For example, in the Senate race, Democratic candidate and State Rep. James Talarico includes references to environmental impact and sharing corporate profit with the public, while Republican candidate and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton discusses the need to keep Chinese technology out of US data centers. Both, however, want data centers to bear their own energy infrastructure-related costs and want to do away with certain tax exemptions for them.

In July, Talarico unveiled his “Hold Data Centers Accountable Plan,” which would end state sales tax incentives, give communities more of a say in data center development, require a closed-loop water system in new data centers to limit consumption, and create federal standards to protect the energy grid and environment. Talarico has also proposed an “AI Dividend” for Americans that would be funded by a tax on “AI-attributable profits.”

For his part, Paxton’s “Texas First Data Center Plan,” unveiled in August, would support Gov. Greg Abbott’s state-level policies, including repealing sales tax exemptions for data centers, requiring them to pay for electricity they use and add to state capacity, and preventing AI data centers from building in rural parts of the state. On the federal level, Paxton says he would co-sponsor an existing bill making it easier for data centers to connect to off-grid power systems, introduce new legislation prohibiting the use of Chinese technology to power US data centers or infrastructure, and hold data center companies criminally liable if the facility “empowers AI chatbots that undermine children’s safety.”

Talarico has also proposed an “AI Dividend” for Americans that would be funded by a tax on “AI-attributable profits”

In the race for the governor’s office, Democratic challenger and State Rep. Gina Hinojosa has accused Abbott, the Republican incumbent, of “flip-flopping” on data centers. Abbott’s office put out a press release last year celebrating a $40 billion Google investment that would include three new data center campuses, but in August 2026, with campaign season heating up, he announced an audit that could slow new facilities connecting to the state energy grid. Hinojosa, who has recently called for a statewide moratorium on data center development, pounced on the perceived inconsistency. “Greg Abbott has zero credibility here. Nobody believes that the arsonist is about to put out the fire,” she said in a social media video.

The outcome of these races remains highly uncertain. Cook Political Report changed its rating for the governor’s race earlier this month from a likely Republican win to one that leans Republican. It says the open field for the Senate race is a toss-up.

Florida gubernatorial race

In Florida, there’s a clash over whether large-scale data centers can be reined in with the right policies or if they should be outright barred in the state. Democratic candidate and former congressman David Jolly has pledged to install a one-year ban on hyperscale data centers on his first day in office, and hasn’t ruled out a permanent extension. In one ad, Jolly puts data centers in the same breath as crime in a list of things he doesn’t want in Florida.

His Republican opponent, Congressman Byron Donalds, has previously supported data center development in the state and said Florida is “wide open” to build without destroying the state’s beauty. He’s more recently changed his tune though, and while he still doesn’t want to outright ban data centers, he’s tried to assure voters that he’d support policies protecting them from associated risks like higher energy costs. In July, Donalds introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would require data center developers to fund the energy and water needed to run their operations. He’s also supported a state law with some similar requirements and environmental guardrails. “In my Florida, if you don’t protect our pocketbooks and our people, you won’t build data centers, period,” he assures voters in one ad. Energy experts have warned, however, that Donalds’ pledge to lean on nuclear and natural gas could actually raise costs for consumers.

Despite these efforts, he’s been branded as “Data Center Donalds” by opponents, and polling suggests he may have to fight for conservative voters who also strongly oppose data center development. An October NBC6/Telemundo Station Group poll found that 45 percent of likely voter respondents opposed data centers in Florida, with 38 percent in support and 17 percent undecided. A higher percentage opposed data centers in their own communities, at 59 percent. Still, the poll found Donalds has a lead of 48 percent to Jolly’s 41 percent, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percent. Ten percent of respondents were still undecided.

Pennsylvania gubernatorial race

In one of the country’s relatively few purple states, both candidates for governor have accused each other of changing their rhetoric on data centers just to get votes. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Republican challenger and state Treasurer Stacy Garrity each appear to have hardened their stances amid the widespread backlash to data center development, even though they previously touted opportunity in such projects.

Shapiro proudly announced a $20 billion investment from Amazon last year that would bring new data centers to the state, and credited Pennsylvania’s new fast track permitting program in helping lure the investment. But this year, Shapiro has tempered his enthusiasm, signing an executive order in August prohibiting nondisclosure agreements for data center developers and taking AI data center proposals off of the fast track. Shapiro has said his views evolved based on community feedback.

But Garrity, too, has seemed to turn against data centers as the election has drawn closer. In a radio interview last year, she said rural parts of the state would be “perfect places to put data centers,” and they’d be largely welcomed based on the economic opportunity they’d bring. She also praised the Amazon investment Shapiro secured at the time, though it’s now a target of some of her attack ads. This year, she has said data center developers must engage the community rather than “jam it down their throats,” and she supports a pause on development lasting no more than three years, according to Spotlight PA.

An early October Quinnipiac University poll of likely Pennsylvania voters found 64 percent believed AI data centers in the state would do more harm than good, with a plus or minus 3.9 percent margin of error. But a far larger portion of Democratic respondents were wary of them, with 80 percent saying they’d do more harm than good. That suggests it may be even more essential for Shapiro to shore up his position for his base, though the poll had him leading 59 percent to Garrity’s 34 percent.

Ohio Senate race

In the battle for Ohio’s Senate seat, data centers are both “the new ingredient (and the new problem),” according to a leaked National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) memo. Republican incumbent Jon Husted and Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown, who’s fighting to win back his former seat, “are in a dead heat,” the NRSC warned in August. And data centers, the group added, “are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

As the NRSC identified, Brown has made his opposition to data centers a central tenet of his campaign, labeling Husted “the face of data centers” in the state. Brown has hammered Husted over his past support for data centers as lieutenant governor, where he helped install tax breaks. Husted has said he believes local communities should be able to decide whether to bring in data centers, and that some may find the revenue useful.

“If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice”

At least as of August, the NRSC still believed voters favored that approach over sweeping bans but acknowledged that current perception is negative. The group warned that losing the Ohio Senate seat could endanger future support for data centers. “If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one,” the memo says.

Husted introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would require large load customers like data centers to cover their own energy costs and the infrastructure upgrades needed to accommodate them. The bill passed the House and was seen as a potential life raft for Husted, but narrowly failed to pass the Senate, even with a handful of Democrats voting in favor. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up, and a RealClear Polling average of recent surveys shows Brown with a slight edge.

Michigan Senate race

Data centers are a hot topic across two key races in Michigan with razor-thin margins. The state is handling dozens of new data center proposals, and both candidates for Michigan’s open Senate seat support a moratorium. Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers supports a one-year pause but opposes a federal ban, while Democratic candidate and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed says there should be “no more data centers until we can do it safely and with federal protections.” Rogers’ moratorium support came days after The Lever reported on his investments that reportedly stand to gain from the buildout.

El-Sayed put his stake in the ground on data centers relatively early, compared to other Democrats across the country. In February, Politico wrote that “underdogs” like El-Sayed were centering data centers in their primary campaigns, raising what’s now a common topic in campaign ads. El-Sayed is also now locked in what the Cook Political Report rates as a dead heat with Rogers, in a race that could determine the balance of power in Congress. Rogers and El-Sayed are competing for a seat currently held by Democrat Gary Peters, who isn’t seeking another term.

In another toss-up race, Democratic organizer William Lawrence is challenging Republican incumbent Tom Barrett for his House seat. Lawrence called for a year-long federal moratorium on new data center construction during his primary campaign, and when he won the nomination, his supporters reportedly chanted, “data centers lost.” In the general election, data centers have continued to be a central theme. Barrett introduced two bills this summer that would strengthen local decision-making on data center development and bar federal lawmakers from signing non-disclosure agreements about data centers. Lawrence’s data center plan includes environmental standards, worker protections, and “zoning buffers” for data center development.

Wisconsin gubernatorial race

Wisconsin is another state where both gubernatorial candidates have backed away from previous support for data centers, but neither has gone as far as to call for a moratorium. Democratic nominee and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, for example, set himself apart from his progressive primary opponent Francesca Hong by declining to oppose a development moratorium that she supported.

Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee, similarly opposes a moratorium in favor of data center guardrails, and voted for a bill allowing faster permitting for data center projects. But Tiffany has still tried to label his opponent as “data center David Crowley,” pointing to past comments he made saying the state shouldn’t “automatically roll back all data center tax incentives.” More recently, Crowley has said he would sign a bill repealing tax subsidies for the facilities. Cook Political Report says the race is a dead heat.

Nevada gubernatorial race

Nevada’s Democratic Party created an entire website branding Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo “data center Joe,” highlighting his past supportive comments about data centers and money his campaign took from AI-connected donors. Lombardo, locked in a tight race to keep his seat, has fought the accusations. He introduced an executive order last month that ties tax incentives to developers covering power costs and meeting water use standards, empowering the state to claw back money from those who violate it. But Democratic challenger and attorney general Aaron Ford has said he’d go further, pausing tax breaks entirely for new data centers.

At the same time, Ford has been criticized for championing a 2015 bill enshrining data center tax breaks. Ford said his thinking has evolved with new information, and that “the data centers of 11 years ago are not the data centers of 2026.” The issue is particularly salient in a state that’s experiencing significant water issues. The Cook Political Report says the race is a toss-up.

Georgia gubernatorial race

Swing state Georgia has been called “one of the nation’s most attractive markets for AI, hyperscale cloud and enterprise data center development,” and its gubernatorial candidates — Democratic nominee and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican nominee and healthcare executive Rick Jackson — have sparred over each other’s data center records. Bottoms supports a pause on development to evaluate environmental and cost effects, while Jackson says it should be up to local communities to decide whether to bring a data center in.

At a recent debate in the toss-up race, Bottoms said her opponent “cannot be trusted” on the topic based on his investment in a Texas data center. Jackson shot back that Bottoms approved and gave tax breaks to multiple data centers as mayor, which Bottoms denied, saying she only approved one non-hyperscale data center that wasn’t near a residential community. While Bottoms led the Invest Atlanta board in 2018, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported, the group approved up to $440 million in bonds for a mixed-use project at Georgia Tech that included a data center. This was not a “direct financing mechanism” but did help the project get tax abatement, the AJC wrote, and its data center was far smaller than those mainly at issue today.

Arizona gubernatorial and AG races

In dry Arizona where concerns about water are a top issue for many voters, the most interesting conflict is within parties, not across them. Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs and Attorney General Kris Mayes are both locked in close races with their respective Republican challengers, Rep. Andy Biggs and state legislator Warren Petersen. But the two Democrats are split over how to regulate data centers: Mayes supports a statewide pause on development, while Hobbs opposes one.

In dry Arizona, the most interesting conflict is within parties, not across them

Mayes says the state should “take a beat” to evaluate water and energy needs, a move Petersen has criticized in a rare outright defense of data centers, saying, “If you like your tech and your phone and your computer and the stuff you can use that for, you probably think data centers are important.” Hobbs, meanwhile, says data centers are here to stay, and the state should instead figure out how to best make them work for communities. That puts her significantly closer to her Republican opponent, who similarly opposes a moratorium.

Iowa gubernatorial race

Iowa’s open governor’s seat is another close race where data centers are taking center stage. The state economic development authority says Iowa’s wind energy and low construction and business costs have attracted developers there, but their growth has also brought concerns to local communities.

Democratic nominee and state auditor Rob Sand has not supported a blanket moratorium but says he would end tax breaks for data centers, make them cover their own costs, and keep NDAs from shielding deals from communities. Republican nominee and businessman Zach Lahn called for a moratorium on new development and eliminating tax incentives for them.

At the same time, tech money has been pouring into many of these races. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, has already spent $45 million in a year. Other super PACs see an opportunity to push for stricter AI policies, like the recently created Tomorrow Together, which launched $4 million in ads for battleground House races, with messages about data center development and AI safety.

Alongside a new M6 iMac, Apple has also unveiled a new 14-inch MacBook Pro powered by M6. The new M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 and will be available to pre-order tomorrow, October 28. 

Apple says: 

Apple today announced the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6, delivering even more performance, powerful on-device AI capabilities, and faster connectivity for college students, business users, creators, and more. The 12-core GPU is up to 30% faster than M5. 

The dual 16-core Neural Engine is up to 1.9x faster than M5. 

Up to 13x faster time to first token performance for LLM prompt processing compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.

fullText:
We’re still a few months away from the official reveal of the Ford Fathom, the automaker’s first next-generation electric vehicle. While we wait, Ford has been whetting our appetite with news about the sub-$30,000 pickup — including today’s announcement about the Fathom’s bidirectional charging capabilities.

With an increasing number of EVs coming out with bidirectional vehicle-to-home (V2H) or vehicle-to-load (V2L) charging capabilities, Ford is trying to position the Fathom as a key entrant — and one that simplifies the system by making it an everyday reality rather than a $10,000 luxury perk. Unlike the discontinued F-150 Lightning, which required a massive, expensive external DC-to-AC wall inverter, the Fathom packs the inverter directly into its onboard “E-box” to pump out over 10 kW of AC power natively.

The Fathom’s built-in inverter converts its battery power into standard household electricity to run appliances, back up a home during an outage, or feed energy back into the grid.

The Ford Fathom’s E-box supplies up to 10kW of power. 

Taking advantage of these features will require additional hardware, though Ford aims to make it significantly cheaper than current options. To send power back to the grid, owners will need the Ford Home Power Station. Ford is targeting a 50 percent discount compared to the existing $1,310 Ford Charge Station Pro. For whole-home backup power during a blackout, owners must pair that station with a backup panel. While that combination typically runs around $5,205, Ford is aiming for an estimated $3,123 — a roughly 40 percent reduction — though finalized pricing for both packages is still pending.

The Fathom, a $28,000 electric pickup truck, will be the first vehicle on Ford’s new Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, an innovative new system designed to maximize aerodynamic range while also reducing production costs so Ford can make a profitable EV. For over a year, the company has been hyping it as its “Model T moment” that will revolutionize nearly everything at the 123-year-old company.

1/3

Another barrier to V2H or V2L charging is red tape from public utilities. Ford’s solution was to team up with five of North America’s biggest power companies — Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E); American Electric Power (AEP); BC Hydro; Consumers Energy; and Exelon — which collectively cover millions of customers in the US and Canada. Ford theorized that whatever rules they agree on will likely become the standard everyone else follows. They agreed to cut the paperwork for basic storm backup, use common plugs and software, and make grid programs automatic.

Cutting the cost of the Ford Home Power Station and Backup Panel is certainly helpful, but homeowners will still face additional costs related to permitting, electrician labor, and heavy-gauge wiring. These could conspire to keep these bidirectional charging features out of reach for some customers.

Still, Ford is intent on keeping the costs low for its new electric truck. With supply chain constraints and trade upheaval, that will remain a central challenge for the automaker as it gets closer to one of the most important vehicle debuts in Ford’s history.

fullText:
Apple is bringing an AI assistant to its suite of productivity apps, including Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. The assistant, which is built on AI models from Apple and OpenAI, can understand a document’s context to perform tasks like designing, animating, and refining slides in Keynote.

In Pages, Apple says the AI assistant can draft, restructure, and tweak written content. It can also calculate, visualize, and organize data in Numbers, while suggesting chart types and building custom tables.

Keynote, Pages, and Numbers now support the Model Context Protocol on macOS 27 or later, allowing third-party AI agents to plug into the apps. The AI assistant is rolling out in beta to devices compatible with Apple Intelligence. It works on devices running iOS 27, iPadOS 27, or macOS 27 or later.

Several other updates are coming to Apple’s creative apps as well, with Pixelmator Pro introducing a Generate Fill feature that allows you to edit part of an image by describing the changes you want to see. Apple says the tool “automatically matches the lighting, perspective, and texture of the surrounding environment so edits blend in.”

Meanwhile, Logic Pro for Mac and iPad is getting a Liquid Glass redesign, along with an AI assistant that Apple says can “set up a vocal track from a single prompt” and edit existing projects. There’s also a redesigned Browser on Mac that uses on-device AI to automatically analyze, classify, and tag added sounds.

Apple is launching an update to Final Cut Pro, too, which brings templates, graphics, titles, and transitions directly into the app through MotionVFX. Apple is also building the Content Hub directly into Final Cut Pro, featuring a library of stock videos, photos, and backgrounds. The updates to Apple’s Creator’s Studio will be available to existing subscribers for free in November.

title: Apple releases iOS 27.2, here’s what’s new
snippet: Apple has officially released iOS 27.2 for iPhone. The update brings a new look to Apple Music, more Siri AI languages, changes to Messages and Podcasts, and Apple Pencil support for iPhone Duo. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Apple has officially released iOS 27.2 for iPhone. The update brings a new look to Apple Music, more Siri AI languages, changes to Messages and Podcasts, and Apple Pencil support for iPhone Duo. Here’s what’s new.

Release notes

Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)

Siri AI can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week

Siri AI can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List

Excluded Apps lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one setting

Granular text selection lets you select and copy just the part of a Siri response you need

Siri AI is available in more languages, with support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Siri AI is not available in the EU or mainland China

Other

Suggestions in Messages help you take action based on the context of your conversations, like adding a Calendar invite for a dinner

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

The Home tab in the Podcasts app offers two separate sections for New Episodes and Continue Playing, letting you find the latest updates from your shows and then pick up where you left off

Friends tab in the Games app provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages

Simple Profiles in the Apple TV app lets everyone in your household have their own profile, with recommendations that fit what they like to watch

FaceTime supports adding a third party sign language interpreter or live captioner to a call

Here’s what we’ve seen from testing as well.

Apple Pencil support for iPhone Duo

iPhone Duo gains support for Apple Pencil with iOS 27.2. Apple originally announced the feature as coming later this year, and it’s arriving with this update.

There is one detail to keep in mind: iPhone Duo works with Apple Pencil (USB-C). Apple Pencil Pro and other Pencil models aren’t supported. More on Apple Pencil support.

Apple Music gets a new look

Apple Music has a new black-and-white app icon that replaces the familiar red design. Inside the app, blue replaces red as the accent color for the selected tab. Apple has also refreshed Music widgets with black backgrounds. More on the Apple Music changes.

Messages, Podcasts, and Apple TV updates

Messages gains Suggested Actions, which offer shortcuts based on the conversation. A message about plans, for example, can include an option to create a calendar event or reminder. Settings also lets you control which types of suggestions appear.

Apple Podcasts separates new episodes from episodes you’ve already started. New Episodes and Continue Playing give each category its own place on the Home tab.

The Apple TV app also adds profiles on iPhone, letting users keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. More on the app updates.

More Siri AI languages and Group FaceTime Dual Capture

Siri AI adds support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

Meanwhile, Dual Capture expands to Group FaceTime. The feature lets you share views from the front and rear cameras simultaneously. More on these additions.

New Home controls

The Home app adds Lock After Closing and Door Left Open options for compatible smart locks. These let you automatically lock a door after it closes or receive an alert if it stays open too long. More on the smart lock features.

HomePod owners also gain a Lock Controls setting after updating both their iPhone and HomePod to 27.2. This prevents unwanted taps from starting audio, while preserving touch responses for features like timers and alarms. More on HomePod Lock Controls.

What about the new Health app?

Apple’s redesigned Health app appeared in earlier iOS 27.2 betas, but Apple removed it before release. The upgrade is still planned for later this year. More on the Health app release timing.

You can install iOS 27.2 by opening Settings > General > Software Update on your iPhone.

title: AI Killed the Homework Era
snippet: Commentary: And it could mean the massacre of grading in general.
fullText:
Grading homework and providing feedback to students is arguably the toughest part of being an educator. During my tenure as a professor, reviewing the results of carefully crafted assignments was at best a barometer of how well I was relaying the concepts and crucial elements of the course. In the era of AI, it’s become an infuriating exercise in futility. 

Discussion posts littered with complex references to materials outside the course’s accepted reading. Students who were instant masters at the subject matter from day one, taking a page from the classic tactic of “forge your mom’s signature the first time so you can keep forging it forever.” 

After reading a story last week about a UC Berkeley math professor who no longer bothers grading his students’ homework because they’re all using AI, I couldn’t help reflecting on my own experience as a professor of practice at the Walter Cronkite School of Journalism and Mass Communication at Arizona State University. With the proliferation of AI tools once ChatGPT launched in late 2022, and tech giants worldwide started following suit, launching increasingly sophisticated chatbots and now AI agents, grading homework became deeply depressing. 

			

More from CNET

In advanced communications courses like the ones I taught, reviewing homework turned into a hypervigilant hunt for the hallmarks of AI-generated text and ideas. The beast was cunning, quick and never slept. My tools for catching it were sorely lacking.

Despite there being no way to verify it, I was fairly certain there were online students in my classes who had never done any of the work themselves the entire course. When those students were given work they could not outsource to AI, like simulations and recorded oral presentations, they reliably struggled to maintain the perfect standard they had set. But when you get A’s all semester, one C or D doesn’t really matter. The AI cheating math still shakes out.

In an effort to keep myself alert to the use of AI tools in completing homework, I always ran a smattering of assignments through a few widely available AI chat tools to compare against student-submitted work. 

Most of the time, this method was inconclusive, but by the time I left teaching earlier this year, I suspected that at least 90% of the students I had online were using AI to do all or part of their work. 

In my very small in-person classes, I had several confrontations over the unauthorized, clandestine use of AI to complete assignments. One in particular made me rethink the purpose of my work.

A student gave a presentation early in the semester, and when asked a few basic questions in front of the class about how they came up with their ideas, the student was flummoxed, unable to explain the circumstances that led to their own creative output. 

We had a talk privately later that day about AI use, and the student admitted to using ChatGPT to create part of their assignment. They agreed to never use it again in my class. On the next assignment, we ended up having the same discussion, and I was given the same promise. It didn’t stick. 

When I went to my supervising dean about the use of AI in my classroom and inquired as to whether this case should be referred to the academic integrity board, they told me it was at my discretion and that, candidly, the university and college were grappling with what stance to take in the face of wide AI adoption. ASU’s stance on AI currently reads, in part: “Our focus is on using AI not only to address educational challenges, but to do so in a way that respects and uplifts all learners.”

Education is about the journey, not the outcome

Some might argue that cheating is a natural impulse. On your taxes, on the Monopoly board. Sometimes putting a thumb on the scale is the only way we feel we can win at a game that looks rigged or too hard to beat. 

But education isn’t a game. Even though school environments can be competitive, learning is not something at which you “win.” It’s a personal journey meant to unlock fluency you can call on at will, like knowing how to speak a language or effortlessly opening a door. 

AI may be viewed as a skeleton key by the students of today, granting instant access to great grades and passable answers that a busy, bored teacher can’t flag as 100% fake. Students who outsource the work of learning take for granted the value in being able to perform expertise with ease, and also risk ruining their credibility at their own peril.

Until our brains are plugged into our computers 24/7, it’s a crutch that educators can’t afford to quibble about any longer.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Rachel Kane
						

						

							Contributor and former Senior Editor						
					

											

								

											Rachel is a freelancer based in Echo Park, Los Angeles and has been writing and producing content for nearly two decades on subjects ranging from tech to fashion, health and lifestyle to entertainment and education. She's currently a Professor of Practice at Arizona State University's Walter Cronkite School of Journalism and Mass Communication, helping to mold the new minds who will inherit the media landscape. She's hoping to prevent the singularity by being polite to chatbots and spends way too much time refining Midjourney prompts.

fullText:
It actually seems like an episode of Black Mirror that it’s legal for a company to buy and sell our personal data without our consent, but that’s the reality in the US. Apple has built some really useful tools to limit future tracking, including App Tracking Transparency, Hide My Email, and iCloud Private Relay, but this doesn’t solve your actual problem, though. What they can’t do is remove the data that has already been collected, bought, and spread across hundreds of broker databases over the past decade.

What data brokers actually have on you

Most people are shocked when they learn just how much information marketers and scammers can find out about them by purchasing it from one of many data brokers. Those long terms and conditions you agree to (but didn’t read) when you download a new app or register with a new website often include simple clauses granting permission to “share data with selected partners.” What that actually means is that data as sensitive as your location history can be sold to data brokers, who then resell it to anyone willing to pay for it.

Data brokers collect personal data from multiple sources to build detailed profiles of individuals. Your cell phone number, home address, Social Security numbers, maiden name, family connections, past employers, car loans, and previous addresses are packaged and sold to marketers and anyone else who wants them (including people who will use them for nefarious purposes). The industry is largely unregulated, which means there are very few guardrails and protections on who can buy this information or what they can do with it.

The security risk absolutely compounds over time. Scammers and hackers who already know your job title, your neighbors’ names, and where you grew up can craft phishing messages that are really hard to spot. For anyone concerned about physical safety, people search sites serve as public, searchable directories that can map your location, your relatives, and your daily patterns to anyone looking.

Can’t you do this yourself?

In most US states, you have a legal right to demand that your information be removed from these databases. Unfortunately, doing so is incredibly time-consuming and deliberately difficult. You have to contact literally hundreds of companies, each of which makes the process difficult on purpose to discourage people from trying. Opt-out forms can be hard to find on a website, the process sometimes requires lengthy application forms, and you cannot make a single request on behalf of your entire family. Each family member must apply separately to have their data removed.

Even if you succeed, there’s nothing to stop brokers from purchasing new data on you and starting the process over again. Doing this properly across hundreds of sites is a part-time job, and the success rate without persistent follow-up is poor. Frankly, none of this should be legal. 

Automated removal with Incogni

Incogni automates this entire process for you, so you can focus on living your life rather than trying to protect your personal data. Once you set up your account with Incogni, it sends legally binding removal requests to 420+ data broker databases on your behalf and handles the follow-up when brokers push back or attempt to re-collect your data. Incogni doesn’t do this once and stop. It keeps repeating the process at regular intervals to ensure your information stays off these databases, rather than being removed a single time.

Incogni’s Unlimited plan extends coverage to 3,000+ additional sites and lets you submit custom removal requests for any site on which you find your information on. You get a dashboard that tracks the status of every request in real time, so you can see what has been removed and what is still in progress. The end result is fewer robocalls, less spam, and a much smaller target on your back for identity thieves and scammers. You get all this without spending hours each week fighting with data brokers.

The basics are always about strong passwords, multi-factor authentication, and recognizing phishing emails. There’s a threat that doesn’t get enough attention during this week: your personal data and your family’s personal data that’s already out there in broker databases, and it brings just as much of a risk as clicking a phishing link. Removing it from the market is one of the most practical safety steps you can take this week to improve your physical and digital safety.

title: Apple addressed at least 329 unique security vulnerabilities across today’s system updates
snippet: Apple has updated its security releases page with details of the vulnerabilities addressed in today’s updates to iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and Safari. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has updated its security releases page with details of the vulnerabilities addressed in today’s updates to iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and Safari. Here are the details.

Apple details security releases from today’s updates

Whenever Apple releases software updates, the company also usually updates its security releases page with details of the vulnerabilities addressed.

Today, the company updated the page with the security content for the following system updates:

Name and information link

Available for

iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2

iPhone 11 and later, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 4th generation and later, iPad Pro 11-inch 2nd generation and later, iPad Air 4th generation and later, iPad 9th generation and later, and iPad mini 6th generation and later

iOS 26.7.2 and iPadOS 26.7.2

iPhone 11 and later, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 3rd generation and later, iPad Pro 11-inch 1st generation and later, iPad Air 3rd generation and later, iPad 8th generation and later, and iPad mini 5th generation and later

watchOS 27.2

visionOS 27.2

Safari 27.2

This update has no published CVE entries.

Apple TV HD and Apple TV 4K 1st generation

In total, Apple addressed 329 unique security vulnerabilities across today’s software releases. Many of these vulnerabilities affect multiple operating systems, resulting in a whopping combined total of 1,265 CVE listings.

These numbers may still increase, as Apple regularly adds new entries and updates existing ones in its security advisories after their initial publication.

Among the most notable security fixes are a CoreMedia issue that could let a malicious app access the camera on an iPhone, iPad, Mac, or Apple Vision Pro without permission (CVE-2026-86990), and an Apple Intelligence vulnerability that could let a remote attacker access sensitive user data on supported iPhones and iPads (CVE-2026-86987).

Apple also addressed a Siri vulnerability in macOS Tahoe that could let an app access sensitive user data (CVE-2026-43736), along with multiple WebKit flaws that could allow maliciously crafted web content to execute arbitrary code.

Specifically, when it comes to WebKit, Apple has been on a security-patching spree in recent months, partly driven by the growing use of AI tools to uncover vulnerabilities. (In today’s updates alone, Apple credited AI tools and research teams for several vulnerabilities across its software.)

Earlier this year, the company also released multiple updates to fix flaws exploited by Coruna and DarkSword on older devices. Both exploit kits used WebKit vulnerabilities as part of attack chains that compromised iPhones running older versions of iOS.

And speaking of older versions of iOS, today’s updates also bring a previously released CoreGraphics fix to devices still running iOS 18 and iPadOS 18. The vulnerability could allow a maliciously crafted file to trigger arbitrary code execution (CVE-2026-86950).

Apple first addressed the issue in updates released last month, warning that it may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals running versions of iOS before iOS 27.

title: Touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro launches this week, here’s how the lineup will look
snippet: This week, Apple will be reversing a decades-long decision to exclude touchscreens from its laptop lineup, and we’ll be getting our first ever touchscreen MacBook in just a number of days. This MacBook Pro will fetch quite a premium, though. Here’s what we know so far. more…
fullText:
This week, Apple will be reversing a decades-long decision to exclude touchscreens from its laptop lineup, and we’ll be getting our first ever touchscreen MacBook in just a number of days. This MacBook Pro will fetch quite a premium, though. Here’s what we know so far.

After the release of the touchscreen MacBook Pro, the MacBook Pro lineup will offer three tiers:

Base model: current design, M6 chip, 14-inch design, lesser thermals

High-end: currently sold M5 Pro and M5 Max 14-inch and 16-inch models, unchanged

Best: upcoming redesigned OLED touchscreen models with lighter designs, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips

In terms of pricing, we can likely expect the upcoming M6 14-inch model to retain the same pricepoint as the existing M5 14-inch model: $1999. At that price, it offers 1TB of storage and 16GB of unified memory, though frankly I wouldn’t be surprised if we saw the return of 512GB at the base tier. 

Earlier this year, Apple re-introduced 256GB as the base storage tier on the Mac mini, despite the fact that there was a brief period where 256GB was fully discontinued.

Beyond that, the existing high-end MacBook Pro models will shift to the middle of the lineup. Nothing about these MacBook Pros will be changing, and their price will likely remain the same. Per Omdia, the existing miniLED displays for MacBook Pro will remain in production through 2028, so it’ll probably be a little while where these models exist in the lineup.

At the top of the lineup, the new OLED touch models will slide in. These MacBook Pros will reportedly be ‘significantly lighter,’ while offering Dynamic Island, OLED, touch displays, and potentially even support for cellular. It’ll be the first major overhaul for the MacBook Pro since 2021.

Pricing

In terms of pricing, the new MacBook lineup will likely look something like this:

MacBook Neo: $699

MacBook Air 13-inch and 15-inch: $1299 and $1499

MacBook Pro 14-inch (M6): $1999

MacBook Pro (current) 14-inch and 16-inch (M5 Pro, M5 Max): $2499 and $2999

MacBook Pro (redesign) 14-inch and 16-inch (M5 Pro, M5 Max): $2999 and $3499

	

The redesign prices are just guesses, though Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says the redesigned models will fetch a ‘significantly higher’ price. It’s possible that the new models will start even higher than what I predicted here.

These new MacBook Pros will certainly be the most exciting Macs in quite some time, though you certainly need to be prepared to pay for it. The older models remaining in the lineup is likely a sign of how pricey these new models will start at.

title: Palmer Luckey’s Anduril is getting into laptops — and claims they’ll be American-made
snippet: BlueChip will be an Arm-based laptop from an arms dealer. | Image: Anduril Anduril and Qualcomm are partnering on a new line of laptops called BlueChip, launching in early 2027. Eventually. The global supply chain of computers and laptops normally involves China, Taiwan, and many other countries, so the first BlueChip laptops will only be "designed and assembled in the United States," per Anduril's official press release. fullText:
Anduril and Qualcomm are partnering on a new line of laptops called BlueChip, launching in early 2027. The first prototype is a ruggedized model using Arm-based Snapdragon X series chips and aimed at the US military, but the ultimate focus of the joint venture is to make laptops entirely in the US. Eventually.

The global supply chain of computers and laptops normally involves China, Taiwan, and many other countries, so the first BlueChip laptops will only be “designed and assembled in the United States,” per Anduril’s official press release. Assembly is planned to be done at Anduril’s Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio.

Anduril and Qualcomm aren’t sharing many details on how they’re going to build enough manufacturing in the US for a laptop that’s 100-percent domestically made. During a virtual Q&A session with media that included The Verge, Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey and Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon laid out the motivations for American-made (or at least, American-assembled) laptops. It’s the talking points you’d expect: keeping US money in the US, the potential for creating domestic jobs, minimizing technological / economic reliance on other countries, and reducing national security vulnerabilities.

1/2BlueChip laptop hardware labeled as “Built in America.” Image: Anduril

When asked what percentage of the BlueChip laptop’s components will be made in the US once it launches in 2027, Luckey said, “TBD. . . Those questions are not settled.” The components Luckey specified that are planned to be American-made from the start are the display glass, the frame around the display, and parts of the ribbon component. “I think most likely the thing that we ship is not going to be 100-percent American.” It sounds like BlueChip’s first laptop will be well below the 65-percent requirement to count as American-made under federal procurement rules.s A promo image provided by Anduril shows hardware stamped with “Built in America.”

As for the chips in BlueChip, Qualcomm’s Amon told The Verge it intends to manufacture processors for this laptop at TSMC Arizona. When The Verge followed up to ask how much money Qualcomm is investing into that, Qualcomm communications rep Yelena Tebcherani said, “We don’t have any more details to share at the moment.”

Anduril’s first potential customer for BlueChip laptops is the same as its drones: the US military. The prototype is a ruggedized computer aimed at military personnel, complete with a rifle strap-style carrying handle — presumably so a soldier can slam the laptop shut, quickly grab it, and get on the move. It will run Windows or two undisclosed versions of Linux.

During the Q&A, Luckey indicated that BlueChip is funded entirely by Anduril and Qualcomm, not government subsidies. He mentioned that Anduril is starting with a military laptop to first service users with the most stringent hardware needs and software security demands. It’s also likely for pursuing those valuable government contracts that could call for large quantities of expensive computers. After the government and defense sectors, Anduril’s next target will be first responders and public safety, before eventually getting to consumer-level laptops — the lowest on the priority list. Luckey mentioned offhandedly, “I’d say the worst case here is that this is going to be a low volume laptop for critical industries and government needs that desperately need something like this to exist.”

Palmer Luckey is of course a controversial figure, with his history of fueling right wing troll farms motivated by his political beliefs. Anduril is better known for making drones and autonomous weapons, while Luckey continues making consumer-facing products like Game Boy clones — often polarizing the communities they’re meant to serve. Bringing a supply chain for computers back to the US and one day manufacturing a fully American-made laptop sounds a tall order. It’s complicated even further once you consider the person and company behind it.

title: Apple knows the iPad mini market, but internet unimpressed by 60Hz
snippet: Apple yesterday officially launched what it describes as “the biggest update ever” to the iPad mini, featuring an OLED screen and a thinner, lighter design. However, while there are a significant number of upgrades, internet commentators were very focused on the one thing Apple didn’t upgrade: that 60Hz display … more…
fullText:
Apple yesterday officially launched what it describes as “the biggest update ever” to the iPad mini, featuring an OLED screen and a thinner, lighter design.

However, while there are a significant number of upgrades, internet commentators were very focused on the one thing Apple didn’t upgrade: that 60Hz display … 

Apple highlighted the new features.

A stunning OLED display in an even thinner and lighter design, a huge leap in performance with A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance. The larger 8.5-inch OLED display, also available with a nano-texture option, delivers higher contrast and more than 2x higher peak brightness than the previous-generation iPad mini for a brilliant and immersive viewing experience. A20 Pro supercharges AI with Neural Accelerators in each GPU core and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. iPad mini now has a 12MP Center Stage front camera on the landscape edge that’s perfect for video calls, an innovative Acoustic Display for an even better audio experience, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support.

Commenters, however, were quick to point to the fact that the refresh rate wasn’t mentioned, with the obvious conclusion that it remains 60Hz instead of being updated to a ProMotion variable refresh rate of 1 to 120Hz.

“700 bucks and no 120hz display?”

“I was someone interested in adding a mini but at 60hz, 128gb, no Face ID I can’t justify the already inflated price tag.”

“60Hz right? in 2026 right? Hell no.”

“60Hz? Next…”

“60Hz in 2026. Apple should be ashamed.”

	

I could include many more quotes, but you get the idea. It’s certainly a surprising omission in a 2026 device, especially when our sister site 9to5Google noted that the closest Android competitor has a 185Hz refresh rate.

The biggest point in Redmagic’s favor is in that display, too. Where Apple is still refusing to give the iPad Mini a 120Hz refresh rate with this latest model – utterly insane in the year two thousand and twenty-six, if I do say so myself – Astra 2 has a 185Hz refresh rate. I’ve not found that inherently better than a standard 120Hz panel, but it’s way better than the 60Hz panel Apple’s latest will still be using.

Now I fully acknowledge that Apple knows the iPad mini market better than any of us do. I’m also aware that it has historically been primarily a business device, used for applications ranging from restaurant waitstaff relaying orders to the kitchen through mobile payment terminals to warehouse inventory systems. None of these types of applications would remotely benefit from a display with a faster refresh rate.

Additionally, when it comes to consumers, I’m sure it’s true that not everyone appreciates the benefits of 120Hz. Some of those in our comments claimed they couldn’t tell the difference, while others said it was only really relevant to gaming. Adding that category of individual purchasers to the majority business market, and Apple has undoubtedly correctly concluded that the majority of its customers simply don’t care about this feature. 

However … Those who do care about it, care about it rather a lot. I don’t know what the unit cost difference would be, but since 120Hz is now standard on a great many cheaper devices, I can’t imagine it’s a substantial one. I can’t help feeling that this is a case where Apple simply should have done the right thing, even if only a minority of buyers would appreciate it.

title: This startup’s self-driving excavators help dig up $600M in new funding
snippet: Bedrock Robotics, which is now valued at $4.1 billion, is particularly focused on autonomous excavators, in part because of a growing shortage of skilled operators.
fullText:
Bedrock Robotics has raised $600 million in a funding round that values the autonomous vehicle technology startup at $4.1 billion, marking a speedy ascent for the two-year-old company. 

The Series C round, co-led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital, comes two months after the startup reached a key milestone: moving its autonomous excavators beyond testing and pilot programs and putting them to work on active construction sites.

Bedrock Robotics has developed a self-driving kit that can be retrofitted onto construction and other worksite vehicles. Excavators outfitted with Bedrock’s autonomous-driving tech are now commercially operating at a Nevada-based water treatment facility, an earthwork site run by Champion Site Prep in Texas, and a 1.2 million-cubic-yard civil sitework project with Zachry Construction Corporation.

Bedrock has raised nearly $1 billion since it was founded in 2024 by a group of autonomous vehicle and robotics industry veterans. Co-founder and CEO Boris Sofman previously led Waymo’s now-shuttered self-driving trucks program. Sofman also co-founded and led Anki Robotics, the maker of the popular Cozmo consumer robot, which shut down in 2019.

Other co-founders include Waymo veterans Kevin Peterson, Bedrock’s chief technology officer, and Ajay Gummalla, who serves as Bedrock’s vice president of engineering and infrastructure. Tom Eliaz, who previously worked at Segment and Twilio, is also a co-founder and VP of engineering and hardware.

The fresh capital will help Bedrock accelerate its transition to commercial work. The company plans to deploy its technology at more construction sites, while expanding the teams and infrastructure needed to support customers in the field.

“We have proven that fully autonomous excavators can perform real work of value alongside the crews and workflows already in place on job sites. The next challenge is delivering that capability to more contractors as a dependable part of how projects get built,” Sofman said in a statement. 

Bedrock is particularly focused on autonomous excavators, in part because of a growing shortage of skilled operators. It takes five years or more to master operating an excavator, according to Bedrock. Meanwhile, a growing number of construction workers are approaching retirement age. The Associated Builders and Contractors, a national construction industry trade association, estimates that more than 40% of construction workers will retire in the next five years.

Bedrock is betting that the industry will increasingly turn to autonomous driving tech to help close that labor gap.

The startup’s newest partner is Haydon, an Arizona-based general contractor that plans to use Bedrock-equipped machines across a range of projects, including advanced manufacturing facilities, water and wastewater plants, data centers, and healthcare facilities.

New investors US Innovative Technology Fund (USIT), Bessemer Venture Partners, and Temasek participated in the round, alongside existing investors 8VC, Georgian, Valor Equity Partners, Xora, Eclipse, Perry Creek Capital, and Nvidia.

The startup also announced two executive hires as it scales commercial operations. Amy Jones Satrom, a veteran of Amazon, Nuro, and Uber, has joined Bedrock as its vice president of operations. Lando Juarez, formerly head of legal for Uber’s autonomous mobility and delivery business, was hired as general counsel.

		Kirsten Korosec is a reporter and editor who has covered the future of transportation from EVs and autonomous vehicles to urban air mobility and in-car tech for more than a decade. She is currently the transportation editor at TechCrunch and co-host of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast. She is also co-founder and co-host of the podcast, “The Autonocast.” She previously wrote for Fortune, The Verge, Bloomberg, MIT Technology Review and CBS Interactive.

title: Gemini for Android rolls out side panel and settings redesign
snippet: Following the Spark-to-Task update, the Gemini app has now rolled out redesigns of the side panel and settings on Android. more…
fullText:
Following the Spark-to-Task update, the Gemini app has now rolled out redesigns of the side panel and settings on Android.

This revamp starts with Google moving search to the top-right corner. The first item in the list remains New chat, with Library appearing next instead of being located near the bottom. 

To avoid cluttering the navigation drawer while still allowing you to view recent chats, Gemini displays only five items before making use of “More,” which expands the list upon tapping. With an AI Ultra subscription, the full list is as follows: New chat, Library, Images, Scheduled, Daily brief, Customize, Students, Videos, and Gems.

Old vs. new

	

Meanwhile, the Gemini app is revamping settings. Instead of having preferences split between the account menu and “Gemini Settings,” Google has consolidated everything into one page. The account menu is now just for switching accounts, leaving Feedback, or getting Help.

The “Settings” page starts with Manage account and Usage limits. Under Preferences, you’ll find Notifications, Personal Intelligence, Avatar, Task settings, Theme (new), Skills, Voice, Media, Device controls, Cart and orders, and Gemini Notebook. There are two other sections:

Data & privacy: Import memory, Contact info from your devices, Gemini Apps Activity, Your public links, and Privacy Help Hub.

Get support: Help, Report a problem, About, and Updates.

The updated side panel and settings rolled out to iOS, macOS, and the web app last week with the launch of Gemini 4 Argon. We’re now seeing wide availability on Android following a server-side update.

That’s why we’re partnering with the United Service Organizations (USO) to bring the HP

title: US government acting illegally over electronic surveillance of its own citizens, say senators
snippet: Two senators with notable expertise in intelligence matters say that the US government is acting illegally over electronic surveillance of its own citizens. They say the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC) has permitted intelligence agencies to continue warrantless interception of messages by US citizens despite failing to comply with the administration’s own privacy promise to allow public review of such rulings … more…
fullText:
Two senators with notable expertise in intelligence matters say that the US government is acting illegally over electronic surveillance of its own citizens.

They say the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC) has permitted intelligence agencies to continue warrantless interception of messages by US citizens despite failing to comply with the administration’s own privacy promise to allow public review of such rulings …

The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) was supposed to allow interception of communications by agents of foreign powers on US soil. It also put in place safeguards intended to ensure proper oversight. Controversially, however, it has also been used to intercept the communications of American citizens without a warrant under a clause known as Section 702.

That latter power is supposed to be granted for 12 months at a time by FISC. Decisions to renew the authorization should be made public within 180 days. It was last renewed back in March, with a deadline for public review expiring on September 13th. 

As Wired reports, however, that has still not happened.

Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September […]

“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”

The report also says that additional oversight through things like internal auditing within the FBI has been abandoned, and it’s no longer possible to track how many times search filters have been used to restrict electronic surveillance to US citizens.

Wyden is the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff formerly chaired the equivalent House committee.

title: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
snippet: The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.
fullText:
SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday. In a statement, SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing”. 

Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing.

SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.

The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets. 

“This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services.

Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.” 

The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses. 

The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business. SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool, and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined.

Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s October 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.

The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits.

While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals. 

Pointing to SpaceX’s “investment-grade” status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads.

“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote on X. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

title: Anduril, Qualcomm launch BlueChip, a new kind of US-made laptop
snippet: Anduril founder Palmer Luckey is vowing to bring computer manufacturing back to the U.S. and by that he doesn't just mean assembly, but every individual component, some of which are exclusively made in China today.
fullText:
Anduril founder Palmer Luckey is vowing to bring computer manufacturing back to the U.S. And by that, he doesn’t just mean assembly, but the production of every individual component, some of which are exclusively made in China today.

Anduril is partnering with Qualcomm to achieve that mission with a new computer called BlueChip, the companies announced Tuesday. BlueChip will be available for preorder in 2027.

While technical details are scant — Anduril hasn’t even finished contracting with all its component suppliers yet, according to Luckey — this first product will be a hardened laptop. It will be designed to withstand the most grueling physical environments and meet the security-conscious needs of the military, government, first responders and law enforcement.

For the first generation, about 90% of its components will be made in the U.S. or in allied countries, Anduril says, most notably its CPU. BlueChip will run on a Snapdragon X Series built at TSCM’s massive new facility in Arizona. The CPU uses the same architecture that powers other laptops, including the Microsoft Surface, Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said during the press conference.

“As of right now, the laptop’s bill of materials is about 90% U.S. and allied [ally countries], and we have a technical roadmap to get to 100% domestic over time,” Luckey said. “The intent in the long run is to have an option that is made entirely in the United States, 100% domestic. And I mean everything. I mean the displays. I mean the metallics. I mean the the magnetics. All of it.”

Right now, for instance, Luckey says he’s found an American supplier for the glass that covers the display, but the display itself is one of several components he says are only manufactured in China.

Anduril’s BlueChip computerImage Credits:Anduril

While Luckey says consumers are welcome to order a BlueChip — the company may even create a waiting list for interested consumers — this first PC won’t be designed for them. For one thing, as a hardened computer, it will be heavy and have battery-life constraints because of the engineering required to  withstand rain, dust, and other rugged conditions.

The bigger point is to offer U.S. government agencies a product that complies with regulations requiring them to buy U.S.-made computers. In this case, the selling point is a transparent supply chain that customers can track and audit.

“These computers are the anti-surveillance computer. You fully control it,” Luckey described in a recent interview. “You know everything that is in it, every single component, and you know every software component that is running on it.”

Anduril is also working to ensure that the Arm-based machine works well with Windows apps, apps built for certain Linux distributions used by the government, and even archaic software that various agencies still run.

While Anduril hasn’t yet announced pricing, Luckey estimates it will cost about 20% more than typical high-end PCs.

“As much as I love BlueChip, if I was just a normal consumer making a rational decision without a kind of patriotic basis, I’d be better off buying a Dell laptop than an Anduril laptop because it’s going to be cheaper. I’m just talking about your average person consumer, right, who doesn’t have any real need for this,” Luckey said.

But Luckey clearly hopes Anduril will eventually make U.S.-made laptops more in line with consumer desires. He said the product is the first in what he envisions as a full line of BlueChip computers, noting that he began his career making devices virtual reality headsets for consumers.

“I’m buying American cars, and then I buy a computer that’s made on the other side of the world, not just China, but you know, Japan, Korea,” he said. “It’s kind of humiliating that as an American and my birthright is computers, in my opinion, because America invented them, that I’m not able to buy an American computer.” 

As for the potentially expensive folly of trying to take on China’s electronics components manufacturing industry single-handedly, Luckey joked about his internal reputation for “being a nut” with such big ideas. (He admits that he pushed his board to spend $900 million to build a factory for a jet before the company had even won a contract.)

“This is not one of those things. My investors do not think I’m a crazy person in this particular area,” he said. In fact, rugged computers are already about a $5 billion market.

title: Honor’s new gaming phone & tablet have 10,000+ mAh batteries, fans, up to 240Hz OLED display
snippet: The Honor Win2 series and the Honor Tablet are pushing the boundaries of mobile tech, with impressive specs, built-in fans, and the same excellent eye care features the company is known for. more…
fullText:
The Honor Win2 series and the Honor Tablet are pushing the boundaries of mobile tech, with impressive specs, built-in fans, and the same excellent eye care features the company is known for.

If you thought refresh rates couldn’t get any higher, it’s time to think again. Honor just announced four new devices, all of which push OLED refresh rates in impressive ways. The most impressive on the docket is probably the Honor Win Tablet, which packs an unbelievable 240Hz OLED display onto an actively cooled 8.4-inch tablet.

Honor looks to be pushing extreme processing speed with an included 15,000rpm fan build into the camera island on the back, which should keep the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 nice and cool. The display sports 6,000-nit peak brightness, 4,400Hz or 5,920Hz PWM dimming (refresh rate-dependent), a 10,000mAh battery with 66W charging, 12GB or 16GB RAM, 256GB or 512GB storage, and Honor’s Android 17-based Magic OS 11. The Win Tablet starts at CNY 4,499 (~$670).

The Honor Win2 is this year’s flagship gaming phone from the company, sporting two active cooling fans. One ramps up to 20,000rpm, while the side fan cranks that up to 31,000rpm, ensuring this thing should never, ever overheat despite the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 alleged overheating issues.

	

The Win2 sports a new top-of-the-line OLED panel with 10,000-nit peak brightness, a 185Hz refresh rate, 5,920Hz PWM dimming, 16GB RAM, 1TB of storage, a 200MP 1/1.4-inch main camera with OIS, 10,100mAh battery (not a typo!), 100W wired and 80W wireless charging, IP68/69/69K ratings, and Honor’s Android 17-based Magic OS 11. Holy cow what a flagship, and it starts at CNY 5,499 (~$990).

And if that’s not enough for you, there’s also the Honor Win2 RT, which dials the processor back just a tad to a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, keeps the active cooling fan, uses a physically smaller 200MP camera sensor, and even somehow increases the battery capacity to 12,070mAh. This one starts at CNY 4,199 (~$630).

Lastly, the Honor Win Turbo is the company’s mid-range offering for the line, packing a Snapdragon 8s Gen 4, drops the main camera to 50MP, and ditches the active cooling fan, but still retains the absurdly amazing 12,070mAh battery of the Win2 RT. The Win Turbo starts at CNY 3,299 (~$500).

Like the previous Honor Win series, this one appears to be largely relegated to China only. Honor confirmed to us that there won’t be a global release, but that doesn’t count specific regional releases out of the question.

During the beta cycle for macOS 27.2, users reported a particularly frustrating bug that caused windows in Electron-based apps to randomly stop responding to dragging attempts. Restarting the Mac temporarily resolved the issue, but the problem could eventually return.

The bug appears to have been fixed in last week’s Release Candidate, which carried a different release build than today’s release, which is 26B123. Importantly, users with beta updates enabled may need to disable them to see the new build in Software Update.

Today Apple unveiled its biggest update to the iPad mini yet, but if you’re looking to buy one, there’s a key limitation of the A20 Pro chip in every configuration but one.

A20 Pro chip in iPad mini drops CPU core and Dual 16-core Neural Engine in most configurations

Apple’s new iPad mini comes with significant upgrades like the larger display, thinner design, OLED display, and a powerful A20 Pro chip.

But if you’re interested in buying the iPad mini, not all models are created equal.

In fact, every configuration except the highest 512GB model includes a less powerful, binned A20 Pro chip.

According to Apple’s tech specs page, here’s the breakdown of the A20 Pro across different storage configurations.

Models with 128GB or 256GB storage:

5-core CPU with 2 super cores and 3 efficiency cores

7-core GPU

Neural Accelerators

Hardware-accelerated ray tracing

16-core Neural Engine

Models with 512GB storage:

6-core CPU with 2 super cores and 4 efficiency cores

7-core GPU

Neural Accelerators

Hardware-accelerated ray tracing

Dual 16-core Neural Engine

It’s not unusual for Apple to use binned chips at times in its products. But in most cases, the only drawback of those chips is having one less CPU or GPU core.

With iPad mini, you not only lose a CPU core, you also don’t get the Dual 16-core Neural Engine.

That feature is exclusive to high-end 512GB models. So both the 128GB and 256GB models—the majority of configurations—have only a 16-core Neural Engine.

	

It’s a significant limitation, and especially unfortunate since it applies to most models that Apple will sell.

The iPad mini has a higher than ever starting price of $699, and if you want the model with a full-featured A20 Pro chip, it will set you back $999 (or more, depending on cellular and nano-texture choices).

title: Uh-oh, it sounds like the iPhone Duo keeps cracking and users aren’t happy about it
snippet: A small number of early adopters of the much-hyped new foldable phone from Apple have complained of screens cracking.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

12:22 PM PDT · October 26, 2026

Image Credits:Apple

		

							

											
									

					

	

The launch of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s hotly anticipated foldable phone, is off to a rough start. The phone was announced at this year’s Surprise and Shine event, with Apple promising that it had finally gotten a notoriously tricky form factor right.

Now, however, Bloomberg reports that early Duo users have been complaining about screens cracking “after just hours or days of use.” Some users have reported hearing a loud crunching noise, followed by the appearance of a crack. Others have reported display malfunctions.

404 Media has also reported that early adopters are dealing with “big fat creases down the middle of the [$2,000] folding screen.”

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for comment and will update this story if it responds. The company told Bloomberg that it was “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units.”

Creating a functional foldable phone has long been an ambition in Silicon Valley, but many of the models released so far have suffered from similar maladies. Apple promised that it had cracked the code, but these early complaints suggest it may not have solved the problem after all.

title: OLED iPad mini 8 debuting this week: Here’s what’s coming, and how much it’ll cost
snippet: For the first time since 2021, Apple will be overhauling the iPad mini with new display technology. It also marks the first chip refresh since 2024. Here’s what Apple has in store for this all-new iPad mini. more…
fullText:
For the first time since 2021, Apple will be overhauling the iPad mini with new display technology. It also marks the first chip refresh since 2024. Here’s what Apple has in store for this all-new iPad mini.

OLED display

This is certainly the rumor you’ve heard the most. The next iPad mini will feature an OLED display. It won’t be Tandem OLED like the iPad Pro, though you’ll still get more vibrant colors, improved contrast, and a brighter display.

However, it’s unclear if Apple will ship a 120Hz ProMotion display. The new iPad mini might end up being 60Hz still. Let’s hope that isn’t the case.

A20 Pro chip

The current iPad mini features Apple’s 3nm A17 Pro chip with 8GB of memory. Rumors suggest that this new iPad mini will offer the A20 Pro chip with 12gb of memory, allowing it to run Apple’s most advanced on-device models locally, which gives you some improved voice/dictation features with Siri AI.

Beyond Siri AI, the A20 Pro should be a rather notable jump in performance from the A17 Pro, with a roughly 60% improvement in multi-core CPU performance, and a 166% improvement in GPU performance.

Water resistance

	

Apple is working on making the iPad mini water-resistant, with a new casing and redesigned speakers that’ll help push out water ingress. This’ll potentially make the iPad mini the first ever water-resistant iPad.

Pricing

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the upcoming iPad mini with OLED and the A20 Pro chip could potentially start at $799, a substantial increase from the current $599 starting price of iPad mini. It’s unclear if it’ll continue to start with 128GB of base storage at that price point, though one could hope that the company ships 256GB to lessen the blow.
