title: Arc browser gets a sunset date, and users have two months to move on
snippet: The Browser Company announced plans to discontinue its flagship Arc browser in favor of a new browser project called Dia. Today, Arc received a sunset date that gives users exactly two months to move on from the discontinued app. more…
fullText:
The Browser Company announced plans to discontinue its flagship Arc browser in favor of a new browser project called Dia. Today, Arc received a sunset date that gives users exactly two months to move on from the discontinued app.

Arc will be sunset on December 22

The Arc desktop browser is effectively what put The Browser Company on the map. However, the firm switched its focus to a second shot at taking on the desktop web browser with Dia. 

Since May of last year, we’ve known that Arc development was no longer moving forward. Now The Browser Company is giving users until December 22 to switch from Arc without losing information.

“We’ve decided to sunset Arc on December 22, 2026,” the company announced today. “That’s not an easy sentence to write. We spent years building Arc and celebrating each and every release along the way: we have so much pride and love for what we made alongside the Arc community.”

The announcement goes on to explain why Dia is the solution moving forward.

“Our priority is to deliver best-in-class security for our members. Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI. Dia was built from the ground up to meet today’s security standards, so that’s where our engineering and security teams will focus moving forward.”

Additionally, The Browser Company explains what users can expect when making the jump from Arc to Dia. It flags these four points:

Your passwords, bookmarks, extensions and history come over to Dia seamlessly.

Spaces, Folders, and Tab Groups are in Dia and import over with your data intact.

Dia now surpasses Arc benchmarks in stability, speed, and security.

The browser features you use in Arc are free in Dia, and the AI is optional.

Dia is available for free here. Separately, OpenAI shut down its AI-centric Atlas browser this year in favor of ChatGPT’s in-app browser. Several alternatives still exist on the Mac and beyond.

title: 1Password will let AI agents use your passwords without seeing them
snippet: As AI agents continue to get more capable, account credentials are becoming more of a hang-up. 1Password is today offering its solution – giving AI agents the ability to use your passwords without actually seeing them, all while leaving you in control. more…
fullText:
As AI agents continue to get more capable, account credentials are becoming more of a hang-up. 1Password is today offering its solution – giving AI agents the ability to use your passwords without actually seeing them, all while leaving you in control.

“1Password for Agents” is a new way to connect your password vault to your AI agents, all while leaving things secure. This works be connecting an AI agent like Meta’s Muse to 1Password and letting the agent ask for permission to sign into a website, at which point 1Password will provide the needed information on your approval. 

The actual sign-in is handled by 1Password, not the agent, with your credentials remaining hidden to the agent. 1Password explains:

1Password for Agents lets AI agents sign in without receiving or seeing the credential. When an agent reaches a sign-in form, it uses a unique digital key to verify its identity to 1Password. The person sees which credential it needs and why, and then chooses whether to approve the request. If approved, 1Password fills it directly into the sign-in form. Once the website accepts the login, 1Password removes the credential so the agent can’t read or reuse it as it continues the task.

The process also leaves the rest of your password vault inaccessible to the agent.

	

While there’s still a level of trust, this solution seems far safer than just handing an AI agent your passwords. Right now this integration is limited to Muse and Grok Bot, but support for more agents is in the works, including OpenAI Dots and Anthropic Claude Duet.

title: Japan internet giant GMO says hackers posted stolen customer data
snippet: Japan's GMO Internet is verifying alleged customer data posted by suspected hackers following a cloud service breach.
fullText:
Japanese internet company GMO Internet is investigating a data leak after suspected unauthorized access to its Onamae cloud desktop service, which provides virtualized desktops to financial traders

The IT and internet services giant said on its blog that it believes the attacker has published information allegedly linked to customers and its business. However, the contents are still being verified and the full extent of the incident remains unclear.

GMO Internet has since advised customers to reset their passwords, amid receiving reports of “unauthorized operations” performed on customer trading accounts. The company said 27,000 servers may be affected by the breach.

A spokesperson for GMO Internet did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

The incident comes about a week after the Japanese firm’s cybersecurity unit separately reported finding evidence that a Chinese AI-enabled penetration testing tool called Artex had been used in hacks targeting companies across Japan. However, the company said it has not publicly established a connection between Artex and the breach of Onamae.

The Artex tool was also used to hack financial institutions in South Korea in September, according to a report by CrowdStrike earlier this month. The attacks largely relied on exploiting weak security controls, such as a lack of multi-factor authentication. Artex’s Chinese developer has since stopped public updates and made the AI security tool closed-source after it was linked to cyberattacks targeting banks, per Reuters.

A spokesperson at Japan’s Financial Service Agency (FSA) told TechCrunch that it issued guidance in May urging financial institutions to prepare for a rise in cybersecurity vulnerabilities. 

The regulator called for stronger basic defenses, including “vulnerability management, defense-in-depth and incident preparedness,” while encouraging firms to use AI and other security tools, the spokesperson added.

Here’s the timeline of the Onamae breach.

Oct 21: GMO Internet shut down its Onamae Desktop Cloud service after discovering unauthorized access had occurred to its systems without permission. The IT firm also received an email from hackers demanding about 8 billion yen (~$50 million).

Oct 22: The Japanese company reported the incident to Japanese police and shared another public update.

Oct 24: GMO Internet said it would offer customers compensation and alternative service while seeking help from government agencies.

Oct 25-26: The company began collecting devices from customers to detect malware and better understand the damage.

Oct 27: The Japanese IT firm said a suspected attacker had posted information that appeared to be linked to the company and its customers. GMO said it was still checking whether the information was genuine.

title: Cohere says Alibaba’s Qwen model tried to send a file to Beijing
snippet: An AI model said it wouldn’t use any tools, then tried to send something to a server in Beijing anyway, and while researchers say it’s probably a training quirk and not espionage, the whole thing has people asking how much to trust free Chinese AI.
fullText:
Canadian AI company Cohere said on Monday that it found one of Alibaba’s newest AI models, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, trying to upload a file to a server in Beijing during a routine cybersecurity test, even though the model had said in its own notes that it wouldn’t use any tools.

The incident initially raised fears that the model had undermined a fundamental promise to businesses — that self-hosting an open-weight model keeps data in-house. But those early fears of corporate espionage were short-lived. Researchers quickly dismissed the threat, saying it was likely a byproduct of messy training environments that cause models to unexpectedly act outside their instructions rather than a deliberate attempt to secretly send sensitive information to China.

The incident began on Friday during an evaluation in which the Qwen model was asked to write a rule for catching malware downloads. According to a blog post from Cohere, the model’s written reasoning explicitly stated it would not use any external tools. Yet in the very next step, it attempted to send a test string (a short piece of placeholder text) to an external server before being blocked by a security sandbox. 

Cohere said it could not tell whether the behavior was deliberate or a leftover from its training. 

Asked about the debate over the model’s intent, Cohere co-founder Ivan Zhang told TechCrunch that Cohere has seen its own models pick up strange habits in training simulators.

“It’s really hard to assign intention or motivation. We’ve read our own model traces, we’ve seen reward hacks, and sometimes these models get really creative when it comes to trying to break out their sandboxes,” Zhang said. (Reward hacks are shortcuts a model finds to earn credit without doing a task as intended.)

To teach an AI model to act as an agent that takes actions on its own, companies like Alibaba train it in thousands of practice setups, sort of like flight simulators for software. The model is rewarded every time it finishes a task in a simulator, and it picks up habits along the way. If these practice setups routinely stored files on Alibaba’s cloud servers, models could learn to save files there by default. 

Critics also argued that the incident could have been caused by the way Cohere investigated the behavior, steering the model toward it instead of measuring how often Qwen does it on its own. 

To find what triggered the upload attempt, Cohere supplied the beginning of a network command (an instruction telling one computer to connect to another) and let the model finish it. Because it processed thousands of routine network commands during its training, the model acted like a highly advanced autocomplete — often filling in web addresses, some of them for Alibaba’s servers.

Cohere said the original upload attempt happened without any such help, but that the behavior is rare. 

After developers asked for more evidence, Cohere released the raw traces from its tests on Monday evening on the AI developer platform Hugging Face, along with a script so others could try to reproduce the behavior. 

One initial skeptic, after going through the traces, rated the evidence as strong that Qwen can invent suspicious web addresses, but found no evidence that Alibaba planted a backdoor or that Qwen was deliberately hiding its intent.

The incident lands as governments are deciding how far to push back on Chinese AI. Last week, the Department of Homeland Security ordered federal civilian agencies to remove the Chinese AI developer DeepSeek’s products from their systems.

In its blog post, Cohere called on governments to clarify whether their restrictions on Chinese AI also apply to models running on government computers

“I’m not asking for full regulation of these open weights models,” Zhang told TechCrunch, adding that companies should treat open models like any program downloaded from the internet. 

Cohere, which sells its own AI models to governments, stands to benefit if officials grow warier of free Chinese alternatives.

title: The Future of Wet Cat Food Dispensers Is Here. My Review of Neakasa Riko
snippet: Riko is the first wet cat food feeder to mix meals to order from a supply of freeze-dried food. Here’s how my cat and I liked it.
fullText:
After a health scare a couple of years ago, my cat spent a while on a wet food diet before I finally got him back to dry food with a smart pet feeder. During that time, I learned how tricky wet cat food can be: You need to serve it fresh, and it can’t sit out too long. Leaving the house meant planning my day around the next meal, spending more than on dry kibble and keeping a steady supply of wet food on hand — canned or otherwise.

Although wet cat food was inconvenient, it was the price of keeping my cat healthy and happy at the time. I looked into automatic wet food dispensers, but most required freezer packs to keep the food chilled, and the few refrigerated models held only enough for a day or so.

	

			

	

			

									

						The Best Pet Tech, Tested by CNET Editors					

							

		

So you can imagine my excitement when I learned about the Neakasa Riko, a smart cat feeder that rehydrates food meal by meal. It stores freeze-dried food and water separately — and it’s also somewhat compatible with other dry food. When it’s time to dispense food, it grinds and soaks the food before serving your cat. I spent a month with the Neakasa Riko to see how it might help cat owners. Here’s what I learned.

			

More from CNET

How the Neakasa Riko makes wet food easier

The feeder works best on a hard floor, like the tile one in my kitchen.John Carlsen/CNET

At first glance, you see right away that the Neakasa Riko is not your typical smart cat feeder. The most obvious tells are the 80-ounce water tank on the right-hand side and the retractable feeding bowl below the food hopper. Because it sits directly below a grinder and water jets on the underside of the dry food storage, the retractable bowl lets food sit long enough to rehydrate before a cat digs in. (I doubt many cats will wait for the food to rehydrate.)

While the Riko specifically targets freeze-dried food, Neakasa notes it may also work for air-dried and baked cat food — but it doesn’t recommend using it with extruded kibble. In addition to freeze-dried food, I tried the Riko with my cat’s regular food: Supreme Source. This brand says you can soften food with water as needed, but I noticed the Neakasa Riko doesn’t grind it at all. Early results are promising — mostly because my cat doesn’t seem to care about the texture — but I’m not ready to let the Riko take over the entire feeding process just yet.

Using a mix of freeze-dried food and kibble with the Neakasa Riko might be a great fit for most cats. A few cat food brands already offer such mixes. You’ll still need to figure out the best water-to-food ratio for your cat, but it’s worth considering. Although it can dispense water separately from food, I don’t think it’s a good use of the unit other than possibly having a secondary water source for your cat after mealtime until the next feeding.

The device I tested seems to be an early production model, as it lacks the cleaning brush included in other Riko kits.John Carlsen/CNET

I like that the storage tanks are easy to remove for refilling and cleaning. Helpfully, the unit won’t run without the food hopper’s lid in place, because it’s low enough that most cats could eat food from the hopper rather than the bowl. It even chimes to remind you to put the lid back. As with other smart feeders I’ve used, the Riko has a compartment for desiccant packs to help keep food fresh.

This smart pet feeder comes with two dishwasher-safe stainless steel bowl inserts, making it easier to clean than other smart feeders I’ve used. Interestingly, you calibrate the food dispenser scale with the bowl removed, so you can swap the bowl quickly without recalibrating or zeroing out the scale. It’s a practical solution that keeps your pet’s bowl clean.

My starter kit also included wet wipes to clean the inside of the unit, spare desiccant packs and a limescale cleaner to remove hard water deposits from the water tank. Lastly, there’s an optional rechargeable battery pack, which I didn’t test, but it comes in the Riko Everyday Set. Neakasa claims the battery can provide up to seven days of backup power.

The Neakasa app is good

The Neakasa Riko’s built-in Bluetooth and Wi-Fi connections make it easy to set up and control using the Neakasa app.John Carlsen/CNET

During my time with the app, I found it fairly intuitive and liked that the Riko’s main tab included useful information, such as daily feeding history, quick access to manual and scheduled feeding controls and estimated food and water levels. While the settings menu has quite a few features — such as feeding controls, reminders, calibration, a child lock and deep cleaning — I like that Neakasa organizes them based on what you’re most likely to use.

I’m generally ambivalent about smart feeders making sounds or having displays, as pets generally don’t need these features to know when food hits the bowl. However, the Riko’s mealtime chime is a helpful reminder for pets that might’ve forgotten the food after it started to rehydrate.

Although Neakasa markets the Riko to cat owners, it also works for small dogs.John Carlsen/CNET

Similarly, the Riko’s small display shows the feeder’s status. When idle, you can also set the display to show a clock, simple icon or custom text. However, the custom text always scrolls, even when it’s short enough to display all at once. I found this movement distracting, so I opted for a simple heart icon instead. Likewise, you can turn the display off entirely or set it to a Do Not Disturb schedule for nighttime — the same goes for the sound settings.

The Neakasa Riko doesn’t integrate with smart home systems. This is understandable, as the main appeal is scheduling feeding times and monitoring pet food intake. While I’m sure that aggregating this information in a platform such as Home Assistant may benefit some power users, other smart home compatibility features — like automating lighting, smart locks and energy tracking — don’t seem important. For example, the only automations I would want with a smart feeder are lights changing color to indicate an error or low food level.

Putting the Neakasa Riko to the test

By slowly ramping up over the first few days through trial and error, you can eventually find an equilibrium for how large each meal should be to avoid leftovers.John Carlsen/CNET

Switching a cat to a new type of food is usually a long process, as most brands recommend slowly phasing in the new food over many days until they transition completely. Because my cat’s diet is already stable, I didn’t want to subject him to a completely new food paradigm — not to mention the high cost of freeze-dried chicken. As a result, my testing with the Neakasa Riko mostly involved replacing daily treats. This way, I can enrich his existing diet with rehydrated chicken while getting a feel for how the Riko operates.

It took a few feedings to dial in the best water-to-freeze-dried-chicken ratio. I started with equal amounts of food and water, which apparently wasn’t appetizing to my cat, who took most of a day to eat a serving. My concern with this is that I don’t want food sitting out and spoiling. Fortunately, the solution was simply adding more water to each serving. In my case, I found a 1:4 food-to-water ratio was the sweet spot — the cat usually ate everything within a few minutes.

As much as I like that the Neakasa Riko retracts the bowl when too much food remains uneaten, the safety retraction threshold must be 10 grams or higher — you can choose a value between 10 and 60 grams — so it won’t work if you’re feeding only small amounts of food. If you’re dispensing a lot of food, it’s worth testing how much your cat will eat and how quickly.

While I didn’t need the feature, the Riko can add a little extra moisture to food that sits out longer than an hour, helping keep it moist.John Carlsen/CNET

I don’t recommend leaving your cat home alone with the feeder for multiple meals until you’re sure it can meet your cat’s needs. This way, you can avoid coming home to a hungry kitty because the Neakasa Riko’s food safety feature has kicked in. (You can disable the setting, but leaving wet food out to spoil isn’t worth the risk.)

One quirk I noticed about the Riko is the way it handles scheduling. Notably, each feeding was an hour after my schedule. I’m not sure why — there’s no Daylight Saving Time setting, and my time zone was correct. The fix was easy: I moved the schedule up an hour. While you can adjust the rehydration time for manual feedings, the scheduled ones seem to take about 20 minutes. I like that this provides plenty of time for water to soak in.

Once the bowl is empty, it stays out until the next food or water distribution. At first, I found this behavior perplexing because I assumed the bowl would retract when empty to keep it out of the way. However, I think this is a good feature for two reasons. First, it gives your pet a chance to lick the bowl clean or get the last tiny morsels. Second, it keeps the bowl easily accessible for when you want to swap it for a clean one, something I do whenever I ran the dishwasher.

Is the Neakasa Riko worth it?

Keep in mind that freeze-dried food isn’t just meat—it also includes essential nutrients to form a complete meal. Freeze-dried treats are cheaper, but may not be as nutritious.John Carlsen/CNET

The real benefits come from the convenience and improvements to your cat’s quality of life. For $240, the Neakasa Riko fills a useful niche, especially if you want to diversify your cat’s diet with nutritious freeze-dried food or softened kibble. Outside of a few scenarios, my gut says it isn’t a complete replacement for wet food.

To support my intuition, I compared the prices of canned cat food and freeze-dried cat food. The average price per daily serving of freeze-dried cat food — based on a 10-pound adult cat — from brands such as Weruva, Instinct and Stella & Chewy’s is roughly $5.18. That’s nearly five times as much as the $1.05 from budget canned brands such as Friskies and Meow Mix. It’s also $0.90 more than premium canned brands such as Sheba and Fancy Feast, which average $4.28 per serving. While Instinct is more competitive than the premium brands, at $3.67 per serving, you’re still paying $110 a month to feed it exclusively to your cat.

Smart pet tech rarely saves money, so expect potentially expensive freeze-dried meals or moistened kibble.John Carlsen/CNET

Even premium dry kibble brands are much cheaper per serving. For example, my cat’s food costs about $30 per 11-pound bag and lasts nearly two months at $0.48 per serving. It’s cheaper than most budget canned food, but still pricier than Walmart’s Special Kitty canned food brand ($0.23 per serving) — budget kibble brands offer even more savings. (The cheapest kibble may include added filler that isn’t nutritious — ask your vet for good options that won’t break the bank.)

When you factor in the cost of traditional canned wet food, competing feeders come out ahead on meal costs. The $170 Petlibro PLAF109 uses a simple refrigeration system to keep three meals fresh — Petlibro doesn’t guarantee freshness beyond three days, but this is an excellent compromise for sticking with canned food. If you want up to six meals, the $262 PetSafe FreshFeed can keep them fresh for up to six days. While you can find cheaper smart wet food dispenser designs from generic brands, none seemed particularly noteworthy in my research.

Should you buy the Neakasa Riko?

The Neakasa Riko can supplement an existing feeding regimen without breaking your budget in one of four ways: limited daily feedings, vacation feedings, health monitoring and dispensing normal dry kibble.David Watsky/CNET

Setting aside meal costs, the Neakasa Riko is easily the most convenient smart feeder for wet cat food. It holds up to 10 days of meals and uses less energy than refrigeration. Plus, you don’t have to fill individual meal compartments. At $240, it sits comfortably between Petlibro and PetSafe. The Neakasa Riko’s biggest advantage is that it can dispense most kinds of dry pet food, plus freeze-dried food. You can likely get great results with standard dry food, but you may need to settle for moist (or soggy) morsels rather than the soft texture of canned cat food.

It also bridges the gap with standard dry food feeders, keeping Riko as an option for wet or dry food as your pet’s needs change. I think Riko is a better long-term value than the $190 PetLibro Granary Vision 2 I tested recently, mostly because it doesn’t require an expensive subscription. Even without PetLibro’s subscriptions, Riko’s added wet food capability more than justifies the initial price difference. However, on the dry food front, I’m inclined to stick with the $100 PawSync as my preferred smart pet feeder.

There’s certainly a case for choosing the Neakasa Riko, especially if you want an excellent way to manage wet food. Still, using it exclusively with freeze-dried food will strain all but the most robust pet food budgets.
excerpt:
After a health scare a couple of years ago, my cat spent a while on a wet food diet before I finally got him back to dry food with a smart pet feeder. During that time, I learned how tricky wet cat food can be: You need to serve it fresh, and it can’t sit out too long. Leaving the house meant planning my day around the next meal, spending more than on dry kibble and keeping a steady supply of wet food on hand — canned or otherwise.

Although wet cat food was inconvenient, it was the price of keeping my cat healthy and happy at the time. I looked into automatic wet food dispensers, but most required freezer packs to keep the food chilled, and the few refrigerated models held only enough for a day or so.

title: Galaxy Watch user reports burn overnight; this isn’t the first time
snippet: One Galaxy Watch 5 Pro user reported burns and blisters on their skin after sleeping with their watch under what can only be considered normal operation. more…
fullText:
One Galaxy Watch 5 Pro user reported burns and blisters on their skin after sleeping with their watch under what can only be considered normal operation.

A post on Reddit shows blisters and red marks on a Galaxy Watch 5 Pro user’s arm (via Android Authority). Red marks and irritation aren’t all that uncommon for users, but they’re generally categorized as contact dermatitis. The blisters are new, though.

They claim the watch was on their wrist from the moment they went to bed after charging it to full, but that the battery had drained by the time they woke up. A dead battery might indicate the Galaxy Watch 5 Pro was active enough to burn through the 590mAh cell throughout the night. The user also notes their watch refused to power on after the incident.

When a lithium-ion battery depletes itself in a matter of hours, it puts off some considerable heat. So a burn this bad sits nowhere outside the realm of possibilities.

	

This isn’t the first time we’ve seen reports like this. Samsung’s Galaxy Watch lineup is, for the most part, consistently safe. We’ve tested them for years and have never had overheating issues that leave visible markings on skin. Still, reported battery issues are not all that uncommon. It’s even affected the Galaxy Ring.

Users have reported suspected overheating with their Galaxy Watch Ultra, Watch Ultra 2, Galaxy Watch 8, and a few other models in the past, but none of them seem to have affected the user as much as the most recent Watch 5 Pro report. An argument could be made for contact dermatitis on some older posts, but this report holds more water – or fluid.

What’s your experience with skin irritation from Samsung’s watches? Tell your story in the comments.

title: Wyze Bulb Cam upgraded with better camera, 360-degree rotation, and color lights
snippet: Following up on one of our favorite smart home gadgets of last year, the Wyze Bulb Cam Pan Color adds a more powerful camera and a color light bulb. more…
fullText:
Following up on one of our favorite smart home gadgets of last year, the Wyze Bulb Cam Pan Color adds a more powerful camera and a color light bulb.

The Wyze Bulb Cam is a simple pitch. Take a normal light bulb socket, add a camera and a controllable light to it. It’s effective and easy to set up, and something we really enjoyed while spending some time with it last year. 

Now, Wyze is delivering an upgrade.

The Wyze Bulb Cam Pan Color brings exactly what the name implies – a pan camera and a color light bulb. The $99 camera works in the same way, screwing into an E26 light bulb socket and needing no additional power or setup. Just screw it in, flip the switch, and pair it to your app. 

	

The new additions here include 360-degree motion tracking through the motorized base, as well as 180-degree tilt. That can automatically track subjects or switch between preset waypoints. The camera itself is also upgraded with color night vision and a 2.5K sensor. 

The light bulb is also massively upgraded, jumping from max brightness of 800 lumens up to 1,100 lumens. It’s also full RGB now, supporting “16 million colors” and a white range from 1800K to 6500K. You can also pair additional bulbs. 

As with the prior model, there’s local microSD card storage on top of Wyze’s cloud-backed Cam Plus subscription.

Meanwhile, you can still buy the existing Wyze Bulb Cam for just shy of $50 if you don’t need the added functionality.

title: Google will target ads based on Gmail, Photos data if Personal Intelligence is enabled
snippet: If you’re an Android user, you’ve probably trusted Google with mountains of your own personal data over the last couple of decades. Now, a new privacy policy update suggests that the company is finally dipping into that data to target personalized ads, and you can’t opt out with disabling Personal Intelligence. more…
fullText:
If you’re an Android user, you’ve probably trusted Google with mountains of your own personal data over the last couple of decades. Now, a new privacy policy update suggests that the company is finally dipping into that data to target personalized ads, and you can’t opt out with disabling Personal Intelligence.

As spotted by Android Authority (via The Verge), Google’s new privacy policy update — which went into effect one week ago on October 16th — adds new language surrounding how the company uses data from Gmail, Drive, and Photos to target ads. Previously, the policy specifically stated that personalized ads were not “based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos,” but following this change, the sentence no longer stops there. Google now continues on with a pretty big caveat: “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”

	

Obviously, that sentence reads about as intentionally vague as possible, so let’s draw a clearer circle around it: this is a change that revolves around Google’s AI initiative, and the choice the company is referring to here is the decision to enable Personal Intelligence across your account. Personal Intelligence first began rolling out in beta at the start of this year, and allows for Gemini to share data between various apps, including Gmail, Photos, Search, Drive, and more.

You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.

In other words, while Google hasn’t explicitly revealed your cloud storage, inbox, or photo collection to advertisers, it has opened the door to allowing advertisers to target ads based on that connected content as it appears in spaces like Search. The company still says advertisers won’t be able to see personally identifying details, including your name and email address, to advertisers without your permission; that language remains unchanged from previous policy versions.

	

Personal Intelligence remains opt-in (for the time being), but if this sort of change freaks you out, you might want to verify your Google account settings are where you want them to be. To do so, head to Data & privacy under your My Account page, selection Personalization settings, then select Manage Personalized Recommendations in Search services. You can also disable Personalized Recommendations entirely by clicking the Turn off button on this page.

title: Next week’s MacBook Pro could be huge upgrade, but with one problem
snippet: Apple has a fully redesigned MacBook Pro launching next week that promises to be a major upgrade, except in one key area. more…
fullText:
Apple has a fully redesigned MacBook Pro launching next week that promises to be a major upgrade, except in one key area.

New MacBook Pro will reportedly have no performance boost, use current M5 Pro and Max chips

Next week on October 28 at its ‘Pro and tell’ event, Apple is expected to unveil a redesigned MacBook Pro with major improvements.

The new model is rumored to feature:

brand new industrial design

significantly lighter and a bit thinner

OLED display

touchscreen

Dynamic Island

no notch

wildcard: possibly a C2 cellular modem

If most or all of these rumors prove true, it’s going to be a big upgrade for the MacBook Pro.

But there’s one crucial area that’s not expected to improve: performance.

Per Mark Gurman, the new MacBook Pro will include the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips that first debuted nearly eight months ago. That means a product that specializes in performance is going to offer zero performance boosts.

It’s an odd move, and reportedly the result of Apple skipping M6 Pro and Max chips altogether in favor of fast-tracking the M7 Pro and Max for 2027.

Considering how expensive the MacBook Pro is already, and the premium this new model is likely to bring, we may be looking at a ~$2,999 starting price for a model that’s no faster than before. 

	

Perhaps Apple will replace the current M5 Pro and M5 Max models entirely at the same price point. I would love that, but it’s probably wishful thinking in our memory-crisis moment. 

Overall, I’m fascinated to see how Apple pitches the new MacBook Pro to prospective upgraders. Will Pro users who passed on M5 Pro and M5 Max chips earlier this year all of a sudden be convinced now? We’ll have to wait and see.

How likely are you to upgrade to the new MacBook Pro? Let us know in the comments.

title: This New Simulation of the Early Universe Is Massive, Detailed and Gorgeous
snippet: The Lumina Project spans 2 billion years and will allow scientists to test theories and predictions about the origins of the cosmos.
fullText:
The origin of the universe is one of the greatest scientific mysteries of all time. Scientists have developed numerous theories and testable predictions about how the universe began, including the Big Bang model, cosmic inflation and quantum-cosmology proposals.

To test those theories, researchers from the Center for Astrophysics, a collaboration between Harvard and the Smithsonian, assembled the Lumina Project, a simulation of the early universe far larger than any prior one. 

The details of the simulation, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (PDF), describe how regular matter, dark matter and radiation likely interacted during the first 2 billion years of the universe, covering a region equivalent to a cube roughly 1.5 billion light-years on each side. 

			

More from CNET

For reference, the prior champion for the largest early-universe simulation was the Thesan simulation in 2022, which simulated about a billion years of the early universe across a region roughly equivalent to a 300-million-light-year cube.

It does all of this in incredible detail, largely due to observations made by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope and other telescopes that spend considerable time observing the oldest celestial objects. By looking at those ancient space objects, scientists have been able to piece together at least some ideas of what the early universe may have looked like. 

There’s a lot of science at work here

The simulation was made on the Frontier supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee. Frontier has around 37,000 GPUs across its system, and the Lumina Project used about 15,000 of them. 

That’s what helped the simulation become the largest and most detailed simulation ever made, giving researchers plenty of unique features to work with. 

One example is helium reionization, a process that scientists believe took place in the early universe. Back then, the universe was so hot that virtually all matter was ionized, meaning it consisted of charged particles. When the universe cooled about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, atoms started combining together to make regular hydrogen and helium. Then, a short time later (comparatively speaking), the first generation of stars emerged and emitted enough ultraviolet light to reionize nearby hydrogen and helium atoms. 

“Lumina follows both hydrogen and helium reionization,” Zier told CNET in an email. “This allows us to study these processes together in one self-consistent simulation, meaning it captures reionization as it occurred while allowing its effects to immediately influence the evolving universe within the model.”

Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and an author on the paper, said the team is incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina. “For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation,” Smith said in a statement. 

The main function of Lumina is to help scientists test and confirm theories about the early universe and gauge whether their understanding of physics aligns with the simulation’s results. 

The team has already used the simulation to make some interesting predictions, including that there were “fewer massive galaxies” in the early universe than James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest. The simulation also houses the mysterious little red dots spotted by JWST, which some scientists now believe are black hole stars. 

Stunning imagery of the early universe

A side benefit is that the simulation has some truly gorgeous imagery, showing off a lot of interactions of the early universe, including gases at various temperatures mixing together, chemical reactions and the locations of early galaxies and stars. Since the simulation also fills in where dark matter and dark energy would be, the entire thing is a gorgeous litany of colorful clouds, threads and filaments. 

Take the above video, for instance. It starts with a wide shot of the entire Lumina simulation volume, then zooms into a single galaxy in virtually empty space, showing how vast this simulation really is. Try pausing the video at almost any point to capture a really cool screenshot.

This next video flies the viewer through a massive halo within the simulation. It starts by adding in various layers, such as dark matter density, gas temperature, gas metallicity (how much heavier elements there are in the cosmic gas, and stellar light. At the end of the video, the layers are turned off, and what you’re left with is a cluster of galaxies.

The Lumina Project has 15 spectacular videos, showcasing everything from gas densities to hydrogen and helium reionization.

title: Report: Apple gains ground in China as smartphone shipments hit 14-year low in Q3
snippet: Rising memory prices continue to weigh on the global smartphone market, with shipments in China alone falling 10% year over year in Q3. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Rising memory prices continue to weigh on the global smartphone market, with shipments in China alone falling 10% year over year in Q3. Here are the details.

Apple gains ground despite market downturn

A few days ago, IDC reported that smartphone shipments in China fell 15.4% year over year in Q3 2026, with Apple increasing its share of that total to 17.8% despite a 4.3% decline in iPhone shipments.

The report echoed the broader global trend, with IDC estimating that worldwide smartphone shipments fell a record 22% year over year during the quarter, while Apple recorded the smallest decline among the top five manufacturers, at just 4%.

Now, a new report from Counterpoint Research paints a similar picture of China’s smartphone market in Q3, although its estimates differ somewhat from IDC’s.

According to the report, smartphone shipments in China hit a 14-year low during Q3 2026, with a 10% decline year over year.

Apple, on the other hand, accounted for 19.5% of smartphone shipments in China during the period, a 4.8-percentage-point increase year over year. The company was second only to Huawei, which held a 21.3% share, up 5.3 percentage points from a year earlier.

In fact, these were the only two among the top six brands to gain shipment share year over year, with vivo down 2.8 percentage points to 15.2%, OPPO down 1.3 points to 15.1%, Xiaomi down 1.6 points to 13.5%, HONOR down 2.2 points to 12.7%, and other manufacturers collectively down 2 points to 2.8%.

Notably, Apple went from sixth to second place in overall shipments, which Counterpoint attributes in part to the strong launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series:

Apple ranked second with a 19.5% market share in Q3. The iPhone 18 Pro series saw a strong launch in China, with sales in the first three weeks up 23.5% YoY compared with the iPhone 17 Pro series. The delayed launch of the base iPhone 18 may have encouraged some consumers to trade up to the Pro models, supporting their early sales momentum.

Looking ahead, Counterpoint noted that rising smartphone prices are leading consumers to delay upgrades, wait for promotional periods, or turn to refurbished devices, potentially putting further pressure on demand in Q4.

title: iFixit tears down iPhone Duo, finds possible causes of early screen failures
snippet: iFixit’s teardown of the iPhone Duo is up, revealing some interesting (and some worrisome) details about what it calls the most repairable foldable phone yet. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
iFixit’s teardown of the iPhone Duo is up, revealing some interesting (and some worrisome) details about what it calls the most repairable foldable phone yet. Here are the details.

You know the drill: new iPhone, now iFixit teardown

iFixit’s much-anticipated teardown of the iPhone Duo is now live. Among the many interesting findings of its disassembly process, perhaps the most positively surprising one is its repairability score: the iPhone Duo gets a 5 out of 10, which iFixit says is the highest score it has ever given a foldable smartphone.

Granted, this is a provisional score, pending the availability of replacement parts, but it’s still an encouraging result for Apple’s first foldable.

As usual, the teardown is very detailed, and I encourage you to watch the video below and read iFixit’s in-depth blog post here.

Unsurprisingly, much of the teardown focuses on the hinge, which is the biggest news of this iPhone. As iFixit notes, Apple’s patents had already been offering clues about its design for years. Still, now that it’s here, the teardown reveals an even more intricate and fascinating mechanism than those filings suggested.

iFixit’s teardown starts with its now-traditional fluorescent dust test, which lets the team track how dust particles enter the device as they disassemble it.

The iPhone Duo has an IP68 rating, which means it’s dust-tight and can withstand submersion in water up to 6 meters deep for 30 minutes.

Right off the bat, they notice that the hinge starts making crunchy sounds after the dust test. As the teardown progresses, though, they find that relatively little dust has made its way into the hinge, especially compared to other foldable phones they’ve tested.

The hinge itself features an intricate combination of gears, springs, and interconnected metal joints, along with a waterdrop design that makes room for the display to bend without folding too sharply. This waterdrop design is rather commonplace for foldable phones by now, though Apple’s implementation adds some interesting engineering tricks of its own.

Apple also uses curved guides to control how the joints move, to reduce the stress placed on the display as the phone opens and closes.

About those screen failures

Speaking of stress, however, iFixit has found some possible culprits for the early screen failures reported by iPhone Duo owners, many of whom have described hearing a crunch while folding or unfolding the device, followed by bright lines appearing across the inner display.

Interestingly, many of the reported failures appear to occur around the same area of the display, near the transition between the opening for the cable connecting the two halves and the central hinge support.

Using CT scans, teardown footage, and Apple’s patents, iFixit built a 3D model of the hinge to investigate the possible causes of the damage.

One possibility is that a central support bar isn’t retracting properly as the phone closes, potentially putting excessive pressure on the display. Another involves the curved rails that guide the hinge’s movement, which rise above the surrounding components during folding and could, in theory, interfere with the screen if they fail to move as intended.

iFixit also points out that several structural edges and components converge around the affected area, potentially concentrating stress on the delicate display layers.

iFixit’s teardown doesn’t definitively establish what’s causing the failures, but the similarities between the reported damage and the hinge’s internal geometry give the team some promising leads for further investigation.

Other interesting tidbits

iFixit’s teardown also takes a closer look at the iPhone Duo’s matte nano-texture display, which Apple explains helps disguise the crease by scattering reflected light. Under a microscope, the team found a surface covered in tiny rounded bumps that diffuse reflections, making the crease less noticeable.

Another interesting discovery came from examining the display’s pixels under a microscope. iFixit noticed that some of the subpixels are oval-shaped and oriented in different directions, rather than following a uniform pattern.

iFixit noted that an Apple patent suggests that this arrangement could help reduce diffraction artifacts, potentially making the crease even less noticeable. The teardown blog post offers a fascinating look at the pattern and how Apple may be using it to make reflections less distracting.

And speaking of pixels, iFixit also examined the area above the inner display’s selfie camera. Much like the under-display infrared camera on the iPhone 18 Pro, the Duo uses a modified pixel pattern with larger gaps that allow light to reach the camera underneath. In this area, the pixels also become rounder and more regularly arranged.

Lastly on the display, iFixit notes that the bezel surrounding the inner screen can be removed without breaking, thanks to Apple’s use of clips rather than relying entirely on adhesive. The outer display is also surprisingly easy to remove, which is particularly good news, given that several internal repairs require removing it first.

	

Moving on to the batteries, iFixit shows how Apple has positioned the two cells, one beneath the back glass and the other beneath the outer display (which means that replacing both requires opening up both halves of the phone). The larger battery has a capacity of 11.567 Wh, while the smaller one is rated at 7.506 Wh, for a combined 19.073 Wh.

iFixit also praises Apple’s use of electrically releasable adhesive on both batteries, allowing them to be removed without forceful prying. The team called it the best battery-removal experience it has seen in a foldable smartphone.

The teardown also explores the iPhone Duo’s new logic board design, the display’s multiple layers and how they move independently to accommodate folding, and you can watch it in full below:

title: Apple wins again in copyright infringement battle over Apple TV thriller series
snippet: The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit today upheld a verdict from early last year that cleared Apple of allegations that one of its hit thriller series was copied from an independent film. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit today upheld a verdict from early last year that cleared Apple of allegations that one of its hit thriller series was copied from an independent film. Here are the details.

‘Servant’ cleared of copyright infringement allegations

When Apple announced its streaming platform, then known as Apple TV+, one of the many original productions it had in the works was M. Night Shyamalan’s psychological thriller Servant.

Starring Lauren Ambrose (Six Feet Under), Toby Kebbell (RocknRolla), Nell Tiger Free (The First Omen), and Rupert Grint (Snatch), the series “follows a Philadelphia couple in mourning after an unspeakable tragedy creates a rift in their marriage and opens the door for a mysterious force to enter their home,” per Apple TV’s synopsis.

Shortly after Servant premiered, however, Italian-born director Francesca Gregorini sued Apple and Shyamalan, alleging that the show stole the plot from her 2013 film “The Truth About Emanuel.” She sought as much as $81 million in damages.

While Servant ran for four seasons, wrapping up in 2023, the lawsuit dragged on until January last year, when a jury unanimously ruled in favor of Apple and Shyamalan. Jurors found that the show’s creators had not had access to Gregorini’s film before developing the series.

Gregorini subsequently appealed the verdict, challenging two aspects of the trial.

First, she argued that the jury should have received more detailed instructions on what constitutes “widespread dissemination,” including whether her film was sufficiently well known within the entertainment industry for the creators of Servant to have potentially encountered it.

She also challenged the trial judge’s decision to accept the verdict without first answering a question from jurors seeking clarification on the term “widespread dissemination.”

Today, as reported by Reuters, the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit rejected both arguments and upheld the jury’s verdict in Apple’s favor.

In its decision, the appeals court found that the jury instructions accurately reflected the applicable law and that the trial judge was not required to provide a more detailed definition of what it means for a work to be “widely disseminated.”

It also ruled that the judge did not abuse her discretion by accepting the jury’s unanimous verdict without first answering the jurors’ question.

title: Google says Gemini 4 Argon ranks well behind Claude and GPT-6 for Android coding
snippet: Google has updated its Android Bench list for showing how good AI models are at Android coding assistance, with Gemini 4 Argon ranking way behind that of the latest Claude and GPT models. more…
fullText:
Google has updated its Android Bench list for showing how good AI models are at Android coding assistance, with Gemini 4 Argon ranking way behind that of the latest Claude and GPT models.

The Android Bench was introduced early this year as a way for Android developers to get a quick way to see what AI models were best suited to Android coding assistance based on a test from Google. That test took into account aspects of AI use that are specific to Android coding and best practices in Android development. As Google has continued its tests and ranking new models, it has also included the average cost as a part of the benchmark so that developers can make the best decision for their needs.

With the October 26 update, Google has added the reasoning level used for each model, as well as adding results for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, as well as Google’s own Gemini 4 Argon.

Currently topping the chart is Claude Sonnet 5.5, with a pass rate of 40% and a completion rate of 80.9%. Claude Opus 5.5, added to the list in early October, comes in second place. 

	

OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol might be the most interesting addition here, coming in at a pass rate of 29.3% and completion rate of 82.8%, but a cost of just $99.50 compared to Claude’s $1,574.90 cost for its first place finish. 

But it’s Google’s own Gemini 4 Argon that makes a rather underwhelming debut, sitting well behind other frontier models in fifth place. It lags behind Claude Fable 5.1 at a mere 21.3% pass rate, 81.8% completion rate, and an average cost of $267.70. 

In a report shortly after Google’s announcement of Gemini 4 Argon, some internal voices claimed that the model “struggles to handle certain coding tasks,” though Google stood by its capabilities.

title: Samsung reportedly slashes production plans for millions of Galaxy phones
snippet: As RAMageddon rages on, brands are making tough choices including price hikes and refocused lineups. According to a new report, Samsung plans to cut production for millions of entry-level and mid-range Galaxy phones. more…
fullText:
As RAMageddon rages on, brands are making tough choices including price hikes and refocused lineups. According to a new report, Samsung plans to cut production for millions of entry-level and mid-range Galaxy phones.

ETNews reports that Samsung is cutting production of Galaxy A smartphones by “approximately 20%.” The cuts are being made to reallocate those resources for Samsung’s flagship products, as those pricier products are more likely to make a profit in current market conditions. For mid-range devices, inflated costs of memory and chipsets now make up around half of the overall cost of production.

This 20% cut to Galaxy A devices is said to account for roughly 10 million units, with further cuts planned going into 2027 (translated):

Component orders for the fourth quarter have decreased by about 20% compared to the production plan at the beginning of the year. On an annual basis, this represents a decrease of about 10 million units. The situation is critical as Samsung Electronics’ Mobile Communications (MX) division is suffering a loss this year… The stance is to cut Galaxy A series production by more than 10% next year as well.

While Samsung does make less on its Galaxy A series, the company’s entry-level and mid-range devices make up a huge share of Samsung’s overall sales. The best-selling Samsung phones are almost always entry-level or mid-range Galaxy A devices, though the Galaxy S26 series finally broke that record earlier this year.

title: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max was exciting until I found out about the price
snippet: RAMageddon sucks folks. Over the past few weeks I’ve been using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, a phone I’ve been pretty enthralled by, but its price tag really killed the hype on this one. more…
fullText:
RAMageddon sucks folks. Over the past few weeks I’ve been using the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, a phone I’ve been pretty enthralled by, but its price tag really killed the hype on this one.

The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is €1,799. You’re not reading that wrong. This non-foldable, MediaTek-powered Android flagship costs just a little bit less than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (€1,999). 

It’s not really Oppo’s fault, and it’s not like the company is alone in this struggle. A comparable Galaxy S26 Ultra in Europe isn’t much cheaper at €1,769, and Xiaomi is also rumored to be running into wildly high prices for its next launch in Europe too. This is just the current state of the tech industry as a whole, largely thanks to AI companies. 

But the reactions to Oppo’s pricing have not been quiet, and not just for the European model. Some users on Reddit mention how Oppo’s price matches the latest iPhone 18 Pro Max, how pricing in some regions is disproportionately high, and how you can still get the Find X9 Ultra for less. And I’m right there in that same train of thought.

	

As mentioned in our review, you’ll be happy with the Find X10 Pro Max. It performs well, has great cameras, and killer battery life, but this price tag really stings in a market where prices are already exceptionally high. 

Review: The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is a gut punch in a post-OnePlus world

Mirroring that last example, I’d happily go for the Find X9 Ultra, especially if I could get it for less. Even the Find X9 Pro seems like a better deal for many – some have pointed out that last year’s flagship has more memory and a bigger battery in Europe for hundreds less. You can get a Find X9 Pro in Europe right now for around €1,000~, way less than the newer model.

Find X9 Pro and Ultra both deliver more phone for less money

You might be able to get the Find X10 Pro Max for a deal, though. Some UK buyers point out offers they were able to take advantage of, but nothing changes that Oppo’s latest flagship is very expensive. 

Have you been considering the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max? Would you pay full price for it? Let us know in the comments below.

title: X is nudging users to promote their posts with a pointing hand, and people are confused
snippet: Whose hand is behind this travesty?
fullText:
Image Credits:TechCrunch	

	

						

11:34 PM PDT · October 26, 2026

											

			

Some interface changes and nudges, like bright buttons urging you to subscribe in apps, are mildly annoying but easy to ignore. Others are so in your face that you want to throw your phone in a river. X’s new push to get users to promote their posts is firmly in that category.

Over the last 24 hours, a growing number of users have posted that a mysterious hand pointing to the “promote” button suddenly showed up while they were writing a post. This has irked people across the board.

With Halloween around the corner, it could be a prank meant to spook users, though X hasn’t said so. And even users who wanted to promote a post and spend money might be scared off after seeing the hand.

WTF @elonmusk, if I wanted jump scares I would've watched a horror movie instead. 

P.S. this hand popped out of nowhere and conveniently when the words "engagement farming" are in the tweet. pic.twitter.com/NWxt81AYie

— Ershad Kaleebullah (@r3dash) October 27, 2026

TBPN podcast’s president Dylan Abruscato said that this engagement trick was the “most Nikita-coded thing I’ve ever seen,” a nod to the growth tactics associated with Nikita Bier, X’s former head of product.

I was just about to post when this huge, in-your-face arm popped up pointing at the promote button (yes, this is a real screenshot)

The most Nikita coded thing I’ve ever seen. So obstructive, yet so effective pic.twitter.com/TOI2puhliO

— Dylan Abruscato (@DylanAbruscato) October 26, 2026

Bier left the platform in August after almost a year at the helm. On Monday, Bier’s former boss and ex-head of product for Snap and Discord, Peter Sellis, posted that he has taken over as X’s product chief.

I’m joining the team at @X to lead Product.

I am a huge believer in @SpaceX's mission to extend human consciousness to the stars, so it’s time to make shitposting multiplanetary.

X is the best way to find out what’s happening in the world right now and talk about it. The team…

— Peter Sellis (@petersellis) October 26, 2026

It’s unclear if the hand is Sellis’s doing. We have reached out to X for a comment, and will update our story if we hear back.

Tech is in a weird place right now. There are plenty of exciting developments in AI, tons of new hardware, and rapidly growing ideas, but it’s all surrounded by the effect today’s tech is having on society. So, what tech is making you happy right now?

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. This article spawned from my time recently with new tech including Googlebook, the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, and the Mac Mini that I recently purchased.

Let me explain.

	

In the 10+ years I’ve been working in this industry, Googlebook is the first big launch that left me unable to find the upsides. Even after reviewing the otherwise excellent HP Googlebook 14, I’m still struggling to find anything to be optimistic about. And that largely boils down to the timing, as we discussed in last week’s Weekender issue. Googlebook is not only a platform that’s less capable than its competitors, but also wants to demand more from customers for it, all in a time where our resources as customers are more strained than ever. That same train of thought also comes into the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max that I reviewed earlier this week. It’s a great smartphone, one I think I’ll keep using for a while yet, but it’s also obscenely expensive, not really to the fault of Oppo directly. That’s just the tech industry we’re dealing with right now – heck, it’s the economy as a whole we’re dealing with right now.

So, that Mac Mini I bought. That came out of a limited-time deal where the M4 Mac Mini was $650. I’m still a Windows guy at the end of the day, but as PC components only become harder to find and, frankly, to afford, a $650 Mac Mini was by far the most logical way for me to eke more out of my gaming PC that’s already overdue for some component replacements. 

All of that is to say, the tech industry right now is full of a lot of tougher choices when it comes to the bottom line. As a reviewer, that’s been a tough conversation to balance, and it has me thinking not just about how we’ll interact with new devices going forward, but also where to find the optimism in the tech I’m using.

Here are some recent examples of tech that have brought me a smile:

The Oppo Enco X4 earbuds that I used alongside the Find X10 Pro Max are the harder-to-buy sibling to the stellar OnePlus Buds Pro 3, and they’re just utterly wonderful to use with such an excellent sound profile. 

As I’ve been working up my review of the Fitbit Edge, I’m reminded just how much I’ve come to adore the Fitbit Air for its simple and refreshing take on a wearable – I look forward to going back to it soon. 

There’s delight in the simplest ideas; the Statik Powerstand cable I went hands-on with this week immediately sparked a bit of joy from the moment I picked it up, knowing I’d just found a new staple for my bag. 

So, that’s my question to you.

What tech is making you happy right now? Is it a new gadget you picked up, or just the simple fact that your existing device is still up and running? Regardless of your outlook on the tech industry as a whole right now, it’s a stressful time out there, so let’s all focus on the positives for a minute…

title: Google says Chrome’s Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection mode makes users 10x safer
snippet: Chrome today announced the latest features for Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection. Google says this mode makes users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared to Standard Protection. more…
fullText:
Chrome today announced the latest features for Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection. Google says this mode makes users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared to Standard Protection.

Chrome is adding suspicious site warnings in the address bar “when a page exhibits deceptive patterns commonly associated with known malicious sites.” There are two tiers:

Suspicious sites (lower confidence verdict, possible risk of user harm)

Dangerous sites (high confidence verdict, high risk of user harm)

Suspicious sites (above) will trigger a shield icon in the Omnibox, with a dialog box letting you “Mark as safe” or go “Back to safety.” 

Dangerous site alerts (below) will continue to appear as a “full-page red interstitial warning.”

	

Meanwhile, Chrome is continuing to boost scam detection by leveraging Gemini models in the cloud after using on-device approaches. This protects Enhanced Protection users from a broader range of threats, including fake antivirus and browser update scams.

This model evaluates page content to analyze key indicators, such as the brand represented, the intent of the page, and a scam likeliness score, giving us rich threat data needed to identify deceptive sites.

Safe Browsing uses the Gemini analysis “in combination with domain reputation and other security signals.” Google will process page content ephemerally, “meaning it is never logged, retained, or used to train models.”

The final Enhanced Protection update defends against ClickFix social engineering that “tricks users into manually copying and executing malicious commands on their own computers in order to ‘fix’ a fake issue.” In reality, this is used to “carry out malicious actions such as downloading and setting up malware.”

Because these utilities are native to the system and trusted by security software, bad actors use them to blend in and hide their activity, and by shifting the download process out of the browser and into the terminal, attackers completely sidestep existing Chrome and Safe Browsing download protections.

When a potential ClickFix script is copied, Chrome will remove personally identifiable information from the clipboard and send it to Safe Browsing for further analysis. The browser shows a warning if a “dangerous verdict is returned.”

This system is designed to be high precision, in order to protect users in real time while minimizing disruption to legitimate developer activity.

Enhanced Protection was introduced in 2020, and Google said it was enabled by 1 billion users in 2025. It can be enabled in Chrome Settings > Privacy and security > Security.

title: The Galaxy S26 Ultra just hit its lowest price in months
snippet: If you are in the market for a new device, you cannot go wrong with the Galaxy S26 Ultra with a deal bringing the device below $950 on Amazon right now. more…
fullText:
If you are in the market for a new device, you cannot go wrong with the Galaxy S26 Ultra with a deal bringing the device below $950 on Amazon right now.

title: OpenAI Has a Surprising Defense Against Election Deepfakes
snippet: ChatGPT is cracking down on photorealistic, political deepfakes ahead of next week’s US midterm elections.
fullText:
One of the biggest problems of the AI age is that AI deepfakes are now so realistic that they’re practically indistinguishable from real photos. That matters a lot during election season, when voters are looking for reliable, truthful information on their candidates and polling sites. OpenAI is implementing a new safeguard to prevent people from making political deepfakes.

The US midterm election is only a week away on Nov. 3. Tech issues are taking center stage in many races, especially as AI and data center concerns rise for folks across the country. (Check out CNET’s guide to spotting political scams.)

If you were to go into ChatGPT today and ask it to generate an image “depicting election interference or that may discourage voting,” as OpenAI put it in an Oct. 20 update, the chatbot would create the image, given it doesn’t violate any other content guidelines. But it will be in an illustrated or cartoon style — all requests to have the image appear photorealistic should be ignored.

			

More from CNET

For example, CNET asked ChatGPT to create an image of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers standing outside a polling location. Every such prompt generated an image in a cartoon style. A photorealistic version of this kind of image would likely spark anxiety, if not outright panic, for voters.

Every edit request for ChatGPT to make an image of ICE officers outside a polling location generated a picture in a cartoon style to avoid confusion for people who see it.Screenshot by Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

The idea is to make it harder for bad actors to create realistic political deepfakes that could interfere with or question the integrity of an election without stymying people’s ability to create political content in general. In another example, CNET Managing Editor Jon Reed couldn’t trick ChatGPT into creating a photojournalist-style image that showed a voting machine recording the wrong choice.

Voting machines recording results other than a voter’s selection is a common election myth.Screenshot by Jon Reed/CNET

“The problem with deepfakes isn’t social commentary, it’s deception. So our aim is to degrade the evidentiary value of an image, while preserving room for illustrations and social commentary,” Josh Lawson, OpenAI’s head of elections, told CNET. The goal is to “make our platform less useful to bad actors by adding another layer of friction,” he said. 

This cartoonification of AI images is a practical way to make political deepfakes a little harder to create. Improving AI image models, like ChatGPT Images 2.5, is a double-edged sword. Newer models make fewer errors or hallucinations, making better content for creators. But removing those flubs makes it even harder for everyone else to identify AI-created content with the naked eye. Verification or AI labeling methods have tried to help, but those methods aren’t industry-wide nor foolproof.

When I asked Gemini maker Google about any precautions it is taking specifically for AI images, a spokesperson pointed me to its midterm election policy, which says the company is “rolling out additional protections to limit the creation of misleading election-related images” but doesn’t include any details on how. 

Anthropic doesn’t have a traditional image or video generator, and a spokesperson told CNET that any attempts to use Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections violate its policies. The company also posted this general election guidance earlier this month.

Claude refused to make a photorealistic image with potentially “sensitive election-related” content.Screenshot by Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

There’s no guarantee that OpenAI will keep this system in place once the election cycle is over. But it’s a solid sign from one of the biggest AI labs that it is taking its role in safeguarding American elections’ integrity at least somewhat seriously.

For more, check out what to do when you’ve been deepfaked and everything to know about the Take It Down Act.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Katelyn Chedraoui
						

						

							Reporter 2						
					

											

								

											Katelyn is a reporter with CNET covering artificial intelligence, including chatbots, image and video generators. Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens. She graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill with a degree in media and journalism. You can reach her at kchedraoui@cnet.com.

title: Chrome 156 for Googlebook rolling out with 14 updates across sites, shortcuts, more
snippet: Google is rolling out Chrome 156 for Googlebooks with a slew of improvements and bug fixes. This follows the last browser update two weeks ago. more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out Chrome 156 for Googlebooks with a slew of improvements and bug fixes. This follows the last browser update two weeks ago.

In terms of “New Features,” there’s “Hover Tooltips in the AI Mode Menu: Items in the address bar’s AI Mode menu now show tooltips on mouse hover.”

The remaining 13 updates today are classified as “Improvements.” On the keyboard shortcuts front:

Alt+Tab: Alt+Tab now switches windows on Fullscreen sites and apps when keyboard lock is on, as it does on ChromeOS, Mac and Windows. Users no longer need to hold Esc to exit before switching tabs.

Alt+Shift+Enter Shortcut: Alt+Shift+Enter now opens the typed query in a new background tab and keeps you on the current page.

Up/Down Arrows in Multi-Line Address Bar Text: Up/Down arrows now move the cursor between lines for easier editing when typed text wraps to multiple lines. Suggestions are hidden.

Specific website improvements include:

	

Google Docs: Enabled copying of large selections and tables in Google Docs. 

Facebook Live Video: Performance improvement of Facebook Live streams.

Stability fixes: Stability improvements were made across 1Password and other extensions, third party apps, and Chrome tab functionality.

Site Icons: Site and Google icons appear correctly when clicking into the address bar from a webpage or search results page. Stale site icons are removed when the URL bar is cleared.

There are some meaningful usability fixes:

Close Third-Party Sign-In Prompts: The close (X) button will close third-party sign-in prompts correctly. 

File Downloads: Added “Save As” dialog support to choose download save locations, and fixed a naming issue with duplicate file downloads so they open correctly in apps.

Right-Click on Incognito New Tab Page: Context menu now opens when right-clicking links on the Incognito new tab page.

Finally, the AI Mode updates continue with:

AI Mode Animation Timing: The AI Mode animation waits for the expansion to complete before playing and plays more consistently.

“Add to your search”: The menu for adding tabs and files to an AI Mode search now has an “Add to your search” header.

“View your AI Mode history”: The address bar now correctly displays “Ask anything” hint text and blinking cursor.

We’re seeing Chrome 156 for Googlebook OS widely rolling out via the Play Store today. It comes a week after the stable release started on desktop and mobile (not fully available for Android phones and tablets yet).
