title: iPhone Duo tested to destruction, including removing nanotexture layer
snippet: It’s kind of wild that there’s an entire YouTube niche in which people buy the latest expensive gadgets and then find creative ways to destroy them. JerryRigEverything is one of the bigger names, and he didn’t hold back when it came to a destruction test of the iPhone Duo. In addition to subjecting the display to everything from a knife to chainmail armor, he removed the nanotexture layer and said that it kind of looks better … more…
fullText:
It’s kind of wild that there’s an entire YouTube niche in which people buy the latest expensive gadgets and then find creative ways to destroy them. JerryRigEverything is one of the bigger names, and he didn’t hold back when it came to a destruction test of the iPhone Duo.

In addition to subjecting the display to everything from a knife to chainmail armor, he removed the nanotexture layer and said that it kind of looks better … 

The first piece of bad news he discovers is that the inner display begins showing scratches at just level 2 hardness on a 10-point scale. You can even create visible grooves with a fingernail. The good news, however, is that the nano-texture display does an excellent job at hiding imperfections when the screen is on.

The iPhone scratches at a level two with deeper grooves at a level fingernail. While the screen is on, these scratches just magically disappear, just like that center crease disappears. It’s like in the construction industry. It’s very common to paint hallways and big rooms in aneggshell or satin finish instead of gloss because the non-shiny finishes hide imperfections really well. The keys and coins are leaving marks along with the medieval chainmail armor as one often has. And with the screen on, the imperfections are just totally disappearing. It’s an incredibly brilliant move on Apple’s part to have a matte display on the iPhone Duo, but when the screen turns off, those imperfections do come back.

While the iPhone Duo has a dust and waterproofing rating of IP68, theoretically meaning that it’s completely dustproof, the extreme testing used here shows that there are limits. While dust may not enter the casing, you can pour over about a beach’s worth to get enough of it trapped in the hinge mechanism that the device no longer closes.

Apple warns against removing the nanotexture layer yourself, as you can easily damage the display beneath it, but of course that didn’t stop Jerry. He found that while the display is much more reflective without it, it kind of looks better.

Yeah, the glares are back, but so are the colors. One looks like a vibrant, fresh AMOLED display, and the other looks like it has Vaseline smeared all over the top. It’s a tough trade-off, and I’m by no means telling people to take off the nanotexture layer. To be honest, you’ll probably end up breaking it, but personally, I think now it kind of looks better.

Of course, in addition to glare, the crease becomes much more visible alongside all of those scratches.

Finally, by exerting a huge amount of force to bend the hinge the wrong way, he damages the screen in the same way we’ve seen with the cracking issue in a small number of Duos.

Mostly the video is just a bit of fun, but while the dust test was certainly an extreme one, I would certainly be cautious using the Duo on a beach; best keep your chainmail armor away from it too.

fullText:
Google is holding off on a sleep breathing quality feature it promised for the Fitbit Air. It launched for the Pixel Watch last month.

Under the Your Health Guardian umbrella of features, Google recently announced several new features for its fitness trackers. That includes not only the Pixel Watch series, but the Fitbit Air and even the newly announced Fitbit Edge. That suite provides access to blood pressure trends, insulin resistance trends, and sleep breathing quality.

Sleep Breathing Quality launched first on Pixel Watches and will come to Fitbit Air soon.

When Google first announced these features, they made sure to include that detail in the press release so as not to get Fitbit Air users’ hopes up. At the time, Google said sleep breathing quality and other features in the Your Health Guardian suite would be added to the screenless tracker “later this year.” It didn’t note that only two of the three features would be released for the Fitbit Air.

	

That being said, neither the comment nor the original press release lays out a detailed timeline for sleep breathing quality trends, specifically. For now, the Pixel Watch 3, Pixel Watch 4, and Pixel Watch 5 are able to set sleep quality, insulin trends, and blood pressure trends on their devices with the Health Guardian feature.

Fitbit Air users will need to wait a little longer.

title: The wide folds are coming; foldable display shipments to increase by 44% in 2026, analysts say
snippet: Samsung is expected to play a major role in what analysts predict will be a 44% increase in foldable display shipments in 2026, thanks to the popularity of wider foldables. more…
fullText:
Samsung is expected to play a major role in what analysts predict will be a 44% increase in foldable display shipments in 2026, thanks to the popularity of wider foldables.

Samsung provides display panels for both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, both of which have gained a massive amount of attention in the last couple of months. That’s credited to the form factor – a refreshing change from the tall and narrow Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, or the devices that emulate the same experience.

Analysts at Omdia reported their forecast for 2026 in the wake of renewed interest in foldables, driven by Samsung and Apple. The report states that foldable AMOLED display shipments are expected to increase by 44% year-over-year. That includes shipments for any foldable displays, but it’s signaled by the surge of wide foldables released or rumored this year.

That increase would be driven by Samsung, if the prediction plays out perfectly. Samsung currently holds a majority lead in foldable display shipments, but it’s possible its slice grows to 66% in 2026. Omdia predicts that current Chinese manufacturers with high shipments will see a decline as demand from Apple and Samsung grows.

	

It’s unlikely we’ll see Samsung and Apple dominate the wide fold market. Motorola is expected to launch a similar foldable, and more will chase the size and shape Apple landed on for its first foldable iPhone.

fullText:
Lighting effects can make or break your TV room, gaming setup, etc. SwitchBot’s RGBICWW Light Bars take a different approach from most products, with dedicated cool-white and warm-white LEDs alongside the color zones. The end result means real white light for work and reading, and 12-zone RGBIC color for movies. It all works over Wi-Fi/Matter as well, so you don’t need a hub.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

RGB color mixing can produce something that technically looks white on a wall, but it’s not the same quality of light you’d want to read or work under for hours. If you work in an office building, you know what I am talking about. SwitchBot’s RGBICWW Light Bars use separate cool-white and warm-white LEDs that produce actual white light with adjustable color temperature that can go from 2200K up to 6500K, and they dim as well. It can produce up to 800 lumens across the pair.

On the color side, each bar has six independently controllable RGBIC zones, so you have 12 zones across the pair. This lets you run multi-color gradients rather than a single color across the entire bar. There are 26 preset dynamic effects and six music-reactive modes powered by a built-in microphone, so you don’t need a separate sensor to sync the lights to sound.

Matter over Wi-Fi

The light bars connect to Apple Home natively over Matter via Wi-Fi without needing a SwitchBot Hub. The integration covers the basics: on/off, brightness, color temperature, and color control via the Home app or Siri.

The deeper color zone control, music modes, dynamic effects, and scene building all live in the SwitchBot app rather than Apple Home, which is standard for Matter accessories at this level of feature complexity. A wired physical controller is also included for quick changes to the lights as well. I am a big fan of when smart home products offer a physical button option as well.

The lights include built-in magnets so you can attach the bars directly to compatible metal surfaces, with adhesive being an option as well. They can be mounted horizontally, vertically, rear-mounted behind a monitor or TV, or set upright with the included desktop stands.

Wrap up

SwitchBot built just about everything you’d want here. The attention to color detail is fantastic. Matter over Wi-Fi means you can buy it and have it directly connected to Apple Home/HomeKit without a hub, while still having flexibility for the future.

title: The iPhone Duo Has Passed 75,000 Folds in Our Fold-a-Phone Testing Machine. Can It Beat the Galaxy Z Fold 8?
snippet: We’re folding Apple’s iPhone Duo 900 times an hour to test how its hinge will last.
fullText:
Apple’s first-ever foldable phone — the iPhone Duo — launched Friday and was met with long lines and product sellouts. We braved three hours at the Apple Store on Friday to snag our own testing model for our lab in Louisville, Kentucky, where I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations.

Now the big question? How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of 8:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, we’ve passed 75,000 folds.

The goal is simple. On Friday afternoon, my team and I loaded the iPhone Duo into a proprietary machine we built to test foldable phones like Apple’s and Samsung’s rival Galaxy Z Fold 8, which we’ve also already started testing. I’ve overseen the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone. (Read on for how CNET tests foldable phones.)

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone. 

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge. 

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience. 

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo. 

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube today from 1-5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

Matthew Murray/CNET

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

How CNET’s Fold-a-Phone tests foldable phones like the iPhone Duo

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day. 

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Matthew Murray/CNET

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test. 

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Matthew Murray
						

						

							Lab Director						
					

										

								

											As lab director for the CNET Group, Matthew leads the Labs team, which helps coordinate and conduct product testing for CNET and other Ziff Davis editorial brands including PCMag and ZDNET. He previously spent eight years as head of testing at Future plc, and before that eight years as an analyst and writer at PCMag. His technology writing has also appeared in publications including Computer Shopper, ExtremeTech, Tom's Guide, Laptop and Backstage.

fullText:
The Vivo V80 sports flagship design quality, a massive 7200mAh battery, Center-Stage selfie camera, IP68/69 ingress protection, and one of the wildest AI camera modes I’ve seen yet.

When I think of the smartphone industry’s best cameras, Vivo or Oppo usually comes to mind. While both companies offer good experiences on any phone they sell, their best features often appear only on flagship models. But the Vivo V80, which retails for just ₹62,999 (~$660), features the company’s new flagship AI camera mode, and that might be the single most interesting thing about the release for me.

Let’s get the full specs out of the way first. The Vivo V80’s got a 6.59-inch 144Hz OLED display, featuring 1.5k resolution, true 10-bit colors (no dithering), and 4320Hz PWM dimming at low brightness (plus an option for full DC dimming). Inside is a Snapdragon 7 Gen 4, 8GB RAM, and that massive 7200mAh battery with 90W charging. Good stuff.

The Vivo V80 uses a main 50MP Sony LYTIA 700V sensor, a 3x optical 50MP Sony IMX882 telephoto camera, an 8MP or 12MP ultrawide camera (region-dependent), and a 50MP ZEISS center-stage 90-degree selfie camera. The phone is available in India, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and other regions in the coming weeks.

	

To illustrate just how interesting the new AI Creation camera mode is, I took a bunch of photos using the same mode on the Vivo X500. That phone is about $300 more expensive, but it features the same AI Creation mode as the Vivo V80. The results are nothing short of jaw-dropping at times. Let’s start with the hike I took this weekend.

It was a gorgeous autumn day, but the sporadic cloud cover was really killing the vibe of my photos. The lighting was annoyingly flat, and the colors my eyes were seeing in the leaves weren’t being picked up on camera at all. So I swiped over to the AI Creation mode and hit the shutter button. The rest was all automated.

The amount of depth and color this mode added truly blew my mind. When you open the mode and point the viewfinder toward something, it scans the scene and automatically applies the style it thinks will be best. It’ll also give you two additional modes to quickly select from, or you can jump into the full UI and choose the one you want.

From here, you can also choose to have Vivo’s AI automatically remove anyone in the photo, and it does an impeccable job, too; no circling required! Original images are always available in Vivo’s Albums app, and you can select a different style after taking the photo.

This mode is 100% cloud processing, though, so you might need to wait to see the processing results if you were somewhere like I was with no signal. Processing takes about one minute per photo, and up to 10 images can be processed simultaneously. If there’s a processing limit per day, I didn’t find it. While the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 in the Vivo V80 could probably handle some of the processing, this ensures you get the best quality without much wait time.

The “Travel” category creates genuinely convincing effects like the Sunlight style. Vivo has several other options that are more dramatic and, therefore, obviously edited-looking. In the header image, I grabbed one of my son’s swords and asked him to take a picture of me. The sword and the room are fully real in these pictures, but the lighting and effects are all automatically generated by Vivo.

All of these, too, were quite convincing, despite obviously being stylized. I particularly love the mist one, although I’m not sure how often anyone would use most of these. They’re clearly only for niche dramatic photos, but hey, maybe you love that sort of thing. The rest of the options available under the “Landscape” category were initially convincing, but zooming in just a bit reveals some very obvious AI editing.

So all of this is amazing, but there’s one big problem that I’m not thrilled about: Vivo doesn’t use SynthID or another more standardized way of noting that these images are edited with AI. If you delve into the EXIF data, you can find “ai_creation” in the comments field, but Gemini apparently isn’t smart enough to understand that yet.

Most likely, Gemini and the rest will figure this out in time, but I don’t care much for AI editing tools that don’t automatically mark them as such. Vivo, if you’re reading this, please add SynthID or another way for AI tools to identify these as automated. Otherwise, this is a dope mode that I love seeing proliferate to more affordable phones like the Vivo V80, especially in the age of RAMageddon.

title: Some iPhone Duo displays are cracking, seemingly all in the same way
snippet: Following the iPhone Duo launch on Friday, a number of owners are reporting that their inner screens have cracked and broken on their own (top image via scary_duck23 on Reddit). The affected units all seem to break in the same way. The screen cracks down the center line of the hinge, and a horizontal block of pixels on the screen is then stuck glowing white. Update: Apple says it is aware of an issue affecting a small number of iPhone Duo units. more…
fullText:
Following the iPhone Duo launch on Friday, a number of owners are reporting that their inner screens have cracked and broken on their own (top image via scary_duck23 on Reddit). 

The affected units all seem to break in the same way. The screen cracks down the center line of the hinge, and a horizontal block of pixels on the screen is then stuck glowing white. Update: Apple says it is aware of an issue affecting a small number of iPhone Duo units.

The scale of the issue remains unclear. We’ve seen about ten unique instances so far, with many posting their (similar) experiences on the iPhone Duo subreddit. 

The amount of time it takes for the cracking to happen varies, but obviously it doesn’t take too long since customers have only been able to start unboxing the device since Friday morning. A couple of people even said theirs cracked during the first setup process. 

From what we’ve seen so far, most buyers experiencing this problem have been able to return to the Apple Store and get a straight device replacement. 

People who bought from carriers may have had less luck, as the carriers do not have immediate stock to give out a replacement. One person said they were told that they must have dropped the phone to cause the damage, and that it was on them to pay for repair.

In terms of why this is happening, there is a working theory that a batch of iPhone Duos have a defective hinge component. The suggestion is a piece of the hinge is slightly misaligned, and pokes upwards onto the inner screen, causing the breakage.

Some on social media have suggested that users should not close the iPhone Duo by pressing in the center of the inner display, and perhaps that contributes to this issue occurring. It is unclear if this is actually relevant advice. Officially, Apple has not given any guidance on how users are expected to handle the phone when folding and unfolding it.

While the reports are concerning, it is worth remembering that Apple has probably shipped hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of units already and only a small percentage of people have had their phone break on them. Hopefully, most people will be able to enjoy using their new iPhone Duo without issue.

title: Google explains how to fix time zones on Android amid changes in Canada
snippet: As Canada makes changes around Daylight Savings, Google is explaining how to deal wiith the time zone change on your Android phone. more…
fullText:
As Canada makes changes around Daylight Savings, Google is explaining how to deal wiith the time zone change on your Android phone.

When Daylight Saving Time comes to an end next month, parts of Canada will not be rolling back their clocks as the time change becomes permanent. Manitoba announced the change in September, with other parts of the country, including Alberta and British Columbia, also no longer changing their times twice a year, but different provinces and territories are making their own choices regarding which time to stick with.

Google, in a post, subtly acknowledges that things could get a little messy with these time zone changes and your Android phone.

Time is usually set automatically on Android, and it sounds like that will still happen for the most part. Google says to “apply any pending updates from your phone’s manufacturer and Google, and then restart your device” if your phone’s time is incorrect on November 1 after the changes kick in.

	

But if there are still problems, you can make adjustments in the Settings of your Android device:

If you are still seeing an incorrect time or time zone, you can enable location-based time zone detection:

Open Settings.

Search for Date and Time.

Enable “Automatic time zone”.

Enable “Use location for time zone”.

or set the time zone manually:

Open Settings.

Search for Date and Time.

Disable “Automatic time zone”.

Choose “Time Zone”.

Choose “Region”.

Choose “Canada”.

Choose a time zone with the right offset.

title: Watch out, YouTube — Instagram goes from short-form to 90-minute videos
snippet: After years in which every social platform (even LinkedIn!) aggressively pursued short-form video, this is a notable shift in strategy for Instagram.
fullText:
If you could have 1 million followers on any social media platform, which would you choose? There is a correct answer, and it’s YouTube, assuming you’d like to get paid for your work. But Instagram’s latest update could upend YouTube’s long-held position as the most lucrative platform for creators, if only Instagram plays its cards right.

Instagram announced on Monday that it’s testing a new type of video upload that will allow creators to share “Features,” videos up to 90 minutes long. After years in which every social platform (even LinkedIn!) aggressively pursued short-form video, this is a notable shift in strategy for Instagram.

Short-form, vertical video content has defined the internet of the 2020s, but the creators behind these clips don’t actually make much money directly from platforms like Instagram — the Meta-owned platform has some monetization tools like subscriptions, but it doesn’t typically pay creators on a per-view basis.

“You can get paid by the platform directly, you can get paid by a fan, and you can get paid by a brand,” Instagram head Adam Mosseri explained on the Colin and Samir Show, an interview show about the creator economy. “And right now, the way that it works on Instagram primarily is you primarily get paid by brands. Some people get paid by fans. We have still a small performance-based program, but … we spend more money than we make back by a long shot, and so it doesn’t really make sense to scale up because we’re just burning capital.”

YouTube’s payment model is more straightforward: There are ads on videos, and creators enrolled in YouTube’s Partner Program get 55% of the ad revenue YouTube earns from their videos. That adds up. The platform said last year that it paid more than $100 billion to creators, artists, and media companies in the previous four years.

Instagram and TikTok haven’t been able to replicate YouTube’s model with short-form content, which is inherently trickier to monetize than longer videos because there’s less room to place ads. Many creators see those accounts more like promotional arms for their YouTube channels than meaningful drivers of revenue.

Image Credits:Instagram

Instagram is encouraging creators to upload longer videos, as it already did eight years ago with the now-defunct IGTV. It’s possible that its parent company, Meta, which makes its billions on advertising, will put ads in those long-form videos, too.

If Meta does add ads, could Instagram meaningfully compete with the YouTube Partner Program for the first time?

“It’s too early to share a long-term monetization model, but we’re exploring ways for creators to earn from brands, fans, and Instagram, including performance-based incentives,” a Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch. “Over time, we think there will be compounding benefits for creators to tell new stories, reach new audiences, and find new partners, which should lead to many monetization opportunities.”

It’s not a particularly promising answer, but it’s also not a no.

Mosseri explained in a video announcement why the platform is suddenly embracing long-form content after scrapping its old video product, IGTV.

“For a long time, I have been against doing long-form video on Instagram,” Mosseri said, noting that shorter content like Reels drives more shares and DMs among users. Instagram VP of Product Tessa Lyons, who has been advocating for this change, finally convinced Mosseri to give long form another shot.

“Reels is still going to be a core part of Instagram. But when you want to go deeper with the creators you love and the content that they’re creating, you should be able to do that on Instagram,” Lyons said in the video.

In other words, Instagram would rather keep fans on its own platform to enjoy both short- and long-form content from a creator than lose them to YouTube. Instagram is testing a feature called “Clips as Reels,” which lets creators make Reels out of their long-form content. The Reels link viewers to the longer video. Viewers can also save the longer video to send to the Instagram app on their TV.

Instagram is currently testing “Features” and “Clips as Reels” in Brazil and will now expand to the U.S. in a small test. The platform is also working on improved discovery features for Live video and a hub on a creator’s profile for episodic Reels, meaning a series of connected Reels similar to TikTok’s playlist feature.

“The thing that the team has been working on that we’re excited to share with you is trying to make it so that the short-form and the long-form video can be symbiotic,” Mosseri said. “We’re going to try to support these different types of formats, both in the mobile app, but also on the TV app, which I think is … going to take some time to get right. But I’m actually very excited about it, and we’re very committed to it long term.”

She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. She is the co-host of Wow If True, a podcast about internet culture, with science fiction author Isabel J. Kim. title: Modretro’s Chromatic is more transparent and cheaper than ever; how could I not love it?
snippet: As a retro gamer, I’ve tried all manner of consoles aiming to replace my OG Game Boy Color, but not many that scratch the itch of the recently released Chromatic Transparent from Modretro. It’s, honestly, the best way to replicate the feeling of the original hardware while improving in so many key ways. more…
fullText:
As a retro gamer, I’ve tried all manner of consoles aiming to replace my OG Game Boy Color, but not many that scratch the itch of the recently released Chromatic Transparent from Modretro. It’s, honestly, the best way to replicate the feeling of the original hardware while improving in so many key ways.

I have a decent number of original gaming consoles from the 90s, but the Game Boy is arguably the handheld that I covet the most. I was a little too young to really enjoy the DMG model, but the Game Boy Color was the first EDC I ever owned. It still has a special place in my heart that very few things can match.

Luckily for me, my parents didn’t throw my original clear “Atomic Purple” Game Boy Color away under the guise of ditching clutter at home. It’s a piece of art, one that I love dearly, but it’s missing out on the fundamentals of a good gadget by 2026 standards.

Using original hardware isn’t always ideal. You miss out on a backlit display, the battery longevity is often subpar, and, in the interests of hardware preservation, I don’t want to break something that means so much to me.

	

That’s kind of why I picked up the original Modretro Chromatic last year. That is a high-end FPGA Game Boy clone that replicates software emulation with hardware-level logic recreation. You’re able to play original cartridges with supremely accurate visuals, sounds, timing, all that good stuff.

The original Chromatic was kind of pricey at over $200 with the Sapphire glass display and all-metal chassis. Sure, those are “nice-to-haves,” but the new Modretro Chromatic Transparent lowers the price of entry and adds back in the transparent tech highlight of my youth for under $150 – with a copy of Tetris. Maybe you need to be a 90s kid to truly understand the appeal. I’m just glad that brands are at least offering us these kinds of options again.

I’ve been carrying this thing for a few weeks in my sidebag in place of my orange Chromatic, and it’s a different beast in many ways. Being able to play all of my favorite Game Boy games isn’t anything new, and sure, I could use an emulator on my phone, but there’s nothing quite like playing as Nintendo intended.

From a purely holistic standpoint, you’re going back to the slow, intentional gaming that is completely vanilla. Mod-free, methodical gaming that feels intentional. I love emulation as much as anyone, but playing at 1x speed rather than trying to speedrun the grinding of Pokémon is a throwback.

Okay, it’s not a gadget for everyone. It’s more of a fancy thing that old heads will adore because it literally does one thing exceptionally well. The screen is 1:1, and includes the all-important backlighting. It does downgrade the scratch protection to Gorilla Glass, but that is far better than what the original Game Boy could ever claim.

By default, it takes three AA batteries, or you can pick up a rechargeable battery pack that charges up through the USB-C port. The port does a little more, like letting you stream to Discord and update on-device firmware. Make no mistake, the Chromatic Transparent is made for the modern era, despite doing one thing and one thing only.

I was sent the green Chromatic Clear, and it’s almost jewel-like, which demands attention. I like that it isn’t quite neon; the smoky color feels premium despite the material difference from the original Chromatic. It will pick up scuffs and dings. Personally, I see that as a patina that means I’m playing my favorite games, which, in my opinion, we should all do more of. Although some of my original carts need battery replacements, I’m using a flash cart to play through my collection.

The buttons are not quite 1:1 with the original Game Boy Color. I’d say they’re a little “stiffer” but feel about as close as you could get without being outright replicas. I know some people won’t like the D-pad. It’s marginally harder to roll through the four directions than an actual Game Boy, so some games may play a little differently.

My only major criticism is that the volume scroll wheel is too easy to adjust without intent. So be aware that you might inadvertently increase the volume while launching the Modretro settings menu.

On that, the speaker is a solitary downward-firing mono speaker, and it gets loud with no distortion. It’s amazing to hear the earworm of the Tetris theme playing at full blast, but remember to tone the volume down when you’re in public.

For anyone wondering why you wouldn’t use an original Game Boy Color to play your games, well, that’s a very fair comment. However, to get a modded Game Boy Color that has all the same functionality, it actually costs upwards of $150 from most reputable sellers on sites like eBay. Modretro is basically undercutting the original with lots of quality-of-life changes with the Chromatic Transparent.

As much as I love this hardware and will covet it in my EDC, you simply cannot separate the company from the controversial founder, Palmer Luckey. To many, the ties to his business ventures outside the gaming space will tarnish the brand. I can understand hesitation, and while I was sent this device for review, you will need to decide for yourself if you are willing to support the company. It would be unfair to omit this; hence, mentioning it.

It would also be a lie if I were not to say I’m smitten with the product. I do wish it were not marked with this extra controversy, as it’s the best way for ardent retro gamers to play through your back catalog of Game Boy titles.

For $150, the Chromatic Transparent is not a cheap way to indulge in some nostalgia. However, it’s undercutting the competition and now has even better colors to choose from.

title: iPhone Duo one day later: Here’s why its quirks don’t make it any less incredible
snippet: Yesterday, I picked up my iPhone Duo at Apple Fifth Avenue, and it’s been a wonder to use. Of course, the phone isn’t perfect, but after my first day of usage, I’m looking forward to daily driving it – even if it has a couple quirks. more…
fullText:
Yesterday, I picked up my iPhone Duo at Apple Fifth Avenue, and it’s been a wonder to use. Of course, the phone isn’t perfect, but after my first day of usage, I’m looking forward to daily driving it – even if it has a couple quirks.

When discussing iPhone Duo, most people are going to talk about the under display FaceTime camera, Touch ID, and app support as compromises. Sure, those are features that make it a lesser experience than a typical iPhone, but personally, I don’t find them as experience-ruining at all.

Last year, Apple impressed many with the iPhone Air. It was incredibly thin, and certainly an engineering marvel to shove everything into that form factor. You felt it though: speaker quality was subpar, you only had a single rear camera, and battery life was lacking compared to any other iPhone. It was by no means unusable, but you had to compromise.

iPhone Duo feels like a full experience

To me, iPhone Duo doesn’t really feel like I’m giving up anything that really matters. Touch ID is a learning curve, but it doesn’t feel like a struggle. The under display FaceTime camera is worse than if it weren’t under display, but in good lighting it looks perfectly fine, especially over video calls.

As for app support, I feel the entire situation was overblown. Many early reviewers were quick to point out the fact that many apps aren’t yet updated for iPhone Duo, while ignoring the fact that they had the phone early and most developers were planning their releases for when consumers would start having devices, not reviewers. In just the past couple days, substantially more apps have been updated for iPhone Duo.

The outside screen also feels like something worth using, not just an afterthought. It’s a smaller screen, and you certainly read less on it than you’d otherwise be able to on a taller display. To me, though, the screen actually feels quite refreshing to use. The keyboard is still full width, you just don’t have to take in as much background context at once. It feels more focused.

That said, there are two things I’ve really felt with iPhone Duo that I’d like to see improved. Luckily, these are mostly software improvements.

Software suggestions

In the first day of using my iPhone Duo, I’ve noticed two things about the device that feel a bit odd. For one, iOS still only allows you to backswipe from the left edge of the device. This feels a bit in conflict with the fact that navigation elements are on the right side of the device. 

When I got my iPhone Duo, I found myself naturally trying to backswipe from the right edge many times. Unfortunately, Apple doesn’t let you do that. This certainly isn’t a make or break for the phone, and I’ve gotten used to reaching over to the left edge of the device, but given the fact that this form factor is otherwise incredibly reachable, I think that would be a nice adjustment.

Another thing I’d like to see improved is unlock with Apple Watch. The feature itself works great, and makes losing Face ID less of a pain. That said, it means if you hand your device to anyone else, they can just unlock it. I think having basic camera-based facial recognition in combination with unlock with Apple Watch would be a nice improvement.

Wrap up

Beyond that though, I’m incredibly happy with iPhone Duo, and I’m excited to use the device more over time and share my experience with you all. Anecdotally, I’ve never had so many people stop me in public and ask about my iPhone, so the Duo seemingly has people excited in a way I haven’t seen in ages. It’s a fun phone.

	

One last thing of note: Apple’s official folio case for iPhone Duo doesn’t seem like a worthwhile product. At $129, the kickstand doesn’t feel super strong, and the front flap creates an awkward situation when taking photos using the outside display. You can’t flip it around the back, since that’d cover the camera, so you just have to leave it floating. I’d skip buying this, and instead wait for third party solutions to fill the gap.

Did you buy an iPhone Duo, or are you still waiting for future iterations? Let us know in the comments.

fullText:
9to5Mac is brought to you by Memoket: Memoket Gem is a 0.4 oz AI wearable that slots beside your Apple Watch. One press captures a conversation, and KITE memory connects it to what you said weeks ago. 20-hour battery. Available now from $168.99 on memoket.ai and Amazon.

While it is great that Siri AI can finally deliver Apple’s promise of an actually useful, personal assistant for the age of AI, expectations surrounding agentic assistants are quickly shifting. But Apple is showing it might not watch from the sidelines again.

Siri AI is great, but it’s also very 2024

Now that Siri AI (which is still officially designated as a beta) has been out for a little more than a month, it seems fair to say that its two defining characteristics are that it’s finally useful, but it can be painfully slow to answer even simple queries.

And while I had spent the better part of the past few months mocking Silicon Valley’s obsession with AI assistants that can book flights and hotels, I hate to admit that the first time Siri AI actually impressed me was when I asked how much I’d paid for a hotel room for an upcoming trip to San Francisco and how far it was from my first appointment in the city. It got both answers exactly right.

Could I have looked this up myself? Sure. But setting aside the fact that I was in the middle of a 10K run at the time, finding that information on my own would undoubtedly have taken longer than it took Siri to give me the answers.

As a result, over the past few months, I’ve found myself increasingly relying on Siri AI for questions like “What was the contact information for that plumber who fixed the kitchen sink leak a couple of years ago?” or “What was the name of that PR person who introduced me to so-and-so?”

Information I know I have somewhere, be it an iMessage conversation or an email receipt, and that although I could just search for it, I’d now rather have Siri AI do it for me.

And for the first time in 15 years, I can ask these questions without already expecting Siri to fail halfway through asking them, only to get frustrated when it inevitably gets it wrong and proves me right.

That’s all well and good. The problem is that Apple has only now caught up with what AI assistants could do in 2024.

Apple’s next AI challenge: Building an agent harness for Siri

Particularly over the past few months, the frontier AI market has increasingly shifted toward agentic assistants, with products from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and xAI (among many others) moving beyond answering questions to actually carrying out tasks on users’ behalf.

I subscribe to ChatGPT, and I’ve been using Codex and ChatGPT Work extensively for everyday tasks involving files and information scattered across my Mac and various cloud services.

And it still feels like magic every time I ask one of these tools to do something that involves opening, creating, editing, or organizing files on my computer, as well as interacting with websites and services I’m logged into, and it actually pulls it off.

The flipside of this is that every time ChatGPT completes one such task, the new Siri AI starts to feel like the old Siri all over again.

It is still early days, for sure, but it already feels like this is yet another area where Apple seems to be falling increasingly behind, as AI labs continue to improve their agentic capabilities, sometimes rolling out major updates just weeks apart, while Apple remains largely tied to its annual software release cycle.

But there’s one important limitation to today’s agentic assistants that I think Apple is particularly well positioned to address.

As impressive as tools like Codex, Dots, and ChatGPT Work can be, they still depend heavily on the user to provide the permissions and the context behind whatever task they’re supposed to accomplish. They can access files, search through emails, and interact with websites, but they generally don’t know what you’re doing, what you’ve been discussing with other people, or what you might need next unless you explicitly tell them.

And as these tools become increasingly capable of operating our computers and phones on our behalf, I suspect the next big leap in their usefulness will come not just from improving what they can do, but from improving their proactive understanding of the user’s context in real time.

That’s where Apple could have an advantage.

Apple has recently shown that it’s finally willing to capitalize on the trust it has spent years building around privacy, even if it means testing the boundaries of what users are comfortable sharing with an AI assistant.

Last month, it introduced two Apple Watch features: Siri Recap, which can automatically generate summaries of conversations throughout the day, and Live Rewind, which lets users retrieve the last 15 seconds of a conversation they may have missed.

Both features rely on the Apple Watch’s microphone to capture information about what’s happening around the user, potentially giving Siri access to an entirely new source of personal context.

Of course, the privacy implications are enormous, particularly because conversations involve other people who haven’t necessarily agreed to have their words processed by an AI assistant.

And while those concerns are certainly worth discussing at length (and are probably why these features have yet to roll out), Apple has repeatedly shown that it’s willing to go to extraordinary lengths to address the privacy challenges that come with giving technology access to sensitive personal information. Just look at the lengths it went to in developing its Reference Image system.

As agentic assistants become more capable, I suspect their biggest limitation will increasingly have less to do with what the underlying models can do, and more with how much we’re willing to let them know about us.

Imagine an assistant that doesn’t just wait for you to ask it to find a document or complete a task, but already understands what you’re working on. One that can gather information in the background so it’s ready when you need it, or even take action on your behalf based on what’s happening around you.

That’s the kind of assistant that could make today’s agentic tools feel as limited as the old Siri (and, increasingly, the new Siri AI) does now.

And while Apple still has plenty of catching up to do when it comes to actually building these capabilities, it is in a much better position to compete in this next phase of AI than it was when the generative AI race first began.

title: WhatsApp starts testing long-awaited scheduled messages on iPhone
snippet: After years of waiting, WhatsApp is finally making one of its most-requested messaging features available to select iPhone beta testers. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After years of waiting, WhatsApp is finally making one of its most-requested messaging features available to select iPhone beta testers. Here are the details.

Scheduled messages are almost here

While Meta doesn’t generally break down active user figures by platform, Mark Zuckerberg said in April last year that WhatsApp had more than 3 billion monthly active users worldwide.

Ironically, despite being used by more than a third of the world’s population, WhatsApp still lacks some features competing platforms have offered for years. Case in point: the ability to schedule messages.

Earlier this year, WABetaInfo reported that code references in WhatsApp’s beta suggested the company was working on a message scheduling feature, although it wasn’t available for testing at the time.

Now, according to the site, the feature is finally rolling out to select iOS beta testers, less than two weeks after making its debut on Android beta.

Image: WABetaInfo

Here’s how the feature works, per WABetaInfo‘s report:

Users can schedule a message from the chat interface. After typing the message into the chat composer, they need to tap and hold the send button. WhatsApp opens the schedule message screen with a date and time picker. Users can scroll through the page and tap the green button at the bottom of the screen to confirm. The button shows the exact delivery time before users schedule the message. After scheduling a message, WhatsApp shows a confirmation in the chat, but it is only visible to the user who scheduled it.

WABetaInfo notes that messages can be scheduled as little as 10 minutes in advance or as far as two weeks in advance, and that scheduled messages appear in a dedicated section within the chat info screen or the group info screen for group chats.

Interestingly, in group chats, scheduled messages are only delivered to users who were already members when the message was scheduled. Anyone who joins the group afterward won’t receive it, even if they join before the message is sent.

The site also says that in addition to scheduling text messages, users can schedule messages containing photos, videos, and links. One current limitation, however, is that users cannot schedule multiple photos or videos at once, meaning each media item must be scheduled separately.

As is often the case with beta features, scheduled messages are only available to select testers, with no way to enable the feature manually. There’s also no word on when it will launch publicly, although with testing now underway on both iOS and Android, a wider rollout could be coming sooner rather than later.

title: iOS 27 adds new Phone app feature that’s an instant favorite
snippet: iOS 27 is packed with new features for apps like Notes, Wallet, Maps, Messages, and more. But one iOS 27 addition that’s especially impressed me is a new Phone feature: Call Context. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is packed with new features for apps like Notes, Wallet, Maps, Messages, and more. But one iOS 27 addition that’s especially impressed me is a new Phone feature: Call Context.

iOS 27’s Call Context feature puts key info on-screen when you’re on the phone with a business

I’m not a big fan of phone calls, so the Phone app isn’t somewhere I spend much time. But last year in iOS 26, the app had two of my favorite new features: Call Screening and Hold Assist.

Now with iOS 27 this year, Apple has again impressed me with a new Phone app feature.

Call Context is an Apple Intelligence feature that automatically surfaces relevant info on the call screen when you’re on the phone with a business.

Per Apple’s website:

Get relevant information while on a call. Call Context can proactively surface relevant information from across your apps when calling a business — like a confirmation code from Mail when you call an airline.

I’ve had the chance to use Call Context several times in iOS 27. And I’ve very quickly concluded that this is the kind of no-brainer addition that should prove popular.

Not long ago I booked flights with Southwest Airlines, and later needed to call them about a change.

When I called, my flight info was automatically put on the screen. My iPhone even offered to read the confirmation number out loud for me on the call.

iOS 27 was also smart enough to include details for another Southwest flight stacked underneath the foremost one. So if Call Context doesn’t show the most relevant info at first, in most cases it should be just a quick tap away.

Call Context is initially available only in English, and it’s limited to iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch models that support Apple Intelligence.

title: LineageOS 24 review: Easier than ever to recommend [Video]
snippet: Times have changed. Prices have changed. Your phone hasn’t changed, but the value of LineageOS 24 certainly has. more…
fullText:
Times have changed. Prices have changed. Your phone hasn’t changed, but the value of LineageOS 24 certainly has.

LineageOS 23 review: The de facto AI-free alternative Android experience [Video]

It’s only been a few months since the LineageOS 23.2 drop, and we’re already here with the full-fat Android 17 release. The initial delays from Google last year might have lingered longer than we hoped, but the Lineage team has been hard at work, and version 24 is now ready to go.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

Simpler installation process

The new online flash tool is, and I don’t say this lightly, the biggest upgrade to how you will flash the Lineage ROM on your devices in the history of the project. It is a fantastic addition and one that lowers the barrier of entry so drastically that it’s now a must for anyone with an older, unsupported handset.

	

However, even with a lower barrier to entry, you still need to follow the traditional flashing process, but it has been simplified. Just download the files and follow the correct order. Because the new method lets you do everything in a browser window, it makes it much easier to recommend – even more so if you already have Lineage installed on your phone.

Open a second browser window, follow the flashing process, and you will have LineageOS 24 running in a few minutes. Just remember that you will need to do a few things ahead of time. Back up your files, maybe restore your phone before you flash Lineage, and you can’t really go wrong.

I’m hopeful that in the future, it’ll be as robust and simple as the Android Flash Tool, but it’s one step at a time. This is still a huge improvement for accessibility.

We cover Google and all the platform updates here, but if you want to de-Google your life, you can ditch the GApps package. If you need the Play Store and Play Services, remember to download the MindTheGapps package before flashing. In the interest of trying LineageOS 24 as intended, we have omitted this from our own installation.

What’s new?

Like previous builds, if you choose to forgo the MindTheGapps package, there are no AI-powered functions unless you install those and link a Google account. If you want Circle to Search and Notification Summaries, then those will be missing unless you sideload those first.

More Material 3 Expressive and QPR1

LineageOS 24 has integrated a lot of the changes that were added with the QPR1 launch for Pixel phones back in September 2026.

App bubbles are the biggest headline addition. This may be limited to the default launcher on Lineage, but it mimics the pop-up floating chathead for your apps that you can stash on the left or right side of your phone display. The same 4 to 5 app limitation also applies, but the functionality is identical to what we’ve seen on Pixel phones.

Wallpaper and style gain the custom icon functionality, but don’t add anything extra. You can choose new shapes, the style, and disable app text labels. Sadly, we are still limited to just one lockscreen clock style, but you can adjust the text thickness to give it a different look.

The Expanded Dark theme has also jumped over so that apps that would ordinarily not have a dedicated dark mode will be themed, but darker tones are also used in apps that support the function. Your mileage may vary with this, so use with caution.

Animations and minor details all match the M3E changes added in QPR1, with all the latest icon changes and Quick Settings panel enhancements. There’s parity with the frontier builds of Android, but with the trademark LineageOS speed and fluidity on top.

Improved apps and controls

During the setup process, there is a system theme picker to get you set up before loading into the OS. I’m not entirely sure if this is new, but it felt like it had changed based on the Lineage 23.2 build I tested earlier this year.

The system update page looks much better, giving key information at a glance now. It’s a more robust section that helps you get updated and stay updated better than in previous versions of LineageOS.

Canvas, the default LineageOS 24 gallery app, is very simple, maybe a little barebones. It has gained some improved editing tools with this release. I do think they could be better, but they do include basic cropping and rotation. options. Basic markup is there with tools to scribble on your images if you need to do that. I haven’t used Snapchat for a while, but it reminds me of the old Snapchat editing toolset.

The Jelly default browser now supports PWA-lite or PWA-like apps when using the “Install shortcut” tool. I’ve found it doesn’t work all the time, but you can use it for services like Instagram and Spotify. It’s pretty useful if you want these lightweight web-based versions of an application, less tracking, and less space usage. This is a great addition.

The new Screen Recording UI is one such area that is improved with an option to record HEVC video directly from the floating panel. This is missing on Pixel phones and might be useful if you want to record high-quality but smaller video files locally.

One of the issues I still have with LineageOS is how the invisible gesture bar or hide feature has been enabled. Certain UI elements don’t fit when you have this disabled, so I would suggest keeping the hint enabled unless you don’t care about some elements feeling squeezed or shunted too close to the bottom display edge. It’s all personal preference at the end of the day.

LineageOS feels different now

I’ve been surface-level testing LineageOS for a good number of years now, and for the most part, I have always been impressed because the ROM gives you the ability to extend the lifespan of a phone or tablet that you’re still happy to use. I tend not to install on a brand new phone, as it defeats the purpose in my mind.

Outside market forces haven’t changed that one iota, but the ballooning costs of basically any and all technology have me thinking more about how flashing Lineage on some of my older devices is going to be a bigger component in my future.

My parents have older phones that are very close to the end of “official” support windows. I’m 100% going to be putting LineageOS 24 on those in the coming months. The peace of mind that comes with security updates and maybe even better performance is almost impossible to ignore now.

Extending the life of your possessions feels like the best way to say f-you to the big tech companies that have all banded together with the modus operandi that’ll we’ll all own nothing and be happy about it. At least there are options like this that still exist. I’m almost certain that I’ll be using this ROM more than I ever expected in the next few years across a wide array of devices I’m responsible for, and long may that continue.

To get started with LineageOS 24 and see all supported devices, click here.

title: Some Galaxy S26 phones are basically paperweights while Samsung fixes a setup bug
snippet: A bug is affecting some Galaxy S26 phones that leaves them essentially useless due to a setup problem. more…
fullText:
A bug is affecting some Galaxy S26 phones that leaves them essentially useless due to a setup problem.

If you can’t get through the initial setup process on your smartphone, it might as well be an expensive paperweight. And that’s exactly the problem right now on some Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra devices, as a bug is causing the setup process to get stuck and leave the device unable to proceed.

Affected devices are left seeing an error saying that “the webpage is unavailable” for an account page on Samsung’s website. This seems to happen during setup, meaning you probably won’t run into the problem unless you reset your device. 

The issue was reported on Samsung’s forums (via SammyFans) with a Samsung representative confirming the cause (translated):

	

Upon reviewing the details you provided, it appears there is an issue following the device UI 9.0 update. The development team has confirmed that this issue occurs when using an unstable system WebView on certain networks… 

Apparently, switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data can serve as a workaround, but your results may vary.

fullText:
iPhone Duo is officially out in the wild, and users keep discovering new details about the device. The latest: there’s a hidden trick that makes opening Control Center significantly easier.

iPhone Duo’s Control Center can be opened in new, more reachable way

When iPhone Duo reviews dropped earlier this week, one common complaint I saw is that in left-handed use, opening Control Center can be a pain.

Like on other iPhones, you open Control Center by swiping down from the top-right corner.

If you’re using iPhone Duo two-handed, that’s not a problem. Or if it’s in your right hand, it might be slightly awkward but still ultimately fine. 

In left-handed use though, even when folded, the device’s extra-wide design makes Control Center more of a challenge to open.

Except it turns out, Apple added a hidden trick that solves that. 

	

As Stephen Robles shows in a video on X, you can instead just tap the new Battery/Wi-Fi/Cellular icon to open Control Center.

This shortcut is much more reachable than a top-right corner swipe. And as Robles demonstrates, when you have a Live Activity running the button moves even further down the screen to become even more reachable.

It’s one of the many unique design implementations iPhone Duo introduces.

title: iPhone Duo’s software restricts an already-small display; Galaxy Z Fold 8 doesn’t
snippet: Apple’s take on a wide foldable isn’t being received without some criticism as it makes its way into the hands of users. The biggest limitation might not even be the hardware. more…
fullText:
Apple’s take on a wide foldable isn’t being received without some criticism as it makes its way into the hands of users. The biggest limitation might not even be the hardware.

Samsung has struggled with the implementation of Android on its foldables. That’s the natural way of things as the form factor has progressed through the years. As the Galaxy Z Fold line has been refined, Google and Samsung have improved Android to be friendlier on big screens.

But this is Apple’s first try, and even on hardware that looks promising, iOS leaves something to be desired on the iPhone Duo.

This comes from a couple of second impressions. One short review via The Verge‘s Allison Johnson notes a couple of small complaints. The first details its usability. Compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the iPhone Duo reportedly feels harder to use with one hand. Because the Fold 8’s taller and narrower physical presence, the cover screen is more easily navigable. That’s a big deal for those of us who gravitated towards the Galaxy Z Fold 8 for its unique outer screen.

	

The iPhone Duo also restricts that small 5.4-inch display by implementing a sidebar, which was intended to make navigation easier. But because the dock sits on the right side, there’s a big chunk of the display that’s essentially left unused. Another post on Twitter/X highlights the severe difference.

In The Verge‘s video, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is set to use a navigation bar instead of gestures, which makes the difference a little less blatant. But for those who use navigation gestures on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, there’s very little wasted screen space.

What Apple is trying to do with the iPhone Duo is to approach a small display with a space-saving solution. By shrinking the space allowed, you stretch media so it appears taller, like on a slab device. But the Galaxy Z Fold 8 proves that leaving the space free for main content works pretty well.

The iPhone Duo is already available, but its availability is limited. Meanwhile, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is continuing to prove a success for Samsung.

If you want to see more from Allison and 9to5Google, be sure to check out her appearance on our episode of The Sideload!

fullText:
Samsung has a bunch of new foldables in store for next year, but also one more coming out this year, and it’s coming out in just a few days according to a new leak.

According to leaker Ice Universe, the device pictured below is the Galaxy W27, a new foldable that Samsung is set to release on October 29.

What is it?

This is just the latest in a yearly tradition of Samsung releasing China-only variants of its Galaxy foldables. Each generation has arrived with some additional flair and usually some fancy packaging too, but the Galaxy W series is just a rebranded version of whatever Samsung’s top foldable is for the year. The one exception was 2024’s Galaxy Z Fold 6 Special Edition, which saw a broader release and served as a stepping stone before Samsung’s major leap in the Galaxy Z Fold 7.

	

For 2026, that’s the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which is what the specs on this new foldable match. The design is certainly matching up, though with a glossy blue back and gold accents around the triple-camera array.

It’s not a surprise that Samsung is continuing on its usual trend with this device, but it is a bit surprising that it’s based on the Ultra and not the standard Galaxy Z Fold 8, the one with the new shape that’s clearly resonating with customers. It’s not like wide foldables aren’t making headway in China either, as Xiaomi’s latest foldable has virtually the same form factor, and Huawei has been putting out wide foldables longer than anyone at this point.

title: Google Pixel’s solution to using Face Unlock in the dark seems to be just blinding you
snippet: Google’s Face Unlock feature on Pixel phones works really well, until the lights go out. The company appears to be building out a new upgrade to this with “active illumination” which is… just turning up the screen brightness. more…
fullText:
Google’s Face Unlock feature on Pixel phones works really well, until the lights go out. The company appears to be building out a new upgrade to this with “active illumination” which is… just turning up the screen brightness.

Face Unlock as it exists on Pixel 8 and newer relies on the camera and Google’s software to deliver biometric authentication that’s actually strong enough to let you unlock secure apps such as banking and password manager apps.  

While the fingerprint sensor serves as a fine backup, not having Face Unlock in dark rooms can be a tiny bit frustrating. And Google’s solution appears to be just raising the screen brightness.

The folks over at Android Authority uncovered a new option being built out in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 2 which is simply titled “Brighten screen in low light.” Google’s summary of the feature reads:

	

Automatically boost screen brightness so Face Unlock works in dim lighting.

Sounds fun in a dark room.

An assortment of strings related to the feature further detail what to expect, with Google seemingly set to offer granular settings around if the feature is used when Bedtime mode, Do Not Disturb, or driving is detected, as well as a setting to tailor just how bright the screen can get.

“Reliable” sounds like it might turn up the brightness higher to ensure an accurate reading from Face Unlock, while “Comfortable” seems to trade brightness for, well, not blinding you. 

	

Some of the strings mention:

Brightness level – Reliable, Comfort – Lower settings may reduce reliability

Complete darkness – Can brighten to find your face when it’s too dark. When turned off, only brightens if your face is partially visible

Bedtime mode – Can brighten when Bedtime mode is on

Driving – Can brighten when a car ride is detected

“When this feature is turned on, the following accessibility settings may temporarily behave differently: extra dim, remove animations, or color inversion”

“Can brighten when Do Not Disturb is on”

It still doesn’t sound like a particularly elegant solution, but it’s certainly better to have the option available. As for when Google might roll this feature out, that also remains to be seen. 

Would you opt to have your screen brightness raise for the sake of using Face Unlock on a Pixel? Let us know in the comments.

title: Retro game emulator Delta looks great on the iPhone Duo
snippet: The popular retro game emulator Delta has today launched a big new 2.0 version, most notably featuring a refreshed Liquid Glass interface and support for the iPhone Duo. The app now has specially-designed controller skins that are optimized for all the different iPhone Duo poses, including some beautiful Nintendo DS layouts that use the full size of the inner display, and cleverly spans the crease when partially folded in book mode in portrait. more…
fullText:
The popular retro game emulator Delta has today launched a big new 2.0 version, most notably featuring a refreshed Liquid Glass interface and support for the iPhone Duo.

The app now has specially-designed controller skins that are optimized for all the different iPhone Duo poses, including some beautiful Nintendo DS layouts that use the full size of the inner display, and cleverly spans the crease when partially folded in book mode in portrait. 

The bigger screen of the iPhone Duo enables some immersive gaming experiences, but the Delta developers have also ensured that the app naturally reflows on the portrait closed outer screen too. 

Another little easter egg is that you can fold the Duo closed to automatically put the DS to sleep, emulating the physical behavior of a real DS console.

Delta also has a special trick when using it in landscape split view alongside another app. You can see it in action in this screenshot, which depicts Delta running side by side with another iPhone Duo app that is playing a video. 

Typically, the iPhone Duo Split View means each app is constrained to 50% of the screen space. But, as shown in this example, because the app exposes the bottom half of the virtual DS as a custom keyboard view, the system allows this ‘keyboard’ to stretch across the full width of the screen, overlapping the unrelated video player app on the other side of the split. 

Aside from iPhone Duo support, the new update also includes Sega Genesis ROM compatibility, improved library navigation, updated audio settings that allow game audio to mix alongside your currently playing music or podcast, and more. 

The premium version of Delta can be unlocked using an In-App Purchase subscription directly through the App Store, now available worldwide. In the US, EU, Brazil, and Japan, you can also support the app directly through Patreon.

title: As iPhone Duo Cracked Screen Reports Surface, a New Teardown Shows a Possible Culprit
snippet: In spite of some display issues, iFixit declares the iPhone Duo “the most repairable foldable” it’s ever tinkered with.
fullText:
With reviews out in the world and real people getting their hands on it, you might assume there’s little left to say about the iPhone Duo that hasn’t already been said. But this is a long-awaited Apple product we’re talking about, and ongoing scrutiny of this show-stealer of a device is not just desirable; it’s pretty much mandatory.

This is because, while we’ve loved using the device so far and think Apple’s first attempt at a foldable is admirable, some early iPhone Duo owners have reported problems with the screen. 

We’re currently conducting our own testing on the screen, folding the iPhone Duo 900 times per hour with a custom-made machine to see how long its hinge will last. At the time of writing, it had passed 55,000 folds without issue, but other people with a Duo haven’t been so lucky. Most commonly, people have reported issues with display cracks and lines of faulty pixels appearing along the hinge, according to MacRumors and Reddit.

			

More from CNET

As quickly as the faults have come to light, repairability experts at iFixit think they might already have discovered the culprit. Using teardown footage, patents and CT scans it collected while breaking down the iPhone Duo to ascertain its repairability score, iFixit built a 3D hinge model to identify where things could be going wrong.

What it found was that the breaks seemed to be occurring in the same place: just below the cable that connects the two screens, in a spot where a bunch of different connectors all meet. 

“All those edges meeting in this spot mean lots of possible culprits,” iFixit’s Elizabeth Chamberlain wrote in a lengthy blog post. “That center pivot looks different from the rest of the hinge. Could it be getting stuck? Could something else be getting stuck?

“Here’s one possible answer. In our closing simulation … the center support bar fails to drop far enough. The screen’s curved fold comes down onto it, creating a small stress hotspot near the reported break location.”

iFixit has created an interactive CT scan that allows you to play around with the Duo and see how the hinge supports, cable and nearby components fit beneath the display.

Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about the faults, but anyone experiencing issues with their iPhone Duo should be protected under warranty at this stage. Apple will charge $999 for inner screen replacement at a later date — whether that makes an AppleCare subscription a worthwhile investment is a choice only you can make.

The ‘most repairable foldable’

Any reports of screen problems are obviously bad news for Apple, but the company does also have reason to be proud of itself. 

iFixit has declared the iPhone Duo “the most repairable foldable smartphone we’ve ever taken apart.” The phone has scored a 5/10 repairability rating, which might not be as impressive as the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max’s scores of 7/10, but still makes Apple the industry leader in terms of foldable repairability.

In its teardown, iFixit called out the trim surrounding the Duo’s screen as being particularly easy to pull away in contrast to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8’s trim, which “crumbled” as it was removed. The flat layout of the Duo’s components also garnered praise from iFixit. Being able to access components like the cameras and logic board without taking the whole device apart makes repairs simpler if any of those components require replacement.

iFixit praised the flat layout of the Duo’s internal components.iFixit/Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

iFixit also praised Apple’s electrically releasable adhesive, which can be used to easily remove the battery by passing a low voltage through it. This is an innovative repair technology that Apple pioneered and is also used across its other devices. It allows the cells to be removed without any bending or prying that could result in a puncture risk to the battery.

Finally, a key part of making tech more repairable is ensuring that the companies making the products also make instruction manuals and official parts accessible to people — whether they’re doing the repairs themselves at home, or taking them to a third-party repair shop. iFixit is still awaiting official parts from Apple, but it praised the company for publishing its repair manual so quickly.

Major points were deducted for the hinge and inner display — both of which would be difficult and time-consuming to repair.

“For a first attempt, Apple has done well,” Chamberlain wrote. “The easy battery removal alone is something we’d like to see on every foldable. But of course we’ll hold Apple accountable for making replacement parts available, and here’s hoping that the next generation of the Duo features a more affordable inner display and a more accessible hinge repair.”

title: YouTube removing ‘Subscriptions’ bottom bar tab on Android, iOS after nearly a decade
snippet: YouTube is making a number of changes to its Android and iOS apps with the launch of custom feeds, including moving Subscriptions out of the bottom bar. more…
fullText:
YouTube is making a number of changes to its Android and iOS apps with the launch of custom feeds, including moving Subscriptions out of the bottom bar.

On mobile, YouTube is “kicking off a series of updates to shape a more seamless Home experience.” This starts with a redesigned top bar with dedicated feeds.

As part of this change, YouTube is removing the Subscriptions tab from its fourth position in the bottom bar. It’s now in the “top bar on the Home tab.” Testing of the redesign started earlier this year. 

“Subs” appears in the second position after “Home” with a red underline that will take some getting used to. This change will break a lot of muscle memory, with Subscriptions appearing in the YouTube bottom bar for nearly a decade (2017).

	

Old vs. new

Meanwhile, after Subs, you’ll see new dedicated feeds for Live, Music, and Movies & TV, with the latter only appearing if you have active subscriptions (such as Primetime Channels). This change has the upside of removing YouTube’s navigation drawer. 

	

More broadly, this change coincides with the launch of custom feeds, which are also available on and sync to the web. This lets you describe “what you want to see in your own words”.

Tap “+” at the top of your Home feed and describe the topic, channels, or vibe you’re looking for (for example, “help me unwind after work with guided meditations under 10 minutes”). You’ll then get a new feed tailored to your interests for you to explore.

They will appear as top tabs in the main feed after Home and Subs so that “you can jump back into them whenever you want.” The prompt box at the top of each feed lets you change it.

Notably, free users “can save up to 3 active custom feeds, while YouTube Premium members can save up to 8.”

Custom feeds are first rolling out on “mobile and desktop in English to U.S. based, signed-in viewers.” It will be available in more countries going forward.
