title: I’ve been using Android’s iPad Mini OLED for months, and it’s the better tiny tablet
snippet: Apple has just released a new iPad Mini with an OLED display and it looks great, but I’ve spent the past few months with Android’s equivalent in the Redmagic Astra 2, and it’s well worth your attention. more…
fullText:
Apple has just released a new iPad Mini with an OLED display and it looks great, but I’ve spent the past few months with Android’s equivalent in the Redmagic Astra 2, and it’s well worth your attention.

The new iPad Mini with OLED is a long-overdue upgrade. As 9to5Mac details, this new tablet delivers an 8.5-inch OLED display, a chassis that’s just 5.4mm thick, and weighs just 255g. By all means, it looks great.

Apple unveils all-new iPad mini: OLED, thinner design, more

But over the past few months, I’ve been using what has now turned out to be a close rival to that tablet. The Redmagic Astra 2 may be a gaming-focused Android tablet, but it matches or even beats the new iPad Mini in some crucial ways.

The 9.04-inch OLED display on the RedMagic Astra 2 is a bit bigger than Apple’s (it’s a slightly thicker and heavier tablet, too), but it’s still very much in that same ballpark. And it’s a gorgeous display. For everything from movies to games, it’s been an absolute pleasure to use. Colors are vivid, blacks are as deep as only OLED can do, and it beats Apple’s peak brightness at 1,600 nits too. 

	

The biggest point in Redmagic’s favor is in that display, too. Where Apple is still refusing to give the iPad Mini a 120Hz refresh rate with this latest model – utterly insane in the year two thousand and twenty-six, if I do say so myself – Astra 2 has a 185Hz refresh rate. I’ve not found that inherently better than a standard 120Hz panel, but it’s way better than the 60Hz panel Apple’s latest will still be using. You do miss out on stylus support on the Astra, though (sadly).

As for performance, Redmagic Astra 2 is packing Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and 12GB of RAM in its base model. Over the past couple of months that performance has been absolutely stellar. Not that that’s a surprise, these are the same core specs as you’ll find in something like the Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Redmagic’s Android skin isn’t particularly heavy either.

I’ve been hooked on Metalstorm throughout the review period, and it runs brilliantly even on max settings on the Astra 2.

It also never gets warm, probably thanks in part to the liquid cooling loop and fan built into the tablet. While the whine of the fan can be heard in super-quiet rooms (like late at night in bed), it’s typically never a problem. Despite the fan, Astra 2 is still IP54 rated, too. 

Battery life is also great to the point where it’s barely a thought, not surprising for an 8,300 mAh cell. Gaming sessions up to an hour barely make a dent, and the standby time is ridiculous. At one point I didn’t have a chance to use the tablet for over a week and it only drained about 25% in that time. When it came time to charge, any USB-C cable works and you’ve got the choice of two ports, so you can easily top off in the way that’s easiest for you while still being able to use USB peripherals if you want. I just found this convenient for being able to choose between the side-mounted charger on my bedside table or the bottom port when I was still actively holding the tablet.

Astra 2’s hardware, by the way, is an aluminum body that’s 6.9mm thick. It has a little glass window on the back with some RGB accents, but it’s overall subtle enough, and you can turn off the RGB entirely.

The software, as mentioned, isn’t all that heavy. It’s certainly not what you’d expect for something marketed as a gaming tablet. Outside of a gamer font (which you can change), the UI doesn’t feel that far off from a Pixel. It’s not the cleanest, but it’s far from the heavy iOS clones you’ll find elsewhere. There are even nice additions such as lockscreen widgets. A customizable switch up top defaults to a gaming mode (which has a full gamer UI and optimizes performance) can serve whatever function you like, including acting as a mute switch or to active the flashlight. 

Meanwhile, there’s also the conversation around price. Apple’s starting price is lower at $699. That said, while the price on Astra 2 is higher at $749 – and that’s the result of a quiet price hike that landed quite literally within the last few days – that’s for the 12GB/256GB model. On Apple’s side, the equivalent iPad Mini lands at $799. Redmagic’s slate is actually a great deal with that in mind, even more so on the 512GB model at $849 compared to Apple’s $999.

title: Google’s new Metal Mesh Fitbit Air band is more versatile than you think
snippet: A metal mesh band might not be right for every watch or wearable, but I can’t say I don’t love using it on the Fitbit Air. more…
fullText:
A metal mesh band might not be right for every watch or wearable, but I can’t say I don’t love using it on the Fitbit Air.

The Fitbit Air has suffered from a lack of band options since launch, and it hasn’t improved very much. The Pokémon Sleep band, while a cool collectible, is still a variation of the Performance Loop strap. The Stephen Curry band is a cool choice, but it suffers from the same lack of elasticity that’s sort of expected from a fabric band.

Google’s new Metal Mesh band, though, is a nice little departure from the existing options. It mounts to the Fitbit Air the same way, with a molded cutout for the small tracker to tuck into. One end of the mesh strap is secured to the plastic Firbit Air case, and a metal loop attaches to the other side. Just like the Performance Loop band, the Metal Mesh strap is secured through that loop and doubles over to secure.

I generally look for a couple of things with mesh bands: a fabric-like lay and a solid clasp. The clasp was a little stiff out of the box, and it took a bit of extra effort to loosen and adjust, but it was painless after the first go. The buckle slides up and down the weave of metal links so you can get the perfect fit. Once secured, putting the strap on is quick. I’d almost go so far as to say it’s easier than strapping down the Performance Loop band.

	

The mesh quality is better than I had expected out of the box. If it falls and conforms to something like fabric, that’s generally a good indicator that it’s secure and made well. A bad mesh band will bunch up or put up some resistance to bending. The Fitbit Air Metal Mesh band doesn’t do that.

It comes in two colors: Champagne Gold and Polished Silver. The Champagne version comes in a bundle, but both colors can be bought separately.

I’ve been wearing the Polished Silver, and it’s so easy to pair with whatever I’m wearing. I haven’t really removed it from my Fitbit Air since putting it on. I love a good fabric band for the versatility, but this has been so comfortable, even during workouts, that I’ve simply never found a reason to take it off. It might not be everyone’s preferred style choice, but it can be worn with almost everything.

Now, a $69.99 price tag might be a deterrent for some. And that goes double for what is a sub-$100 fitness tracker. At the very least, I think this is the best Fitbit Air band Google sells for its screenless Fitbit wearable.

But the Metal Mesh band for the Fitbit Air.

title: Some Galaxy S24, S25 owners say Samsung’s latest update is wrecking battery life
snippet: Samsung’s latest Android 17-based One UI 9 update seems to be causing headaches for some Galaxy S24 and S25 owners, as battery life has gotten considerably worse following the “upgrade.” more…
fullText:
Samsung’s latest Android 17-based One UI 9 update seems to be causing headaches for some Galaxy S24 and S25 owners, as battery life has gotten considerably worse following the “upgrade.”

It’s an age-old story. Major update on a last-gen device and battery life, at least for some users, gets worse. It’s something you hate to see, but it’s a pretty established pattern at this point. 

	

Reports have popped up since the update started rolling out more widely. SammyFans spotted a report of one user whose phone died in just over 5 hours, admittedly on heavy use. Other reports we found on Reddit include increased idle battery drain. Meanwhile, there are also reports on Galaxy S25 series devices, including one user who now has to “charge my phone 3 to 4 times a day,” with others mirroring that problem. 

This seems to be the oddity and not the norm, so far at least. These reports aren’t widespread, nor are droves of other users reporting the exact same problem. Some troubleshooting steps that can help range from a simple reboot, force-stopping rogue apps, or a factory reset. Major system updates like this, as mentioned, just tend to go a little rogue sometimes. 

	

Let us know in the comments if you’re running into any issues!

title: Oppo Find X10 Ultra is in the works, and I can’t wait to try its upgraded cameras
snippet: Not long after the Oppo Find X10 series launched globally, we’re already hearing details about the company’s Ultra model which is set to pack more impressive cameras – and that’s a pretty tall order. more…
fullText:
Not long after the Oppo Find X10 series launched globally, we’re already hearing details about the company’s Ultra model which is set to pack more impressive cameras – and that’s a pretty tall order.

We just reviewed the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max last week and, long story short, it has fantastic cameras. As it turns out, slapping three 200MP sensors into a single phone puts out some excellent images, and the phone around those cameras is pretty great too.

Now, there’s word that Oppo is still building out a Find X10 Ultra despite the impacts of RAMageddon.

Leaker Digital Chat Station says (via GSMArena) that the Oppo Find X10 Ultra is set to include at least two 200MP sensors of its own, but in another league. The cameras confirmed so far include:

	

200MP 1/1.12-inch main sensor, LOFIC

200MP periscope telephoto with 1/1.3-inch sensor, zoom unknown

50MP 10x periscope telephoto

100MP front-facing square sensor camera

That main sensor sounds pretty similar to last year’s Find X9 Ultra, as does that 10x periscope telephoto lens. The other telephoto shooter may not have a confirmed optical zoom length yet, but it’s likely 3x if Oppo is looking to match the Find X9 Ultra, and the sensor size is pretty much unchanged as well. There’s no word on the ultrawide yet, but that seems like an obvious candidate for a 200MP sensor if Oppo is looking to follow up on the Pro Max. Find X9 Ultra had a 50MP shooter here with a 1/1.95-inch sensor.

LOFIC on the main sensor is a new technology that improves dynamic range. It’s also expected to show up on other 2027 flagships, including Galaxy S27 Ultra.

The biggest upgrade here looks to be the front-facing camera, with the move over to a 100MP sensor, twice that of the prior generation, but also a square (1:1) sensor. That would allow for a more flexible shooter akin to the one Apple has been using in its latest iPhones.

Oppo Find X10 Ultra, if it follows the Find X9 Ultra’s pattern, will probably launch around April 2027. After using last year’s model, I can’t wait.

title: Someone built iPhone Duo’s tent mode for Android foldables, but made it even better
snippet: Well, that didn’t take long. As Apple’s iPhone Duo starts to land in the hands of early customers, copycat apps for the Duo’s most well-known features and apps are already landing on Android foldables – not that that’s a bad thing. more…
fullText:
Well, that didn’t take long. As Apple’s iPhone Duo starts to land in the hands of early customers, copycat apps for the Duo’s most well-known features and apps are already landing on Android foldables – not that that’s a bad thing.

One iPhone Duo feature that isn’t widely used on Android is the ability to show information while in “Tent Mode.” The Motorola Razr Fold is one of the few book-style foldables with this feature as a part of its always-on display, but the iPhone Duo’s “StandBy” mode is one that folks could easily want on other devices. Pixel also has similar functionality, but only while charging. 

A new Android app that delivers something pretty close to iPhone Duo’s tent mode is “Foldy.” 

The app is free to use, but requires a premium unlock (90¢/month or $9 lifetime) for its most useful features. On my Galaxy Z Fold 8, the app quickly let me turn tent mode into a useful dual-pane hub that shows the date and time, or data from my calendar. 

	

Its most useful functionality, though, is the ability to turn any Android widget into a pane, opening the door to useful functions such as Google Home or music app controls.

“Foldy” also lets you “train” the app to know when to activate. This works very well, with the app recognizing when the device is partially open and on its side, activating the “StandBy” clone as soon as the conditions are right.

Another example of Android developers quickly coming up with their own takes on iPhone Duo apps is “Foldman,” an app that turns your foldable into a Walkman-style casette player. It’s similar to a Duo app that’s been widely talked about, but with some added bonuses such as YouTube Music integration.

Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music

Is this a bad thing? No! One of the biggest benefits that Apple’s entrance to the foldable space was going to bring was helping to build out new app experiences for Android foldables. I can’t wait for this sort of effort to expand to many more Android apps and experiences.

title: iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is it a Galaxy Fold moment?
snippet: Apple’s first foldable is running into a problem. iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is this a case of a flawed design like Samsung’s original Galaxy Fold, user error, or a bit of both? more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable is running into a problem. iPhone Duo screens are breaking, but is this a case of a flawed design like Samsung’s original Galaxy Fold, user error, or a bit of both?

The earliest days of Android foldables were turbulent, to say the least. The original Galaxy Fold ran into major display issues within just 48 hours of reviewers getting their hands on the phone prior to the official release, leading to Samsung ultimately delaying the Galaxy Fold’s release for months. Part of the issue at the time was that curious minds were removing the top-layer screen protector that, as every foldable now makes abundantly clear, was never meant to be removed. The other problem came in the form of debris that would get under the display and kill the panel from underneath.

During the delay, Samsung ended up making some updates to the Galaxy Fold’s design, including making the top layer extend under the bezel, adding caps to the top and bottom of the hinge to prevent dust and debris from getting under the display panel, and reinforcing the display itself to protect it. At the time, Samsung’s CEO admitted that the launch was “pushed… before it was ready,” leading to the “embarassing” delay.

Galaxy Fold display failures from 2019 from The Verge

Now, Apple seems to be running into its own first-gen foldable issues.

	

As our sister site 9to5Mac highlights, there are a growing number of reports of early iPhone Duo units breaking, with the inner display failing in the exact same way across a number of units. The display fails in the middle, with a green line forming across the right side of the panel before further damage develops over time. 

The cause of the failure, it seems is a flaw in Apple’s hinge design. iFixit hypoethsizes that a support bar isn’t dropping far enough to leave room for the display panel, in turn creating a point of stress that could explain the broken iPhone Duo displays.

Similarly, iFixit’s teardown of the original Galaxy Fold in 2019 seemed to reveal the cause of Samsung’s display failures – and ended up being very much on the right track based on Samsung’s later fixes – though iFixit ended up removing the teardown at Samsung’s request. 

Another YouTuber has found a similar point of failure in the iPhone Duo’s hinge that seems to point to why displays are breaking the in same location. Affected users have found that the hinge has resistance before the display cracks, including an “audible crack.” 

In Samsung’s case, the problem was two-fold (pun intended), with some clear flaws in the hinge design and user error in the removal of the top layer. Samsung responded by delaying the release and making adjustments before re-releasing its first-gen foldable.

In Apple’s case, it’s certainly a bit trickier as this problem wasn’t revealed until the iPhone Duo landed in the hands of customers. The company has yet to issue a formal response to the problem, and affected users seem to be getting mixed messages from support channels. It’s still unclear in the chaos of the iPhone Duo’s launch just how widespread the issue is.

Update: Apple has acknowledged the issue in a statement to 9to5Mac.

Apple responds to reports of iPhone Duo’s inner display cracking

What do you think of the iPhone Duo’s display failures? Coincdence, or a bigger problem?

title: Some seven years later, the iTunes Store is making an unlikely come-back
snippet: Please accept my apologies if the headline made you feel old, but yes, Apple retired the iTunes desktop app way back in 2019. However, a new report says that the iTunes Store is currently experiencing an unlikely seeming revival. This is thanks to a tactic being used by artists like Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande, Charli XCX, Summer Walker, and more … more…
fullText:
Please accept my apologies if the headline made you feel old, but yes, Apple retired the iTunes desktop app way back in 2019. However, a new report says that the iTunes Store is currently experiencing an unlikely seeming revival.

This is thanks to a tactic being used by artists like Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande, Charli XCX, Summer Walker, and more … 

The iTunes Store revolutionized the way people bought music, not only prompting digital sales over physical, but allowing people to buy individual songs rather than an entire album. By the summer of 2019, however, Apple retired the iTunes Mac app in favor of new music, podcasts, and TV apps. 

The world has largely switched to streaming services, with relatively few people buying music outright, but the Financial Times reports that there is a countermovement underway.

The iTunes Store is re-emerging as an unlikely venue for pop stars to hawk collectibles to superfans, reach untapped audiences, and bolster chart positions. Last month, pop superstar Ariana Grande surprise-released a live version of her latest album Petal as an iTunes-only exclusive. This follows a string of iTunes-exclusive releases in recent years from artists such as Taylor Swift, Charli XCX, Doja Cat, Summer Walker and Tinashe.

	

Swift is perhaps the best example. The FT reports that her Life of a Showgirl album did better from physical and digital sales in its first week in the US than it did on streaming services. When Ariana Grande announced a surprise release of a live version of her Petal album on iTunes, it jumped from number 15 to number 6 in the charts. Charli XCX went further by making the B-side songs to her Music, Fashion, Film album an iTunes exclusive.

A report back in February said that Apple was still marketing iTunes to music labels.

Industry experts have mixed views on how well the strategy is likely to work more broadly, but it’s certainly an interesting trend.

title: YouTube says it’s not hiding the dislike button – this is what’s actually happening
snippet: Reports of YouTube moving the dislike button behind a menu have been showing up lately but, according to YouTube itself, this isn’t the change you think it is. more…
fullText:
Reports of YouTube moving the dislike button behind a menu have been showing up lately but, according to YouTube itself, this isn’t the change you think it is.

The dislike button has been a topic of contention in the YouTube community for years now, ever since YouTube removed the count that showed alongside it. So when some users noticed that the dislike button was suddenly no longer visible and hidden behind an overflow menu, there was plenty of confusion around the change.

In a statement to 9to5Google, though, YouTube directly confirms that this is not a test or a change that you’ll see on YouTube videos. Rather, this update to the dislike button’s location appears solely on the video page for a creator’s own video. In other words, you’ll only see this altered location on your own videos.

A YouTube spokesperson explains:

	

We are not testing hiding the dislike button on YouTube for users. We’re introducing a new UI for creators on their own uploaded videos, where dislike is behind the three-dot menu, and as always, they can find their full dislike counts in Studio, alongside other analytics.

And, sure enough, we were able to immediately replicate this behavior when we tested it out on one of our own videos.

title: I needed a dashcam while out running. Meta glasses turned out to be the answer
snippet: I already love to use all of Meta’s AI glasses when I leave the house, and now I’ve got a new reason to love the camera that comes on (almost) every pair. more…
fullText:
I already love to use all of Meta’s AI glasses when I leave the house, and now I’ve got a new reason to love the camera that comes on (almost) every pair.

This summer, I did something I never thought I would do: I started running. “But Nick, why are you running if nothing is chasing you?” my friends joked snarkily. The reality is, yes, I do often run a little faster at times to avoid getting hit by a car, something that’s particularly problematic any time I have to cross a road (even if there’s a crosswalk).

That got me thinking. If cars have dashcams, what could someone do to help document a potential accident? There’s no chance I’m running while holding my phone, and I wouldn’t want it in my pocket either. I also wouldn’t be able to pull it out of one of those armband holsters fast enough to video a potential accident, either. Then I realized the answer was already on my face: my Meta glasses.

I’d already been taking my glasses out on every run to make short video clips to post to my Strava account — with my smartwatch health stats plastered on the video, too — so it made a lot of sense to just take a few more clips along the way. Now I have a personal running dashcam at all times, and it takes less than a second to capture a video whenever I need it.

	

Is this really convenient?

Maybe surprisingly, yes, using Meta glasses as a dashcam is quite convenient. Since I already wore my Meta Nova and Oakley Meta HSTN glasses on regular runs, I didn’t have to significantly change my behavior. I already look out for cars when I cross the street (my mama taught me well); all I have to do now is hold the camera button to start a video recording if I see one coming.

I’ve got my Meta glasses set to record 3 minutes at a time, so I’m not worried about missing a potential problem because the recording got cut short. Once I cross the road, I just press the button again and manually stop the recording.

	

Everything is saved to the glasses until it reconnects to my phone; then everything is synced automatically at that time. It’s as effortless as you can get, and it’s impressively good insurance if anything were to go awry on a run.

If I had to buy a new pair of Meta glasses today, there’s little chance I’d buy one without a camera. While there’s been some negativity surrounding the inclusion of the camera, there are far too many good reasons to have it available to use.

Runners who want to try this should give the Oakley Meta HSTN glasses a shot first, as they’ve got the tightest fit and the most “runner-like” style. Otherwise, the cheaper Meta-branded glasses (read: no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding onboard) are a better budget choice, especially since there’s no functional difference between any of Meta’s latest pairs. And, if you really want to stay away from Meta, Rokid AI Glasses are the best alternative I’ve used to date.

There’s also a built-in smart display on the front that shows things like active connections, charging output, and data activity, plus a multifunction button that can instantly lock the connected computer when you step away. This button is similar to the one you get on the Baseus Nomos NU1 Air Spacemate 12-in-1 dock we tested earlier. It’s a nice little extra for a dock this compact, especially if you regularly move between a laptop-only setup and a proper desk.

The Spacemate RD1 Plus is the more serious workstation option. It packs a built-in 140W GaN power system and can deliver up to 120W across connected devices, while PowerTune 3.0 dynamically splits that power depending on what you have plugged in. Display support also gets a bump, with one HDMI output capable of pushing 4K at up to 120Hz, or dual 4K displays at 60Hz on supported Windows machines.

You also get a much broader mix of connectivity here, including multiple 10Gb/s USB ports, Gigabit Ethernet, SD and microSD card slots, and a 3.5mm audio jack. The built-in display can automatically rotate depending on whether you position the dock horizontally or vertically, keeping charging and connection information readable either way.

title: Someone made a Walkman music player for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and it works with YouTube Music
snippet: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app turns it into a Sony Walkman using your music, YouTube Music, and even Spotify very soon. more…
fullText:
The Galaxy Z Fold 8 app turns it into a Sony Walkman using your music, YouTube Music, and even Spotify very soon.

Foldables sort of walk that dichotomic line between nostalgic and futuristic. They remind us of flip phones from the 2000s, while running on an entirely different decade of tech.

Naturally, a Walkman-style app is a welcome addition to something like the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

One user developed an app called “Foldman” that uses your music from local storage or other apps and plays them in a virtual tape deck. On the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the app’s facade looks just like a cassette player. The app expands to show a wider stereo visual when the phone is opened up.

	

There’s a ton of cool little touches, like a volume slider and running tape counter on the virtual player. And the tape actually transfers from one tape reel to the other instead of a looping animation with no progressive movement! That’s such a nice little detail.

A Walkman-esque app fits so well on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 because of how wide and short the front display is, just like Sony’s original cassette player. That form factor is becoming increasingly popular, and it’s creating opportunities for some cool apps like this.

The app’s developer plans to integrate Spotify within the next couple of days and cautions that this early version has some rough edges. For now, it works with YouTube Music and Apple Music, as well as with files stored locally. The app is free and open source, stripped of ads or tracking.

We never recommend users download APKs outside of verified app stores, so do so at your own risk.

Beyond Spotify, they note that they’re looking into adding support for self-hosted streaming services, so users can use it with their existing library of digital files on their network. For now, it’s a simple little Walkman-style player, and that’s cool enough.

title: Here’s What Happens to Bacon When You Add Water While Cooking
snippet: Water and greasy bacon sound like a recipe for hot splatter. Here’s how the viral hack actually works.
fullText:
Charred and crisp, softer with a chewy middle: no matter how you cook your pork belly, bacon rules the roost among craveable breakfast meats. A handful of ways exist to make the salty strips, but a TikTok cooking hack that calls for a few ounces of water while cooking is making the rounds. The claim is that it even cooks the bacon, prevents dangerous oil splatters and keeps the meat from burning beyond recognition. 

But does it work?

Though I’m a fan of the quick, easy, CNET-approved oven-baking technique and even speedier air fryer method, the water-cooked method allegedly renders the bacon’s fat slowly and consistently, resulting in uniform cooking, fewer splatters and even reduced sodium. 

			

More from CNET

Not one to take social media’s word for it, I put the viral bacon hack to the test.

The water-cooked bacon trick

The technique couldn’t be simpler.Joey Skladany/CNET

The stovetop process is simple: 

Place bacon slices in an oversized skillet so they lie flat. 

Add ¼ cup of water to the skillet and cook over medium heat. 

Allow the water to steam and evaporate. Once the water is gone, lower the heat to medium-low and cook the bacon until it reaches your desired crispiness. 

Remove the cooked bacon from the skillet and place on a paper towel to soak up excess oil. 

I assumed the water would cause grease bombs, but it did the opposite. Joey Skladany/CNET

Ultimately, the water is said to suppress hot grease from popping violently and landing on stovetops or, more importantly, your skin. It also lets the meat cook low and slow before it fries in its own grease, rather than crisping immediately as the skillet heats up.  

Water can also draw out some of the bacon’s sodium, which is ideal for those who find it too salty. 

The results

The bacon turned out crisp with a slight chew.Joey Skladany/CNET

Color me shocked by the results: This cooking tip was executed flawlessly and lived up to the hype. The bacon strips were chewy yet crispy, with no bitter char, and cleanup took mere seconds with a quick wipe with a sponge and towel. (Pro tip: Reserve the leftover bacon grease to cook everything, from vegetables to rice, for added flavor.)

My only gripe was that it took a few minutes longer than using an oven or cast-iron skillet. And, frankly, the cleanup of pesky splatters would far surpass the time it takes to cook with water, at least with the latter tool. 

TikTok cooking tips are a mixed bag, but this bacon hack proved itself a winner.Joey Skladany/CNET

In an industry full of gimmicks and unverifiable shortcuts, it’s nice to sift through the culinary fluff and find something that actually works, especially with an ingredient as universally beloved as bacon. The fact that this trick has trended on TikTok is just a footnote and proof that social media sometimes gets it right. 

Hungry for more tips? Here’s how to recycle frying oil, plus a neat trick for degreasing a frying pan before washing.

title: iPhone Duo review roundup: The same problems Android foldables face, but with Apple’s polish
snippet: Apple’s first foldable has arrived, the better part of a decade after Android laid the groundwork for the form factor. iPhone Duo reviews are here and, while it sounds like a lot of the same problems that plague Android foldables still exist on Apple’s first-gen release, there’s certainly a level of polish there – and I’m not talking about the $9 cloth. more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable has arrived, the better part of a decade after Android laid the groundwork for the form factor. iPhone Duo reviews are here and, while it sounds like a lot of the same problems that plague Android foldables still exist on Apple’s first-gen release, there’s certainly a level of polish there – and I’m not talking about the $9 cloth.

Ahead of the first shipments arriving for customers later this week, the avalanche of iPhone Duo reviews has arrived today and, with it, the first look at what it’s like to live with Apple’s first foldable. 

Starting with our sister site 9to5Mac, of course, Chance used the iPhone Duo for a week and walked away “convinced that this form factor represents the future of the iPhone.” His in-depth review hits on every key aspect of this device, but his ultimate conclusion boils down to this being the future of Apple’s smartphones because the form fact “just makes sense” and that there’s “something special about a compact, notebook-like iPhone that unfolds into a tablet-like experience.”

9to5Mac: iPhone Duo review: The future is foldable

Looking at iPhone Duo reviews from the perspective of someone who’s been using Android foldables as their daily driver for over half a decade at this point, I can’t help but look at Apple’s first attempt and see the foundation it’s building on, but also the places where Apple’s inherent polish comes into play.

	

One big part of that seems to be the inner display. The nanotexture matte finish sounds like a big deal, with it making the crease visually not a problem. It’s still there, Chance stresses in his 9to5Mac review, but you “almost never” notice it visually unless you’re looking for it – just like most Android foldables. He adds that you’re more likely to feel it than see it. 

The app situation clearly seems to be running into the same early problems as Android foldables hit. Apps simply aren’t optimized for a radically new form factor yet. That’s what pushed Android foldables into the “phone that turns into a square tablet” trend they were stuck in for years, despite brands like Oppo and Google coming up with this iPhone Duo form factor way before Apple was a part of the conversation. Apple has the same problem, and it’s not going to be fixed overnight.

That said, it’s clear that it’s going to get cleaned up much quicker. WIRED‘s review opens up mentioning how “in the past day” key apps including “Instagram, Threads, Slack, and even the Google app now have navigational icons on the right rail instead of the bottom center, and the app content is better laid out to make use of the larger screen.”

“Mr Foldable” himself, Michael Fisher, explains in his review how apps that are not optimized are rough, comparing it to the early days of iPad, but that some key players are already stepping up. On top of that, smaller devs are building apps clearly inspired of this new form factor. “Tiny Computers” looks absolutely delightful.

David Imel mentions that “you can scale things up and they work, but they do look silly” in regards to unoptimized apps, and also makes a good point – not everything is going to get updated. iOS apps that aren’t actively maintained anymore are always going to be a mess on this device and, frankly, the scaling features Apple gives you make everything look way worse than an unoptimized app on an Android foldable has ever looked.

Look at the options you get for the yet-to-be-optimized Google Maps. Michael Fisher points out how it still doesn’t take up the whole display and that, if you rotate the phone, it just sends you back to square one. Sounds bad!

Apple’s new sidebar UI, which I still think looks funky, is personally my biggest fear as these wide foldable form factors take over, not because it’s a bad idea – Fisher points out that he actually loves it – but because Android apps will probably take a whole lot longer to adopt it. Seeing where things are starting out on the iPhone Duo, yeah, I’m sticking with that take.

That outer display, too, seems to be a hang up. The Verge says that “most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time.” That’s a problem I ran into a bit with Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and its similar shout and stout form factor, but Apple’s device is even smaller, so I’m not shocked to hear this. 

That same review makes a case for Apple’s app split, saying that “the problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time,” while saying that “the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them.” I’m not sure I agree there – larger canvases and multitasking alone have sold me on a foldable for years – but seeing so many iOS apps going all-in on the new screen size certainly has me feeling a bit envious. 

Another review that caught my eye was from Joanna Stern, where she puts the iPhone Duo “through hell.” There are two things of note here. First, Joanna puts the Duo through over 32,000 folds on top of normal daily use, and the hinge unsurprisingly holds up well. Android brands have laid an incredible foundation here, so even if Apple took its own route, the technology is clearly up to par here for a strong foldable hinge. 

But also pointed out here is a problem that’s been on every single Android foldable I’ve ever used – the iPhone Duo gets warm. Joanna calls the device a “hand warmer” and, apparently, Apple said this was business as usual for the device’s heat management. I was curious if the thicker design of Duo would help alleviate this one, but it seems Apple is dealing with the same issue. It’s a lot harder to cool two halves of a device, and you feel that heat more when there’s more usable space on the device.

Virtually every review mentions how hefty the iPhone Duo’s hardware is, too. This is a problem that Android foldables have been chipping away at generation-by-generation, and that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the poster child for. Smartphone weight continues to be something you don’t notice until it pushes over the edge and, while we’re not at Pixel Fold levels, iPhone Duo is very much at that edge.

Based on these early reviews, Apple didn’t reinvent the foldable, but it’s clear there’s a level of polish on the iPhone Duo that was lacking on Android foldables. Apple has a vision for its foldable and, while it’s tripped up on a few things on attempt #1, it’s undeniably a good start. 

What’s next for Android foldables? I look forward to seeing exactly that…

title: Leaker reveals larger iPhone Duo details, possible Telephoto camera
snippet: Today on Mark Gurman’s Power On podcast, the prolific leaker offered fresh insights into several features in the works for future iPhone Duo models, including larger screen sizes and possibly a Telephoto camera. more…
fullText:
Today on Mark Gurman’s Power On podcast, the prolific leaker offered fresh insights into several features in the works for future iPhone Duo models, including larger screen sizes and possibly a Telephoto camera.

Mark Gurman details Apple’s plans for larger iPhone Duo, says Telephoto is ‘on their list’ for future models

The iPhone Duo isn’t yet available in stores, but Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman already has plenty to share about Apple’s plans for future models.

Today on his Power On podcast, Gurman revealed that Apple is testing iPhone Duo 2 models with Face ID under the outer display, and is exploring ways to add an Action button. You can read more about those details here.

Later in the episode, Gurman looks further out to a 2028 third-gen model that he’s previously reported on.

The iPhone Duo 3 is expected to be slightly larger, and on the podcast Gurman offered specifics on what to expect. He said:

What I heard, just to be specific about the larger screen version of the Duo, is I heard…it’s marginal. It would be that the bigger screen, or the inside screen, increasing by, it’s like, this is rough, like very roughly half an inch. And so, that wouldn’t necessarily make the outer screen much bigger…we’re not talking about an 8.5-inch, 9-inch inner screen. We’re talking about like high sevens, very low eights.

For reference, iPhone Duo currently has a 7.6-inch folding display.

	

Gurman compares the forthcoming change to how Apple gradually sized up its Pro line in recent years. For example, it went from 6.7 inches on iPhone 15 Pro Max to 6.9 inches on iPhone 16 Pro Max.

As part of the conversation, Gurman is also asked if Apple is going to add a Telephoto camera to a future iPhone Duo. He says, “That’s on their list. I don’t know when that’s coming, but that’s gonna be hard to do.” 

He adds that it isn’t a matter of cost, but physics: “I think that’s purely a physics issue in terms of the depth needed. It’s going to be interesting to see how they end up solving that.”

Would you want a slightly larger iPhone Duo, and how important is a Telephoto lens to you? Let us know in the comments.

fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Twelve South has announced a new version of its Airfly dongle that simplifies the pairing process when connecting wireless headphones to devices that don’t natively support Bluetooth. Instead of having to decode flashing or color-changing LEDs, the new Airfly View adds a built-in screen that displays instructions for each step of the pairing process in one of 24 different languages including Japanese, Arabic, Portuguese, and Polish.

The Airfly View is available starting today for $79.99 and includes a carrying case and an adapter for connecting the dongle’s short 3.5mm headphone cable to an airplane’s split headphone jack. That makes it one of Twelve South’s most expensive versions of the Airfly, but the screen is useful for more than just letting you toss the user manual.

The display has a battery level indicator so you can estimate how much of the Airfly View’s estimated 16 hours of battery life remains, and it shows the name of which wireless headphones or earbuds are connected based on how they identify themselves over Bluetooth. That could be useful if you’re juggling a family of flyers who are all traveling with their own headphones.

You can stream audio from a single Airfly View dongle to two connected pairs of wireless headphones simultaneously, but Twelve South also says it “supports Auracast broadcast audio, so it is ready for the next generation of Bluetooth headphones.” That will further expand how many devices can receive audio from a single dongle but is dependent on wireless headphones fully supporting that Auracast feature, and not many currently do.

title: Apple exploring fix for Safari’s cramped layout on the iPhone Duo’s outer display
snippet: In a new post on the WebKit blog highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, Apple’s Jen Simmons said the company is exploring ways to let websites make better use of the iPhone Duo’s outer display. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new post on the WebKit blog highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, Apple’s Jen Simmons said the company is exploring ways to let websites make better use of the iPhone Duo’s outer display. Here are the details.

Apple knows Safari isn’t making full use of iPhone Duo’s outer display

One issue singled out in multiple iPhone Duo reviews (including ours) was the fact that Safari’s right-aligned controls take up a significant portion of the outer display’s limited screen space, leaving websites with an unusually narrow area to show their content.

Here’s what Chance Miller had to say about this in his review, published earlier this week:

But the awkwardness of the iPhone’s 5.4-inch outer display shows up in Safari. The web simply isn’t optimized for this form factor. I’ll talk more about this later, but the right-aligned controls on iPhone Duo eat into the usable screen real estate in Safari especially.

[…]

I can see why Apple chose the design it did for Safari on the iPhone Duo. I don’t think overlapping the controls with the website would’ve made sense. Still, scrolling in Safari is one of the best examples of something that’s better on the inner screen.

For new iPhone Duo users who have also been frustrated by this issue, Apple’s Jen Simmons shared some good news today.

In a post highlighting what’s new in Safari 27.1, including how websites adapt to the iPhone Duo’s different screen sizes and folding positions, Simmons acknowledged that websites currently can’t extend behind the controls on the device’s outer display, and said Apple is exploring ways to address that limitation.

From her post:

We would like to give web designers and developers the ability to design and use that space in more creative ways. Perhaps you want to extend your header background across the full width of the display, for example. It might seem like there’s just one obvious way to make this possible, but really there are many possibilities.

Simmons went on to explain that simply using the HTML viewport meta tag with viewport-fit="cover" to extend websites behind Safari’s controls could cause problems, because many websites don’t properly account for those areas, potentially leaving important content obscured.

Instead, she invited developers to share their ideas as Apple explores a better approach:

We are investigating if there’s a better way to accomplish the same result — something more foolproof and perhaps easier for you to use. If you have ideas, we’d love to hear them. And stay tuned.

If you’re a web developer and have ideas on how Apple could address this limitation, you can read the full WebKit post for details on how to share your feedback.

title: Gemini Notebook now available as Connected App for deeper integration
snippet: Gemini Notebooks are already available in the Gemini app side panel, but Google is now adding deeper Connected App integration. more…
fullText:
Gemini Notebooks are already available in the Gemini app side panel, but Google is now adding deeper Connected App integration.

As a Connected App like Google Workspace or Photos, @Gemini Notebook “allows you to manage and query notebooks directly within your chats using natural language.”

This integration lets you retrieve information from existing notebooks, create new ones, add sources, and save notes. The Gemini app will “automatically detect when to use the Gemini Notebook Connected App for relevant prompts.” For example: 

Create, edit, or delete a notebook (“Create a Gemini Notebook about solar farm market trends”)

Add, update, or delete sources in a notebook (“Add a copy of this chat to my notebook about Bio 101 course”)

List notebooks and their sources (“Show me a list of all the sources in my notebook about US National Parks”)

Answer questions using context from your notebook (“What do my Gemini Notebooks say about butterfly migration?”)

This integration is available now and has been enabled by “default for users globally, except in the European Economic Area, where it will be OFF by default.”

	

@Gemini Notebook is “available to all Google Workspace customers, Workspace Individual subscribers, and users with personal Google accounts.”

title: YouTube starts hiding the dislike button on normal videos
snippet: After removing dislike counts years ago, new UI tests at YouTube are making it harder to even using the dislike button at all. more…
fullText:
After removing dislike counts years ago, new UI tests at YouTube are making it harder to even using the dislike button at all.

Update 10/22: YouTube has confirmed this is not a public-facing test.

YouTube says it’s not hiding the dislike button – this is what’s actually happening

In 2021, YouTube removed the dislike count as a way to “de-weaponize” the button – effort that had been ongoing for years – with YouTube even acknowledging that it was a decision that users might disagree with. Now, following similar changes to Shorts, YouTube appears to be testing further hiding the dislike button.

A report on Twitter/X highlighted by Neowin showcases YouTube hiding the dislike button under an overflow menu, hiding it from view despite the like button remaining front and center. This appears to be on the desktop website, though we couldn’t replicate the same behavior on our end.

	

It’s not the only case of this happening, though.

	

Over the past couple of weeks, reports on Reddit have seen the dislike button vanish, with another web user seeing a slightly different UI to the one above, but with the same result of offloading the button to an overflow menu alongside the “Report” button. 

YouTube runs tests like this frequently, but given the same change was made to the dislike button on Shorts several months ago, it’s all but certain that the same will happen to standard videos.

What do you think of the change?

title: Walter Koenig, Star Trek’s Original Chekov, Dies at 90: ‘He Loved You Too’
snippet: Raise a glass of “wodka” to the Enterprise’s navigator. The actor not only starred in the original series, but in all six original-cast movies.
fullText:
Walter Koenig, known as the cheeky and endearing Russian navigator Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek television series, died on Sunday at 90, The New York Times reports. Koenig played the tart-tongued character for the iconic show’s second and third seasons, and also reprised the role in six Star Trek movies featuring the original cast.

Koenig had a memorable stint in another space-themed show, Babylon 5, playing telepath Alfred Bester. He worked as a screenwriter on shows including Land of the Lost and Family. He voiced Chekov in numerous video games and also wrote several books.

But for many, he’ll forever be remembered as the likable ensign with a Monkees mop-top hairdo and distinct accent. Chekov’s Russian heritage was important to a show that displayed a unified future, where a diverse crew, even including the half-Vulcan Spock, explored the stars together. His Russian accent on words such as “wodka” for vodka and, most famously, “nuclear wessels” for “nuclear vessels” in 1986’s Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home, resulted in fan-favorite quotes. Chekov even once told proud Scotsman and fellow Enterprise crew member Montgomery Scott that “Scotch was invented by a little old lady in Leningrad.” 

			

More from CNET

Koenig was born in Chicago to Russian Jewish immigrant parents from Lithuania. According to his obituary in The New York Times, Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry was told that young viewers thought the stars, William Shatner as Captain Kirk and Leonard Nimoy as Mr. Spock, were too old. Producers hoped younger viewers would be drawn to Koenig and his Davy Jones-esque hair. Be that as it may, Koenig was 30 when cast, only five years younger than Shatner and Nimoy.

Walter Koenig, second from left in the back row, is seen with the cast of the original Star Trek series.Sunset Boulevard/Getty Images

Koenig’s wife, Judy Levitt Koenig, died in 2022. They had two children. In 2012, Koenig was honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. 

In 2008, he served as best man at fellow Star Trek cast member George Takei’s wedding to Brad Altman, with fellow cast member Nichelle Nichols also standing up for the couple. Takei remembered Koenig with a touching Instagram post.

“Walter was more than Chekov,” Takei wrote. “He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too.”

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Gael Cooper

She's been a journalist since 1989, working at Mpls.St.Paul Magazine, Twin Cities Sidewalk, the Minneapolis Star Tribune, and NBC News Digital. She's Gen X in birthdate, word and deed. title: MagSafe Monday: TESSAN’s 6-in-1 charging station replaces every charger on your desk
snippet: One hub/cord to rule them all is a goal most people have for their desk. The TESSAN Magic 65W Charging Station is built to collapse your pile of cords into a single compact hub, and a couple of its design details are really handy as well if you like to hide your power cables. Let’s take a look at it. more…
fullText:
One hub/cord to rule them all is a goal most people have for their desk. The TESSAN Magic 65W Charging Station is built to collapse your pile of cords into a single compact hub, and a couple of its design details are really handy as well if you like to hide your power cables. Let’s take a look at it.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

The Magic 65-watt brings six charging options into one base: two traditional AC outlets, two USB-C ports, a USB-A port, and a MagSafe wireless charging stand. The main USB-C port delivers up to 65 watts, which is enough to fast-charge a MacBook Air or an iPad, so you can leave your power brick in your bag. Keep in mind that 65 watts is the max from that single port, so expect the power to be shared if/when you have several devices plugged in at the same time.

The two AC outlets are a nice touch here for a desk setup, since an external monitor, lamp, or speaker can plug right into the base station. This is super handy if you are trying to snake cables under your desk, etc.

A magnetic stand with a single trade-off

The MagSafe wireless charger doubles as a stand that tilts up to 65 degrees, which puts your iPhone at a nice angle for FaceTime, watching a YouTube Short, or Standby mode. It also handles AirPods charging at 5 watts.

Here’s the trade-off worth knowing before you buy: this isn’t Qi2 certified, so iPhone wireless charging tops out at 7.5W. If you’ve moved to a Qi2 or Qi2.2 charger elsewhere in your house, this will feel slow compared to them. For a quick top-off, it’ll be slow, but for an all-day or overnight charge, it’ll be fine.

The Apple Watch charger, which is built into the station and can be pulled out for use or tucked back in when you don’t need it. I personally don’t wear an Apple Watch, so I love when it’s optional. That’s one less cable dangling off the side of your desk if you do wear one, though 

One of my favorite details is that it has a 0.32-inch ultra-thin flat plug with a 45-degree right-angle design, so the hub can sit flush behind the desk without sticking out from the wall. It also leaves the other outlet on the wall plate open.

Wrap up

The TESSAN Magic 65W Charging Station isn’t the fastest MagSafe charger you can buy, and it doesn’t try to be. What it does well is consolidate your charging and power for your desk, including your external monitor, lamp, and other Apple gear.

You can buy the TESSAN Magic 65W Charging Station from Amazon.

title: Fitbit Edge Review: Too much and too little at the same time
snippet: When Google announced the Fitbit Edge, my assumption was that it would be a great in-between for the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air. In a way, that’s true, but this isn’t the product I thought it was – it’s just a new, slightly better Fitbit that leaves me wanting more. more…
fullText:
When Google announced the Fitbit Edge, my assumption was that it would be a great in-between for the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air. In a way, that’s true, but this isn’t the product I thought it was – it’s just a new, slightly better Fitbit that leaves me wanting more.

At $180, the Fitbit Edge is closer to the lower end of Google’s wearable lineup than it is a proper middle ground. It’s closer to a Fitbit Air with a screen than it is a “Pixel Watch Lite.”

That starts in the software, which has been updated to visually resemble this new era of Google Health. The main “Clock” face brings about a new assortment of options that draw inspiration from the Pixel Watch. There’s a baker’s dozen of these faces available, with the “Modular” series being my personal favorite. 

These support complications just like on Pixel Watch, allowing you to quickly see various data points around fitness tracking, or even pull in weather conditions. It’s not nearly as flexible as Pixel Watch – personal favorite weather data points such as UV index and sunset are missing, for example – but it’s a good glanceable bit of information, something the Air completely lacks.

	

What’s more frustrating than anything about the faces is that it’s all powered through the same basic and clunky interface that Fitbit trackers used for years. It’s incredibly slow and clearly not native to the Health app. It gets the job and works better than I remember it being the last time I used a Fitbit tracker, but it’s still a poor experience compared to the rest of the software.

Using the software on the tracker, you’ve got notifications below the clock and Quick Settings above, with Tiles to either side. It’s very familiar for Pixel Watch owners, and it’s visually a huge upgrade over the Fitbit Charge series. Google’s Material design language is felt throughout and everything is very clean with smooth animations. You can only customize the Tiles via the Google Health app on your phone (through the same clunky UI as faces), with the overwhelming majority being health/fitness-related, with weather and media controls also mixed in. This was the place I found the Edge most useful over the Air. Where tracking a workout on Fitbit Air either required relying on automatic tracking or starting it on your phone, Edge’s display lets you quickly jump into the workout of your choice. The “Quick Start” tile is helpful here, saving your most recent workouts. This was the biggest upgrade I found over the Fitbit Air outside of just, well, having the time shown on the thing on my wrist.

On the note of smartphone notifications, this is where I felt the biggest lacking from Pixel Watch. Inherently, a tiny display like this isn’t going to be as capable or useful as a full smartwatch, but the experience is just not very good. Notification previews can’t scroll through more than the first couple of words from a notification unless you tap “Open,” and incoming notifications also stack in the UI. The side button is used to go “back” in the software, but each notification is treated as its own layer, at least up until a certain point. When several notifications come in at once, this is a dreadful experience. They’re also not working consistently. I couldn’t get notifications working for much of the review period and, after many troubleshooting attempts, they just randomly started working on their own. Jordan Floyd on our video team says he still hasn’t managed to get them up and running. Google tells us that an upcoming Health app update will address notification issues.

Don’t get me wrong, notifications on Fitbit Edge are a huge step forward beyond the Fitbit Charge series, but they’re still not good either.

Apps on Fitbit Edge include the usual Health suite, as well as an alarm clock, Google Maps, a stopwatch, a timer, and a very basic weather app. The Google Maps experience leverages the Edge’s GPS but is really just a mirror of walking directions from your phone. You can’t start navigation on the Edge. The Weather app gets the job done, but it’s incredibly basic and lacks information I’d want outdoors such as UV exposure.

The biggest missing app here is Google Wallet, as the Edge lacks NFC support. Google says hardly anyone used it on the last generation, but I disagree with that logic – the Charge had many other downsides that prevented it from being appealing to those who also wanted Wallet, where the Edge is much closer to a fully usable smartwatch. Lack of mobile payment support is ultimately the biggest dealbreaker for me.

On hardware, Fitbit Edge is very much just an Air with a display.

Compared to a Pixel Watch, wearing the Fitbit Edge feels like wearing nothing. It’s very lightweight and, in turn, comfortable. Google’s bands from Pixel Watch also make the jump here, with the included Active band being just as comfortable as it is on Pixel Watch – though it is a hair magnet, picking up dog hairs far more readily than my Pixel Watch bands ever have. Google also sent over the Magnet Band which, personally, I’m not a fan of. It’s uncomfortable when on and, at least for my wrist, is difficult to put on. The two halves of the band are the same length and, if you sit in between the small and large sizes, it’s hard to get it on since there’s nothing for the band to grip on to until it’s fully connected. I’d rather go for something like the default Fitbit Air band here.

I was disappointed to see a problem from the Charge era make its way to Fitbit Edge. One multiple occasions through the review period, my Edge just fell off my wrist because the band connector failed. This happened once overnight and once as I was just walking through my home. It’s a disconcerting feeling, and was the eventual deal-breaker for me on Fitbit Charge 5 – I nearly lost the tracker while snowboarding, and it was shelved not long after that trip. Fitbit Edge doesn’t seem nearly as prone to this issue, but having it happen twice, with official bands, during my two-week review period is not exactly faith-instilling. A good habit would be to pull on the band to ensure it’s fully seated, but I’d argue this shouldn’t be necessary if you hear it click into place.

The connector here works well for switching bands quickly, but I would have appreciated seeing something new from Google here, especially seeing as it’s not like Fitbit Edge can use bands from the Charge series anyhow.

I reviewed the “Fog” setup with a silver tracker, and I do really appreciate that this splits the difference between a smartwatch and tracker in the looks department. With the right band, this is totally passable in a dressy situation.

Easily my favorite hardware decision here is the physical button on the side of Fitbit Edge. Prior Fitbit tracker toyed with a haptic button that was not at all a true button replacement. Not once was I fooled into thinking I was pressing a button, and the illusion only broke further when trying to turn the device on from an off state. It wasn’t the worst idea in theory, but a physical button is so much more satisfying. Fitbit Edge’s button isn’t the most premium, but it’s very much good enough and a welcome change on Google’s part.

But of course, none of that matters without fitness tracking to back it up.

I wore Fitbit Edge for the better part of two weeks – and only needed to charge once during that time, battery life is great, at least with the always-on display disabled – and used it mainly for tracking treadmill and strength workouts, with stats roughly lining up with the baselines set by Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5. You should never take stats from a fitness tracker as absolute truth, but the Edge is certainly more than capable enough at helping you to establish trends and work towards goals.

That’s all done in conjunction with the Google Health app, which I’ve been using with the Air and Pixel Watch for months at this point. Google Health, like virtually any AI tool, is inherently not perfect, but I’ve certainly come to appreciate it. The app opens to a simple overview of your cardio, steps, and other key data sets before diving into insights from the “Coach” – i.e. Gemini – around your trends. You can speak with “Coach” in natural language to set your goals around fitness, weight loss, strength training, or any number of things.

In that way, this is not the classic Fitbit of years past. This is very much a new experience built on the foundation of the old Fitbit, and one that you’ll either probably come to love, or come to hate. Personally, the experience has really grown on me. The app’s daily notifications summarizing my movement are a good last-minute way to get in some extra movement on quiet days, or a good morale boost when I was particularly active. As a workout novice, it’s also great for helping me figure out strength training workouts that suit my day. If I have more time or want to focus on a specific area, the “Coach” is pretty easy to work with in tailoring your workout. 

It’s not perfect, of course. It still tends to randomly get automatic workouts wrong, but for my needs it has done quite well. As we learned in our Fitbit Air review, though, your results may vary – at the end of the day, this is an AI-powered experience we’re talking about and, as Google itself repeatedly stresses, “AI may make mistakes.”

Of course, you’ll need to pay Google for a monthly subscription to use most of those features. Without Google Health Premium, the Edge is still capable, though, with support for basic step, heart rate, and workout tracking. Health Premium is bundled into the AI Pro plan which also includes Google Home Premium.

As a side note, kudos to Google for continuing on with the ability to use Fitbit Edge in tandem with other Google wearables in the Health app. While I used the Edge almost exclusively over the testing period, there were a couple of short Pixel Watch 5 stints mixed in for specific needs, and the Health app does a great job and syncing everything across not just the app, but each device. That said, it’s a less useful feature on the Edge. Where using a Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch in tandem is a fantastic experience, there’s almost no scenario I can imagine where it makes sense to have a Fitbit Edge alongside either one of those devices.

And therein lies my main takeaway with the Fitbit Edge.

This middle-ground wearable exists in a weird little bubble. It’s not a Pixel Watch, not even close, actually, but it’s also not a Fitbit Air.

I’ve found myself coming to appreciate the Fitbit Air as a way to find some reprieve from a connected lifestyle, with the Pixel Watch then stepping in when I need that connection or the added functionality of apps. The Fitbit Edge gets everything right on the fitness tracking side, but it also doesn’t really feel like it knows what it wants to be. It’s too connected and complex compared to the Air, but also too restricted compared to the Pixel Watch. It’s somehow both too much and too little at the same time.

That said, the Fitbit Edge might just need to be thought of in a specific light – it’s just not something new. This is a Fitbit tracker, an updated version of the same Fitbit tracker that millions have known and loved for years. In that light, it’s rather good, it just depends on whether or not you’ve moved beyond that point. I think I have.

Fitbit Edge starts shipping on October 27.

Fitbit Edge at Google Store

Fitbit Edge at Amazon

Fitbit Edge at Best Buy

					

Inherently a good and capable fitness tracker, Google’s new Fitbit Edge sits in a place where it’s somehow managing to bring too much and too little to the table at the same time.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Excellent battery life

											

Much better software than Fitbit Edge

											

Google Health is a good fitness coach

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

Limited functionality outside of fitness

											

Clunky clock face selector

											

Paid subscription to unlock most features

title: Google Health 5.11 rolling out with Fitbit Air Health Guardian, improved sleep tracking, & more
snippet: Google Health 5.11 is rolling out this week as a rather big update for Fitbit trackers and the Pixel Watch. more…
fullText:
Google Health 5.11 is rolling out this week as a rather big update for Fitbit trackers and the Pixel Watch.

The Improved Automatic Activity Tracking is available now for the Fitbit Air, Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5, with the Fitbit Edge getting the capabilities at launch on October 27.

Tracks more activities: We expanded the number of activities your Fitbit tracker or Pixel Watch can detect from 10 to up to 100, including strength training, swimming, and racket and team sports.

Uses more context: Powered by contextual reasoning, we now factor in more context — including your workout routines, historical data, manual edits — to deliver nearly 2x more accurate detections and cut missed workouts by more than half.2

Logs workouts automatically: Workouts that meet your minimum duration threshold (15 minutes by default) with a sustained elevated heart rate are automatically logged, and a summary is sent to the Google Health app, typically within 30 minutes.

Learns your patterns: When you confirm or edit an activity, you’re improving a feature that learns your unique patterns and uses them to refine its predictions.

The Fitbit Air and Edge are getting two Health Guardian features if you’re a Google Health Premium subscriber. You can set up blood pressure and insulin resistance trends now, with the first report available at the beginning of November.

Blood pressure trends, which allow you to track blood pressure patterns before they can put strain on your heart, will be available in the Health Guardian section of the Health tab if you’ve worn your Fitbit Air for 5 or more consecutive days in October.

Insulin resistance trends, which track monthly shifts in your metabolic health, will be available if you’ve worn your watch for 7 or more days and nights in October.

Blood glucose is now “Glucose” throughout the Google Health app with updated charts and graphs. Additionally:

	

Custom time-in-range goals: You can now set specific time-in-range goals for glucose data from connected continuous glucose monitors. To set a goal, go to the Metabolic section of the Health tab, tap Glucose, open Settings, and select Set goal.

Faster syncing with Lingo by Abbott (US only): You can now connect Lingo by Abbott directly to the Google Health app so your glucose data syncs faster — displaying in the Google Health app within 30 minutes of a reading. If you have a Google Health Premium membership, Google Health Coach³ can also answer questions about your glucose trends. To connect, tap your profile icon in the Google Health app and select Partner Apps.³

Finally, there’s improved Sleep Tracking across wake detection and nap editing:

More accurate awake detection: We’ve improved our sleep tracking to better factor in your steps data so that we can more accurately track short awakenings, like getting up to use the bathroom. 

Easier nap editing: You’re always in control of your sleep data. If a nap ever shows up that doesn’t match your day, you can now easily remove it directly from your nap card.

Version 5.11 is available on iOS and still rolling out for Android users.

fullText:
Today is the 25th anniversary of Apple unveiling the first iPod. And as discovered by Kian on X, the company’s website now has a fun new iPod easter egg.

Apple marks 25th anniversary of iPod introduction with new easter egg

The iPod is 25 years old and has long been discontinued, but it lives on in the hearts of many fans.

And now, a digital version lives on as an easter egg on Apple’s website too.

If you visit music.apple.com and add a path that doesn’t exist, the ‘Page Not Found’ screen now features a fully interactive original iPod model.

You can try it out by visiting music.apple.com/ipod or any other nonexistent version of the domain.

The iPod on the page lets you click through using its buttons to find pre-installed songs. The scroll wheel even works by clicking and dragging it around.

Apple first introduced the iPod on October 23, 2001, and the music you’ll find on this interactive model comes from artists that were popular at the time.

	

You can select songs to play 90-second previews right there in the web interface.

It’s a fun easter egg to play around with and celebrate the iPod’s legacy.

title: Apple TV’s long-awaited Fleetwood Mac documentary finally has a release date
snippet: Nearly two years after it was first announced, Fleetwood Mac fans won’t have to wait much longer for Frank Marshall’s documentary about the legendary band to arrive on Apple TV. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Nearly two years after it was first announced, Fleetwood Mac fans won’t have to wait much longer for Frank Marshall’s documentary about the legendary band to arrive on Apple TV. Here are the details.

’First-ever fully authorized Fleetwood Mac documentary’

Apple TV today confirmed the premiere date and title of its upcoming Fleetwood Mac documentary film, directed by Frank Marshall (The Beach Boys, From Earth to the Moon).

As the platform confirmed earlier today in a post on X, “Fleetwood Mac: The Chain” is set to premiere on Friday, January 29, 2027.

Apple TV says “Fleetwood Mac: The Chain” offers fans “a definitive and unprecedented look at Fleetwood Mac’s story, bringing together the voices, memories and perspectives of Grammy Award-winning Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductees Mick Fleetwood, John McVie, Christine McVie, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks.”

“Fleetwood Mac: The Chain” will join Apple TV’s growing catalog of music documentaries, which already includes “Beastie Boys Story,” “The Velvet Underground,” “Billie Eilish: The World’s a Little Blurry,” “Louis Armstrong’s Black & Blues,” and “Bono: Stories of Surrender,” among others.

Here’s a little more more of what Apple TV had to say about “Fleetwood Mac: The Chain”:

Following their fortuitous meeting in 1974, Mick Fleetwood, John McVie, Christine McVie, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks reflect on their uncompromising 50-plus-year history, from their record-breaking recordings and tours — including never-before-seen footage and exclusive new interviews — through to today. The film explores how the band’s trials and tribulations, personal resilience and musical dexterity combined to create songs that have stood the test of time and are enduring masterpieces. It takes fans through the highs and lows of their brilliant career, illuminating the exceptional ingredients each member brought to the band’s uncommon alchemy — a musical union that sold more than 220 million records worldwide. The documentary explores what allowed this combination of artists to create singular musical work again and again, and what drew them back together and held them there when every possible pressure, both outside and inside the band, threatened to blow them apart.

While there’s no full trailer for “Fleetwood Mac: The Chain” just yet, Apple TV has shared a short teaser on X, which you can watch below:

title: This clever USB-C cable doubles as a stand for your phone [Gallery]
snippet: One of my favorite things about the rise of magnetic wireless charging has been the prevalence of chargers that hold my phone upright on my nightstand. But, when travelling, that tends to be a bit more cumbersome, or at least a little more expensive. The folks over at Statik have come up with a clever solution, a USB-C cable that has a kickstand for your phone with no added bulk. more…
fullText:
One of my favorite things about the rise of magnetic wireless charging has been the prevalence of chargers that hold my phone upright on my nightstand. But, when travelling, that tends to be a bit more cumbersome, or at least a little more expensive. The folks over at Statik have come up with a clever solution, a USB-C cable that has a kickstand for your phone with no added bulk.

The Statik PowerStand is a pretty straightforward idea. A USB-C cable that has a kickstand at the end. Simple idea, plenty of room for a poor implementation, but this is really quite well done.

One end of the braided cable is a standard USB-C plug, while the other side has a right-angle plug on an extended base. Admittedly, it feels a little clunky on its own, but it makes sense once you plug in a device. The USB-C plug is angled slightly and on a raised base, easily connecting to your phone even if it’s in a case. Two foldable “feet” swivel out and let you either stand the phone up vertically – perfect for charging – or put it horizontally for something like watching a video.

The implementation here is really quite good. The vertical orientation is surprisingly well-balanced and I never felt like my phone would just fall over. Don’t get me wrong, a shove will definitely let it fall over, but it’s not just going to fall on its own. The spacing for cases also worked perfectly on a Nomad case I have for my iPhone or my wife’s Peak Design Pixel 10 Pro case, but the plug didn’t feel insecure on my case-less Pixel as a result. 

	

The foldable “feet” also slot into place quickly and lock into position pretty well. It’s a good balance between strength and easily being able to adjust the position.

This isn’t some shoddy cable either. It’s a 240W cable with USB 2.0 data transfer speeds and is measures 6.6ft long too. The braided texture feels sturdy and it’s nice that the design still lets you use the kickstand end with a laptop. 

	

The Statik PowerStand easily earned a permanent spot in my travel bag, and for $20, it’s definitely worth your consideration too. 

Statik, by the way, is the same brand that makes those magnetic cables that are easier to store because they attach to themselves. Another cable in its lineup that the company sent out with the PowerStand is the PowerPivot Pro, an all-in-one cable with USB-C and USB-A ends on one side with a USB-C tip on the other end that can rotate in any direction. I’m not quite as keen on the functionality there, but Statik points out the one place it might come in handy – the car. For Android Auto/CarPlay, I could see this one being good for having your phone perhaps stuffed into a tight spot. It’d been even better, though, if both ends of the cable had these rotating tips. If nothing else, Statik says this is 20x tougher than a normal cable, and I believe it after feeling it in person.

PowerPivot Pro is also available for $20.

title: Older Pixel phones appear to be getting Google’s new 3D emoji
snippet: Google’s redesigned 3D emoji library debuted on the Pixel 11, but might now be slowly appearing on older Pixel devices. more…
fullText:
Google’s redesigned 3D emoji library debuted on the Pixel 11, but might now be slowly appearing on older Pixel devices.

One Pixel 6a user on Reddit shared his new 3D emoji library, noting that his choices switched over from the traditional designs. Given that this is on a Pixel 6a, it signals Google might be slowly switching devices over from 2D to 3D emojis. Only one other commenter shared the same experience, which means the rollout, if it’s actually going live, is very gradual.

Without many other reports, it’s hard to nail down Google’s intended device targets. We know the Pixel 11 is how Google wanted to release the new 3D emoji set, but what comes after has seemed slow. So far, it looks like a majority of devices represented in that thread haven’t received an update. The one user who said they got the new Noto 3D emoji set said they appeared after a Google Play Store update.

Like them or hate them, Google is replacing the standard cartoonish emoji library with 3D designs that closely emulate them on all Pixel devices going forward, starting with Android 17. There are subtle differences across Android’s emoji selection, and they’ll likely take some time getting used to if you’ve been using Android devices for some time.

fullText:
Apple TV’s November lineup includes the return of a beloved comedy, a heist thriller with big stars, the follow-up film to its Oscar winner, and a lot more. Here’s everything new coming to Apple TV in November.

Stick (season 2)

When: November 4

What: TV Show

Genre: Comedy

“Stick” is a sports comedy series created by Jason Keller and starring and executive produced by Owen Wilson. Wilson stars as Pryce Cahill, an over-the-hill, ex-pro golfer whose career was derailed prematurely 20 years ago. After the collapse of his marriage and while working at an Indiana sporting goods store, Pryce hedges his bets, and future, entirely on a troubled 17-year-old golf phenom named Santi (Peter Dager). “Stick” is a heartfelt, feel-good comedy about a found family and their relationships set within the world of golf as it has never been shown before.

Watch Stick on Apple TV
